Full text: Introduction
Broadscale societal crises, or so-called mega-crises, are often followed by an increased spread of false and misleading information, which can have serious consequences for individuals and society at large (Loomba, 2021;Strömbäck et al., 2022). Social media platforms have further exacerbated this challenge by enabling widespread circulation of both accurate and inaccurate information (Brennen et al., 2020;Papakyriakopoulos et al., 2020). The COVID-19 pandemic, for instance, saw a large spread of misleading and false information across social media platforms concerning the deadliness of the virus as well as its causes and origins (Balakrishnan et al., 2022;Önnerfors, 2021). The COVID-19 pandemic is, however, not the only example. Other crises frequently attract attention due to the circulation of false and misleading information concerning them, such as the terrorist attacks and wars (Chen et al., 2022;Hameleers et al., 2024). It is therefore not surprising that research interest in the phenomenon, both in general and in relation to crises more specifically, has accelerated over the past decade (Broda and Strömbäck, 2024). Studies on false and misleading information can be found across fields, including social sciences, psychology, medicine, and computer science (see, for example,Agley and Xiao, 2021;Lewandowsky et al., 2012;Van der Linden, 2020;Rubin et al., 2015).
As noted by prior scholars, the interdisciplinary nature of research has both enhanced our understanding of the phenomenon as well as contributed to a fragmented field. Scholars rarely reference work outside their own discipline. This applies both to studies on false and misleading information in general, where different disciplines have developed largely independently (for a discussion about this, seeBroda and Strömbäck, 2024), and to research specifically focused on societal crises. Journalism and communication scholars have examined the role of false news in shaping political agendas (e.g.,Van der Linden, 2020), while psychological researchers have focused on cognitive processing and memory in relation to misinformation (e.g.,Lewandowsky et al., 2012) and computer scientists have worked on algorithmic solutions to detect and mitigate false and misleading information (e.g.,Chen et al., 2015). Moreover, studies on false and misleading information rarely incorporate theories and concepts from crisis research (such as crisis communication or crisis management). Similarly, crisis communication research tends to engage only to a limited extent with theories and concepts from other disciplines (Johansson and Vigsø, 2020;Palenchar, 2009).
Beyond the lack of theoretical integration across fields, conceptual ambiguity further complicates the picture. As highlighted by other scholars, different terms are sometimes used to refer to the same phenomenon, or the same term is used to refer to different phenomena (for discussion about this, seeBroda and Strömbäck, 2024;Kapantai et al., 2021Wardle, 2018);. For instance, disinformation, misinformation, conspiracy theories, rumours, and fake news are commonly used, but terms like incorrect information, misleading information, and alternative facts also appear in the literature (Broda and Strömbäck, 2024).
The disciplinary fragmentation and conceptual ambiguity hinder the development of a comprehensive understanding of the phenomenon. As argued byBroda and Strömbäck (2024), a more integrated and interdisciplinary approach to the study of false and misleading information is needed, starting with literature reviews. This study therefore aims to provide an overview of the current state of knowledge on false and misleading information during crises across various research fields. Specifically, a scoping review was applied to identify key concepts, methods, relevant factors, and knowledge gaps (Munn et al., 2018). The main focus, however, centred on mapping (1) the factors contributing to the spread of false and misleading information on social media during crises, and (2) the potential consequences of such information at both individual and societal level. We utilize the umbrella term false and misleading information , referring to research on related terms frequently applied in research, such as disinformation, misinformation, false/misleading information, conspiracy theories, rumours, alternative facts, fake news, among others. In total, 179 research studies published between 2014 and 2024, were analysed using quantitative content analysis. By compiling studies from multiple research fields, the overview aims to provide a more holistic view of current state of research, paving the way for interdisciplinary research approaches.
Defining false and misleading information
As noted above, several terms are applied in research to refer to false or misleading information. However, misinformation and disinformation are foundational concepts to describe false and misleading information, occurring across a wide range of different disciplines. While misinformation refers to false information that may be shared without harmful intent, disinformation is spread with the intent to mislead or cause harm (Kapantai et al., 2021). The main difference thus lies in the intent behind it. This also means that information may start as disinformation but spread as misinformation.
In the last decade, the term fake news has also gained prominence, especially in political and media studies (Aïmeur et al., 2023). As noted byBroda and Strömbäck (2024), “fake news both refers to a weaponized label used to attack and undermine the legitimacy of the news media” as well as false or misleading content “presented as legitimate news” (p. 142). Regarding the latter, researchers have developed typologies to categorize fake news.Tandoc et al. (2018)categorize fake news based on its degree of factual content and the creator's intent to mislead. News satire might blend fact and fiction but is understood by its audience as a form of entertainment, whereas fabricated news is entirely fictional and spread with the aim to deceive (Allcott and Gentzkow, 2017). Due to its emphasis in intentional spread to deceive or harm, scholars often use the term interchangeably with disinformation. Further related to the notion of fake news are terms such as alternative facts and post-truth , referring to alternative constructions of realities, evidence and expertise that goes against established evidence and mainstream discourse (Marwick and Partin, 2024).
Relating to crises more specifically, the term infodemic gained renewed attention during the COVID-19 pandemic. It was coined during the SARS outbreak by David Rothkopf in 2003 and refers to the overwhelming amount of information—both accurate and inaccurate—flooding the public during a crisis (Buchanan, 2020). This overflow of information makes it challenging for individuals to identify trustworthy sources and information, potentially leading to confusion about what is true or false. The notion infodemic is related to the term information pollution , referring to “situations where the information supply is contaminated with low-value (e.g., irrelevant, redundant, inaccurate) material” (Malin and Lubienski, 2022, p. 3).
Finally, the term conspiracy theories also gained increased traction in research following the COVID-19 pandemic. This is mainly due to the upsurge in the amount of conspiracy theories that spread online concerning the deadliness and the origins of the virus (Önnerfors, 2021). Conspiracy theories are defined as attempts to explain significant events as the result of secretive, malevolent actions by powerful groups (Douglas, 2021). While conspiracies can be true, conspiracy theories on the other hand are often not grounded in evidence or goes against established evidence. They also tend to carry mis- and disinformation and are, as a consequence, used interchangeably with these concepts. Finally, rumours have also received significant attention in research departing from crises, defined as unverified information that spreads in situations of ambiguity or perceived threat (Bordia and DiFonzo, 2007).
To sum up, terms like misinformation, disinformation, fake news, alternative facts, post-truth, conspiracy theories, infodemic, and rumours are all applied in research addressing false and misleading information. Although they are sometimes used to highlight different facets of the phenomenon, they are also, as noticed by prior scholars, often used interchangeably (for a discussion, see, for example,Broda and Strömbäck, 2024;Kapantai et al., 2021Wardle, 2018);. To get a holistic picture of the current state of knowledge, this research overview applies the umbrella term false and misleading information to refer to all the above terms.
False and misleading information: a scattered research area
Although scholars point to the increased spread of false and misleading information during societal crises, few have conducted comprehensive reviews across fields on its spread and effects during such events. While there are examples of literature reviews focusing on topics such as misinformation or fake news (Tandoc, 2019;Broda and Strömbäck, 2024), disinformation (Benkler et al., 2018;Marwick and Lewis, 2017), and conspiracy theories (Douglas et al., 2019), few of them focus specifically on crisis, with most being focused on the COVID-19 pandemic (see, for instance,Pian et al., 2021;Rocha et al., 2023). However, crises are characterized by uncertainty and high emotional engagement (Canet-Juric et al., 2020;Sellnow and Seeger, 2013), which is likely to increase the spread of false and misleading information online. For instance, studies show a large spread of false and misleading information concerning government policies as well as the causes and origins of the threat during crises (King and Wang, 2023;Lu, 2020;Önnerfors, 2021). Yet, studies on false and misleading information rarely incorporate theories and concepts from crisis research. Similarly, crisis communication research rarely engages with theories and concepts from other disciplines (Johansson and Vigsø, 2020;Palenchar, 2009). The interdisciplinary nature of the phenomenon underlines the need to integrate concepts from various fields, however.
In addition to the above, studies addressing false and misleading information within different disciplines have developed largely independently from each other (for a discussion about this, seeBroda and Strömbäck, 2024). Journalism and communication scholars have examined the role of false news in shaping political agendas and public opinion (e.g.,Van der Linden, 2020). These studies highlight the ways in which false and misleading information can increase polarization, erode trust in traditional news media, and influence public opinion. Meanwhile, psychological researchers have focused on cognitive processing and memory in relation to misinformation (e.g.,Lewandowsky et al., 2012). At the same time, computer scientists have developed machine learning models, automated fact-checking systems, and network-based approaches to identify false and misleading information (e.g.,Y. Chen et al., 2015). Yet, the specific conditions associated with crises require an interdisciplinary approach to the study of false and misleading information, combining knowledge from different fields.
Against this backdrop, a mapping of existing research is needed to synthesize the fragmented findings form prior research. Mapping factors related to the spread and effects of false and misleading information in crises can help reveal gaps in current knowledge and inform future research on the development of interdisciplinary theoretical frameworks. This overview therefore aims to answer two overarching research questions:
RQ1. Which factors have previous research identified as contributing to the spread of false and misleading information on social media during crises?
RQ2. What are the effects identified in previous research related to exposure to false and misleading information on social media during crises?
Methodology
To answer the RQs, a scoping review was conducted. This strategy was chosen because it aligns with the research aims, but also due to the vast number of studies conducted on the topic. Unlike a systematic review, which aims to compile all research on a given subject, a scoping review seeks to gather representative studies to identify patterns and gaps in the existing research concerning theories, methods, or results. Specifically, it aims to identify key terms and concepts within current research, analyse the methods applied, as well as identify factors and current knowledge gaps (Munn et al., 2018).
Timeframe
The studies included in this review were published between 2014 and April 17, 2024. 2014 was chosen as the starting point due to the increased attention given to false and misleading information following key events like the 2016 U.S. presidential election. Close to this period, between 2010 and 2012, there was a widespread adoption of smartphones in Sweden, leading to increased social media use (Andersson, 2023). 2014 and onwards thus marks a period of increased social media usage and increased attention given to the topic of false and misleading information. The results further supported the rationale for choosing 2014 as the starting year, as the number of relevant studies increased significantly after 2016, peaking during the COVID-19 pandemic years and continuing to rise thereafter.
Search strategy and study selection
The initial step in collecting the empirical material involved designing the search thread. To do so, we utilized field-specific databases. Specifically, PsycInfo, ERIC, Cinahl, PubMed, Proquest Social Sciences, and IEEE were used to identify common terms for false and misleading information, crises, and social media across various research domains. Identified terms and concepts were structured into a search string comprising three thematic blocks, along with a fourth block aimed at excluding irrelevant studies. The search string, including the three thematic blocks plus the exclusion block, is presented and discussed below.
The first block targeted terminology used to describe false or misleading information, and the second block focused on terminology for societal crises and specific crisis types. It should be noted that crises not explicitly labelled as such were excluded except for COVID-19. For instance, other epidemics like Zika were excluded unless explicitly referred to as a pandemic or crisis. However, this decision was made after testing the search string and noticing that inclusion of the term “COVID-19” added substantially to the total amount of studies, while the equivalent term such as “Zika” did not. It is therefore likely that including COVID-19 did not significantly alter the proportion of crises cases within health crises 1 . That said, other crises (beyond health crises) may have been excluded if not explicitly stated as one of the crisis types included in the search string, potentially creating an overrepresentation of health crises. Finally, the third block covered social media and associated platforms.
An exclusion block was added to exclude research outside the scope of the study, focusing on, for instance, organizational management of false or misleading information or automatic detection thereof. The exclusion block therefore included terms such as management, automatic detection, and others. It is important to note that it is possible that the exclusion block filtered out relevant studies. For example, studies examining management or leadership strategies as well as the effects of, or spread of, false or misleading information were excluded. The full search string can be found below 2 .
In addition to the predefined search terms and exclusion block, studies were considered eligible if they were written in English and published as peer-reviewed journal articles, book chapters, or conference proceedings were considered eligible for inclusion. A range of publication types were included to ensure coverage of different research fields. However, the language requirement means that relevant studies in other languages were excluded from the material. Finally, studies had to include the predefined search terms in the title, abstract, or keywords and be published between 2014 (2024) and April 17 (2024) to meet the eligibility criteria (as discussed in more detail above under time frame).
Data collection
Eligible studies were identified using Scopus, one of the largest multidisciplinary bibliographic databases. Thus, the field-specific databases (PsycInfo, ERIC, CINAHL, PubMed, ProQuest Social Sciences, and IEEE) were used solely to develop the search strategy and were not used for the final literature search. Scopus was chosen for data collection as it is one of the largest academic databases covering a wide range of research fields. This enabled the identification of studies from diverse disciplines relevant to the research topic.
In line with the aim of a scoping review and to map the characteristics of the research field rather than include all available studies (Munn et al., 2018), a citation-based sampling strategy was adopted. Specifically, citation count was used as an indicator of scientific influence within the respective research field. To ensure that older publications did not have an advantage in the citation ranking, two separate literature searches were conducted from the outset, covering the publication periods 2014–2019 and 2020–April 17, 2024, respectively. Together, the two searches identified 1,189 eligible studies across 27 research fields. Within each search, studies were ranked according to citation count within each research field, and the top 15% most cited publications from each field were selected for further analysis. While citation count was used as an indicator of the scientific influence of a publication within its research field, it should not be interpreted as a measure of study quality. Consequently, relevant studies examining factors associated with the spread or effects of false and misleading information with relatively few citations may have been excluded.
Following the initial screening, 30 articles were excluded after closer review because they did not meet the eligibility criteria. Specifically, this included studies that mentioned the predefined search terms in the abstract but did not operationalize the corresponding concepts in the analysis. Consequently, the final sample consists of 179 unique texts and 275 coded units. A flowchart of the data colleciton process can be found inFigure 1. The number of coded units is higher as some articles were categorized into more than one research field by Scopus based on the journals, books, and conferences associated with a particular scientific text.

Coding and analytical procedures
The collected material was coded using a pre-defined codebook developed by the authors, which was pretested and refined through several iterations. The codebook consists of three sections: 1) metadata (authors, affiliations, journal details, keywords, and research fields), 2) study design (study subjects, crisis type, social media platforms, key concepts, and methodology), and 3) study results (factors contributing to the spread and effects of false information). The coding process was divided among the researchers, with regular meetings to ensure consistency and refine the process. The coded material was analysed applying quantitative content analysis, investigating the frequency of themes within each subsection of the codebook.
Results
Before addressing our main research questions, an overview of the fields and countries represented in research on false and misleading information, types of crises and social media typically studied, as well as the methods employed in the research are provided. After that, the factors contributing to the spread and the effects of false and misleading information are addressed.

Crisis types Most studies focus on global health crises, particularly the COVID-19 pandemic (86 percent) (Table 3). The second-largest crisis type is natural disasters, such as earthquakes (e.g., the 2018 Palu earthquake in Indonesia) and hurricanes (e.g., Maria in Puerto Rico and Harvey in the United States, both in 2017). Other types of crises include terrorism (2.2 percent), such as the Boston Marathon bombing in 2013 and the series of terrorist attacks in several UK cities in 2017. Political crises (1.7 percent) and organizational crises with societal implications (1.1 percent) are less commonly studied. Table 3

Social media platforms 115 out of 179 studies (64.2 percent) address false and misleading information on social media in general, without specifying particular platforms. This approach is especially common in survey-based studies that explore people's perceptions or usage of social media.
The remaining studies focus on specific platforms, with the majority analysing X/Twitter (46.8 percent) or Facebook (17.7 percent), together comprising two-thirds of the platform-specific studies. The third most frequently studied platform is the Chinese social media site Sina Weibo (10 percent) (Table 4). Most research analysing specific social media platforms focuses on one platform at a time. Very few studies (5 in total) compare two or more platforms.

Methods Most of the studies are empirical studies, accounting for 76 percent. Other types of studies, such as reviews, meta-studies, and theoretical studies, each comprise approximately 7 percent. The most applied methods are survey studies and quantitative content analysis, which together encompass nearly half of all studies. Survey research is the predominant method across almost all research fields (seeTable 5). Only three studies utilized data from panel surveys. Finally, there are examples of studies employing sentiment analysis, conceptual analysis, document analysis, and case studies. Table 5

Factors contributing to dissemination and effects of exposure To analyse the factors contributing to the dissemination of false and misleading information, as well as its effects, the analysis does not rely on the total number of collected articles ( N = 179). Instead, it is based on the frequency with which various dissemination factors or effects at the individual, organizational, or societal levels were coded. Since multiple dissemination factors and effects can be coded for each article, the dataset expands to a total of N = 214. Most variables related to dissemination are found within the social sciences (35.3 percent), followed by computer science (19.3 percent) and medicine (13.4 percent).
The largest proportion of investigated factors related to effects is found within the social sciences (27.4 percent), followed by medicine (20 percent) and computer science (16.8 percent).
Factors contributing to dissemination Factors influencing the dissemination of false and misleading information can be categorized into individual-level factors (e.g., attitudes, personality traits, cognition, emotions), content-related factors (e.g., framing and content markers), technologies and platforms (e.g., AI and platform functionalities), and societal structures (e.g., economic or political contexts). Among these, individual-level factors constitute the most examined variables (69 percent), followed by content-related factors (19.3 percent) and platform-specific factors (7.6 percent) (seeTable 8). As noted earlier, most studies in the dataset rely on cross-sectional data, which limits the ability to analyse causal mechanisms. Table 8

Since no factors related to AI applications are present in the material, the category has been excluded from the table.
At the individual level, perceptions are the most frequently studied factor in understanding people's propensity to spread false and misleading information on social media, accounting for 25.2 percent. Several studies have, for example, analysed the influence of political attitudes and trust (e.g.,Agley and Xiao, 2021;Das et al., 2021Freiling et al., 2023;;Recuero et al., 2022Stecula and Pickup, 2021;;Su, 2021;van Mulukom et al., 2022). These studies also discussed the potential for a backfire effect , a strengthened belief in false or misleading information following fact-checking, among individuals whose attitudes align with the false or misleading information (Sharevski et al. 2022).
Studies focusing on cognition account for 11.8 percent of the research, with particular attention to phenomena such as information overload (Bermes, 2021). Emotions have also been examined to some extent (10.1 percent). For example, one study explored the interaction between emotions (anxiety) and perceptions (ideology) (Freiling et al., 2023).
Relatively few studies have investigated the influence of personality traits (5.9 percent) and behaviour (8.4 percent). In relation to personality traits, altruism has for instance been studied as a driver behind information spreading (e.g.,Apuke and Omar, 2021). Regarding behaviour, some studies have analysed the impact of media consumption habits, focusing particularly on the influence of social and political alternative media (e.g.,Romer and Jamieson, 2021). Additionally, some studies have explored the interaction between social media use and cognition (e.g.,Stecula and Pickup, 2021). Finally, the interaction between social media use and emotions has also been examined (e.g.,Su, 2021; e.g.Freiling et al., 2023),.
Moving beyond the individual level, framing and packaging of information (framing and cues) account for 19.3 percent of the total factors investigated. Studies have analysed elements such as tone (sentiment), efficacy information (guidance on how to respond to the crisis), and characteristics of the information source (e.g.,King and Wang, 2023;Song et al., 2022;Jung et al., 2020).
Platform-specific features or technologies account for 7.6 percent of the total dissemination factors in the material. These studies primarily focus on platform affordances, such as the ability to share material across platforms and the impact of positive feedback mechanisms, such as likes (e.g.,Agarwala et al., 2023;Ginossar et al., 2022). Finally, structural factors at the societal level constitute 3.4 percent of the total dissemination factors and have primarily focused on the political context ( N = 2).
Effects of exposure and dissemination Like factors contributing to dissemination, the effects of false and misleading information can be categorized into impacts on individuals, organizations, and society at large. Effects on individuals constituted the largest portion of the collected material, accounting for 87.4 percent, followed by societal-level effects at 12.6 percent (seeTable 9). No organizational effects were identified in the dataset. As with studies on dissemination, most of the research rely on cross-sectional data. Table 9

At the individual level, behavioural effects were the most studied, accounting for 39 percent of the research. These studies primarily addressed behaviour in the context of COVID-19, examining the relationship between exposure to, or belief in, false and misleading information on an individuals’ likelihood of adhering to restrictions and willingness to vaccinate (e.g.,Jennings et al., 2021;Lee et al., 2020;van Mulukom et al., 2022;Romer and Jamieson, 2020;Sallam et al., 2021;Zimmerman et al., 2023). Some studies have also discussed the potential effects of coordinated disinformation campaigns (such as “The Plandemic”) (e.g.,Nazar and Pieters, 2021).
Perception-related effects (27.4 percent) were the second most common, focusing on factors such as politically motivated reasoning (i.e., the tendency to believe information that aligns with already established attitudes and beliefs), threat perceptions, and the third-person effect (i.e., the tendency to believe that others are more susceptible to false or misleading information than oneself) (e.g.,Das et al., 2021;Liu and Huang, 2020;van Mulukom et al., 2022;Yang and Tian, 2021).
Few studies have explored the effects of false and misleading information on emotions or affective states (11.6 percent), focusing mainly on the influence on anxiety and stress levels (e.g.,Khan, 2021;Lee et al., 2020;Rocha et al., 2023). The effects on cognition (such as knowledge) have also been explored to a lesser extent (9.5 percent), but examples include studies examining the role of self-reported media literacy in relation to belief in false and misleading information (e.g.,Borah et al., 2022).
Finally, a relatively small portion examines effects on society at large (12.6 percent). However, it is important to emphasize that the exclusion keyword management in the search string may have contributed to the exclusion of studies investigating both the effects and management of false and misleading information. The most studies societal effect is economic effects (6.3 percent) (Bernard et al., 2021).
Conclusions This interdisciplinary review is based on an analysis of 179 scientific studies on false and misleading information on social media during societal crises from 2014 to 2024. The focus has been on explaining the spread of such information and identifying its effects. Several key conclusions can be drawn from the review.
Starting with broader general patterns, the results first show that COVID-19 has dominated research on false and misleading information over the past decade. The pandemic was not only a global crisis with significant impacts but also the most frequently studied topic in this field. A critical question is how much of the knowledge gained from research during the pandemic can be generalized to other types of crises. Although most studies originate from the social sciences, a substantial portion comes from medical research. This proportion would likely have been smaller if the pandemic had not dominated the sample. It is therefore crucial for future research to extend beyond the pandemic to ensure that findings can be applied to other types of crises.
Second, research tends to view social media as a homogeneous phenomenon. Notably, 64 percent of the studies examined social media without specifying which platforms were being analysed. When individual platforms were the focus, X/Twitter was the most studied. However, social media is not a monolithic entity; referring to “social media” without specifying platforms is as imprecise as referring to “media” in general. Understanding what respondents mean when referring to “social media” can be challenging. Moreover, there is a lack of research on newer platforms like TikTok and Snapchat.
Finally, cross-sectional survey studies are most common for studying false and misleading information on social media. Given the importance of determining the spread and effects of false and misleading information, the lack of studies establishing causality is striking. Experiments and panel studies, both of which can confirm cause-and-effect relationships, are underrepresented. Future research should focus more on identifying causal mechanisms behind the spread and effects of false and misleading information.
Addressing the research questions, the results show that prior research has mainly focused on individual-centred explanations and effects. Approximately two-thirds of the studies attribute the spread of misinformation to individual factors. The dominance of the individual perspective is even greater in studies examining effects, with over 80 percent focusing on individuals. These studies often explain the spread of false and misleading information based on people's perceptions. However, crises are affective-laden events where emotions play a significant role in human behaviour. It is likely that emotions such as anger or anxiety interact with cognitive factors or personality traits, influencing the likelihood of people spreading false or misleading information. Likewise, exposure to and belief in false information may trigger strong emotions that, in turn, affect behaviour in various ways. Future research should pay greater attention to the role of emotions in both the spread and effects of misinformation.
Moreover , structural factors influencing the spread and effects of false and misleading information are absent. This limits our understanding of how structural factors interact with individual behaviours. One reason for this may be that studying individuals is methodologically easier than analysing societal-level influences. However, research on false and misleading information must expand beyond individual-level explanations to consider broader societal dynamics. This includes examining the role of media systems, political contexts, and platform algorithms, as well as how these structures interact with individual behaviours and perceptions. Future research should adopt a more holistic approach to fully understand the phenomenon.
Lastly, technological aspects and applications are rarely explored. It is striking how few studies focus on examining AI applications, and research on deepfakes is entirely absent. Given the rapid advancements in these technologies and their potential impact, this gap is particularly noteworthy. One likely reason is that AI-related false and misleading information has only recently become a central societal concern, and academic research takes time to develop. Our selection criteria may have further contributed to this, including studies with the highest number of citations. Nevertheless, future studies on misinformation during societal crises must address the role of AI and emerging technologies in shaping the spread and impact of false and misleading information.
Taken together, what is lacking is an interdisciplinary research agenda that accounts for the context-specific dynamics of crises. The spread of false and misleading information during crises represents a complex problem at the intersection of psychology, technology, and communication. Moving forward, research should adopt interdisciplinary approaches that examine how key drivers identified in this review, such as crisis-induced emotional states and motivated reasoning, interact. At the same time, future studies should move beyond only focusing on individual-level factors and also incorporate structural and technological dimensions, which remain underexplored. Doing so would support the development of frameworks that integrate context-specific dynamics with broader theoretical mechanisms to explain and mitigate false and misleading information during crises.
Of course, this study is not without its limitations. Most notable is the inclusion of the term COVID-19 in the search string, which may have generated an overrepresentation of that case in relation to other crises types. Moreover, the exclusion block might have (unintentionally) led to an exclusion of relevant studies. However, the strategy was deemed necessary given the large number of studies published on the topic. Future reviews should therefore aim to replicate the findings while also further refining the search string and method, for instance by using computational and automatised methods.

A Multimodal Fake News Detection Model Based on Adaptive Binary Osprey Optimization Algorithm and Cross-Modal Disentangled Fusion

Author: Xu, Dai1    ; Lu, Guoqiang2; Li Jiaxue3    1 School of Finance, Jilin University of Finance and Economics, Changchun 130117, China; daixusissi@jlufe.edu.cn, Jilin Provincial Key Laboratory of Fintech, Changchun 130117, China2 School of Health Management, Mudanjiang Medical University, Mudanjiang 157011, China; luguoqiang_123@163.com3 Institute of National Development and Security Studies, Jilin University, Changchun 130012, China

Publication info: Xu, Dai; Lu, Guoqiang; Li Jiaxue. 

https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/multimodal-fake-news-detection-model-based-on/docview/3389335817/se-2?accountid=14696

Abstract: With the rapid growth of social media, online news has become increasingly multimodal, combining textual and visual information, posing new challenges for fake news detection. Existing methods often suffer from redundant features, distribution differences across modalities, and insufficient modeling of semantic interactions. To address these issues, this paper proposes an Adaptive Binary Osprey Optimization Algorithm and Cross-modal Disentangled Fusion model (ABOOA-CDF). First, an Adaptive Binary Osprey Optimization Algorithm (ABOOA) is developed for multimodal feature selection by integrating chaotic initialization, adaptive search, and binary mapping strategies to identify informative feature subsets. Then, a Cross-modal Relation Disentanglement Module (CRDM) is introduced to decompose multimodal representations into shared, discrepant, and complementary components, thereby enhancing semantic relationship modeling. Furthermore, an Adaptive Semantic Fusion Module (ASFM) dynamically learns fusion weights to generate discriminative multimodal representations. Experimental results demonstrate that ABOOA-CDF effectively improves detection performance. Compared with MFO and OOA, the proposed method achieves Accuracy improvements of 1.02 and 2.66 percentage points, respectively, verifying its effectiveness in feature optimization, cross-modal relation modeling, and semantic fusion.

Full text: 1. Introduction With the rapid development of Internet technologies and social media platforms, the creation and dissemination of news have significantly changed. News can now spread rapidly across online websites, enabling information to reach a large audience quickly. However, the openness and convenience of online communication have also accelerated the dissemination of fake news, posing serious threats to public opinion, social stability, and information security. Consequently, accurate fake news detection has become an important research topic in natural language processing, multimedia analysis, and intelligent information processing.
Early fake news detection methods mainly rely on textual information and use handcrafted features alongside traditional machine learning classifiers. Although these approaches achieve reasonable performance in specific scenarios, they are limited in modeling complex semantics, contextual dependencies, and implicit logical relationships. With the advancement of deep learning, neural representation learning has significantly improved the extraction of semantic features from text, providing more effective solutions for fake news detection [1]. Nevertheless, real-world news often comprises multiple modalities, such as text and images. Depending solely on textual information is therefore insufficient to capture the complete characteristics of news content [2].
The increasing prevalence of multimodal news has promoted extensive research on multimodal fake news detection. Existing approaches typically integrate textual and visual representations and exploit cross-modal interactions to determine news credibility, thereby alleviating the limitations of single-modal methods [3,4]. Despite these developments, text and image modalities differ significantly in their representations, semantic patterns, and feature distributions. The interaction between them may simultaneously contain shared semantic content, complementary clues, and inconsistent information. Although existing approaches generally capture such relationships through feature fusion or cross-modal interaction mechanisms, they seldom explicitly characterize various semantic relationship types. Consequently, the discriminative information contained in multimodal data may not be fully utilized.
Recent progress in cross-modal representation learning and contrastive learning has further strengthened semantic alignment between different modalities [5]. In addition, multimodal contrastive learning enhanced with external knowledge has improved the quality of representations in complex news scenarios [6]. Beyond semantic alignment, disentanglement-based approaches have been explored to separate shared and modality-specific information in multimodal data [7]. Nevertheless, existing multimodal fake news detection methods still focus on overall semantic consistency, neglecting fine-grained cross-modal relationships. This limitation reduces their ability to capture discriminative cues embedded in multimodal content. Therefore, effectively disentangling different types of cross-modal relationships remains a key challenge in multimodal fake news detection.
Another challenge arises from the high dimensionality of multimodal representations. After feature extraction, textual and visual features often contain considerable redundancy and weakly relevant information. These redundant features increase computational complexity and may degrade classification performance. Swarm intelligence optimization algorithms have been widely adopted for feature selection due to their strong global search capabilities and gradient-free optimization. Representative methods, such as the Whale Optimization Algorithm (WOA) and Sparrow Search Algorithm (SSA), have demonstrated promising performance in feature subset optimization [8,9]. More recently, newly developed nature-inspired optimization algorithms have further expanded the solution space for complex optimization problems [10]. However, existing algorithms still suffer from unstable search behavior and premature convergence when solving high-dimensional binary feature selection problems, limiting their effectiveness in multimodal fake news detection.
To address these issues, this paper proposes an Adaptive Binary Osprey Optimization Algorithm and Cross-modal Disentangled Fusion (ABOOA-CDF) for multimodal fake news detection. The proposed framework combines adaptive feature optimization with fine-grained cross-modal relation modeling to improve the quality of multimodal representations and enhance detection performance.
The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows.
(1) . An Adaptive Binary Osprey Optimization Algorithm (ABOOA) is proposed for high-dimensional binary feature selection. By incorporating circle chaotic initialization, an adaptive search strategy, and a binary mapping mechanism, the proposed algorithm improves search efficiency and selects more informative feature subsets.
(2) . A Cross-modal Relation Disentanglement Module (CRDM) is developed to model different semantic relationships between text and images explicitly. The module decomposes cross-modal representations into shared, discrepant, and complementary components, reducing interference among different types of semantic information.
(3) . An Adaptive Semantic Fusion Module (ASFM) is designed to dynamically assign fusion weights according to the semantic characteristics of each sample, enabling more effective integration of multimodal representations.
(4) . Extensive experiments are conducted on real-world multimodal fake news datasets. The proposed method achieves the best overall performance, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed framework.
2. Related Work 2.1. Unimodal Fake News Detection Early fake news detection mainly relies on textual content and exploits linguistic patterns, propagation characteristics, and handcrafted statistical features to distinguish fake news from real news. Conventional approaches typically extract features from word frequency, topic distribution, sentiment polarity, and user behavior, and then employ machine learning classifiers such as Support Vector Machines (SVM), Decision Trees, and Random Forests for classification. Although these methods are computationally efficient and easy to implement, their performance heavily depends on manually designed features. Consequently, they often fail to capture deep semantic representations and complex contextual dependencies, especially when processing fake news with diverse writing styles and implicit semantic patterns [11,12].
The rapid development of deep learning has significantly advanced unimodal fake news detection. Neural representation learning enables automatic extraction of latent patterns from news content and propagation behavior, reducing reliance on manual feature engineering. Deep neural networks can model complex nonlinear relationships and therefore provide more discriminative representations for fake news identification [13]. In parallel, approaches that incorporate user interactions and propagation structures further improve detection performance by exploiting the dynamic dissemination process of online news [14].
More recently, pretrained language models have substantially enhanced text-based fake news detection. Contextual representations learned from large-scale corpora enable dynamic interpretation of word meanings across contexts, thereby improving the modeling of complex semantics and long-range dependencies. Transformer-based pretrained models have demonstrated strong generalization ability in text classification and have gradually become the foundation of modern fake news detection systems [15]. Building upon this framework, RoBERTa further refines the pretraining strategy and optimization process, producing more robust language representations for complex classification tasks [16].
Despite these advances, text-only approaches still exhibit several limitations. News articles can be intentionally manipulated through paraphrasing, implicit expressions, or semantic reconstruction, making authenticity difficult to determine solely from textual evidence. Furthermore, online news generally combines text with images and other complementary media. Ignoring these heterogeneous sources prevents models from fully exploiting the available evidence. As a result, unimodal methods often struggle in real-world scenarios and require additional multimodal information to improve detection accuracy [17].
Overall, unimodal fake news detection has evolved from handcrafted feature engineering to deep representation learning and, more recently, pretrained language modeling. These developments have established a solid foundation for subsequent research. Although online news increasingly incorporates multiple modalities, relying solely on textual information is no longer sufficient. Therefore, integrating heterogeneous data sources has become an important direction for improving fake news detection.
2.2. Multimodal Fake News Detection The rapid growth of social media has transformed online news from pure text into multimodal content that combines text, images, videos, and other media. Text describes events, facts, and opinions, whereas images provide complementary visual evidence, such as people, scenes, and contextual information. By jointly exploiting these heterogeneous sources, multimodal fake news detection provides a more comprehensive understanding of news content than text-only approaches. Therefore, it has become a major research direction in fake news detection.
Early fake news detection methods mainly rely on textual representations or social propagation information, where deep learning models are developed to capture semantic features and structural patterns from single-source data [18,19,20]. However, these approaches struggle to leverage complementary information across modalities, motivating the development of multimodal fake news detection methods.
With the development of multimodal fake news detection, researchers focus on learning joint representations of textual and visual content. These approaches extract features from different modalities and project them into a shared feature space for credibility assessment. The Event Adversarial Neural Network (EANN) introduces event adversarial learning to reduce the influence of event distribution bias, thereby improving generalization across unseen events [21]. Subsequently, attention shifts to visual information. Multi-domain visual modeling methods explore object regions, scene context, and visual semantics to enhance visual representations and improve detection performance in complex news scenarios [22].
As cross-modal learning advances, research has gradually shifted from joint representation learning to semantic relationship modeling. Text and images may exhibit semantic consistency, conflicts, or missing correspondence. Modeling all interactions within a unified representation is often insufficient to capture these diverse relationships. SAFE improves the identification of inconsistent image–text pairs through a similarity-aware mechanism [23]. Multi-view representation learning further models cross-modal interactions from textual semantics, visual patterns, and high-level semantic perspectives, leading to more discriminative multimodal representations [24]. In addition, similarity-aware prompt learning strengthens semantic alignment between modalities by optimizing prompt representations, further improving cross-modal understanding [25].
Recent advances in vision-language pretraining have driven multimodal fake news detection toward knowledge-enhanced frameworks. Prompt-based methods effectively leverage prior knowledge embedded in vision-language models, achieving better performance in few-shot settings and early-stage fake news detection [26]. Emotion-aware prompt learning further integrates textual sentiment, visual semantics, and cross-modal interactions to improve the modeling of complex semantic relationships [27]. Meanwhile, adaptive feature selection, multimodal large language models, and cross-modal entity consistency have been incorporated into fake news detection. These techniques improve misinformation recognition by dynamically selecting informative features, incorporating external knowledge, and modeling entity correspondence across modalities [28,29,30]. Recent studies have further extended multimodal fake news detection to knowledge-enriched and multi-domain settings [31]. More recently, fine-grained attribution analysis and multi-perspective evidence verification have further enhanced reasoning capability and prediction reliability [32,33].
Overall, multimodal fake news detection has evolved from shallow feature fusion to fine-grained cross-modal relationship modeling and knowledge-enhanced learning, leading to substantial improvements in detection performance. Nevertheless, several challenges persist. Most existing methods still rely on a unified representation space, making it difficult to distinguish shared, discrepant, and complementary semantic information. In addition, multimodal representations often contain redundant features that reduce learning efficiency. The relative importance of different modalities also varies across news samples, whereas existing fusion strategies generally employ fixed or insufficiently adaptive mechanisms. Therefore, effective feature selection, fine-grained modeling of heterogeneous cross-modal relationships, and adaptive fusion of multimodal evidence remain important directions for future research.
3. Methodology This paper proposes a multimodal fake news detection model based on the Adaptive Binary Osprey Optimization Algorithm and Cross-modal Disentangled Fusion (ABOOA-CDF). The framework consists of three sequential stages: feature optimization, relation disentanglement, and semantic fusion. First, the Adaptive Binary Osprey Optimization Algorithm (ABOOA) is employed to select informative features from both image and text modalities. Circle chaotic initialization, an adaptive search strategy, and a binary mapping mechanism are incorporated to optimize the feature subset while reducing redundant information. Next, the Cross-modal Relation Disentanglement Module (CRDM) projects visual and textual features into a unified representation space. The cross-modal information is then decomposed into three complementary components: shared, discrepant, and complementary. This disentangled representation improves the discrimination of semantic relationships across different modalities. Finally, the Adaptive Semantic Fusion Module (ASFM) dynamically assigns fusion weights to the three relation components according to their contributions. The resulting fused representation is fed into a fully connected layer followed by a Softmax classifier to predict the authenticity of the news. The overall architecture of the proposed model is illustrated in Figure 1.
3.1. Multimodal Feature Extraction Multimodal fake news detection requires both textual semantics and visual evidence. The text modality conveys news, opinions, and emotional expressions, whereas the image modality provides complementary information, such as scenes, objects, and visual context. To provide reliable inputs for subsequent feature selection and cross-modal relation modeling, text and image features are extracted separately.
3.1.1. Text Feature Extraction News articles exhibit strong contextual dependencies, where the meaning of each word is influenced by its surrounding context. To capture bidirectional semantic information, a Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) network is adopted for text encoding [34].
Given the tokenized text of the i -th news sample, the sequence is defined as (1) P i = w i , 1 , w i , 2 , … , w i , L
where P i denotes the text sequence, w i , k represents the k -th token, and L is the sequence length. Each token is first mapped into a continuous embedding vector. (2) e i , k = E m b w i , k
where e i , k is the embedding of w i , k , and Emb ( ⋅ ) denotes the embedding function.
The forward and backward LSTM networks then process the embedding sequence. (3) h → i , k = LSTM f ( e i , k , h → i , k − 1 )
(4) h ← i , k = LSTM b ( e i , k , h ← i , k + 1 )
where h → i , k and h ← i , k denote the forward and backward hidden states, respectively. The hidden representations from both directions are concatenated to obtain the contextual representation. (5) h i , k = [ h → i , k ; h ← i , k ]
where [;] denotes feature concatenation. To generate a global representation of the entire text, average pooling is applied over all hidden states. (6) g i t = 1 L ∑ k = 1 L h i , k

g i t denotes the global textual representation of the i -th news sample. Finally, a nonlinear transformation is employed to obtain the text feature. (7) E i t = ϕ ( W t 0 ⋅ g i t + b t 0 )
where E i t is the extracted text feature, W t 0 and b t 0 are learnable parameters, and ϕ ( ⋅ ) denotes the activation function.
3.1.2. Image Feature Extraction Images provide visual evidence that complements textual information. To preserve both low-level visual structures and high-level semantic information, ResNet50 and CLIP are jointly employed for image encoding. ResNet50 extracts structural visual patterns such as scenes, textures, and objects [35], while CLIP produces image representations aligned with the shared vision-language semantic space [36].
Let I i denote the image corresponding to the i -th news sample. Deep visual features are first extracted using ResNet50 without its final classification layer. (8) r i = GAP ( ResNet 50 ( I i ) )
where r i denotes the visual feature extracted by ResNet50, and GAP ( ⋅ ) represents global average pooling. The CLIP image encoder then encodes the image. (9) c i = CLIP i m g ( I i )

c i denotes the semantic image representation generated by CLIP. Since these two feature types have different distributions and dimensionalities, nonlinear transformations are first applied. (10) r ^ i = ϕ ( W r ⋅ r i + b r )
(11) c ^ i = ϕ ( W c ⋅ c i + b c )

r ^ i and c ^ i denote the transformed ResNet50 and CLIP features, respectively. W r , W c , b r , and b c are learnable parameters. The transformed features are concatenated to form the joint image representation. (12) g i v = [ r ^ i ; c ^ i ]

g i v denotes the fused visual representation. A projection layer is then applied to obtain the final image feature. (13) E i v = ϕ ( W v 0 ⋅ g i v + b v 0 )
where E i v is the extracted image feature, and W v 0 and b v 0 are learnable parameters.
In summary, BiLSTM is employed to extract the textual feature E i t , while ResNet50 and CLIP are jointly used to obtain the image feature E i v . These features are fed into the ABOOA feature selection module to remove redundant dimensions and retain more discriminative multimodal information. The selected text and image features, denoted as F t and F v , are subsequently used as inputs to the Cross-modal Relation Disentanglement Module (CRDM).
3.2. Osprey Optimization Algorithm (OOA) The Osprey Optimization Algorithm (OOA) is a swarm intelligence optimization method proposed by Dehghani et al. based on the hunting behavior of ospreys in nature [37]. OOA simulates the processes of prey detection, target diving, and prey capture to achieve global exploration and local exploitation in the search space. The algorithm consists of two stages: global exploration (prey localization) and local exploitation (prey capture).
3.2.1. Global Exploration Stage (Prey Localization) At the beginning of hunting, an osprey circles above the water to search for prey. After identifying a promising region, it moves toward the target. In OOA, each osprey represents a search agent, while the prey location corresponds to a potential optimal solution. During optimization, each agent updates its position according to a selected prey candidate and its current position.
Step 1: Construct the Candidate Prey Set
For the i -th osprey, all individuals with better fitness than the current solution are collected to form the candidate prey set. (14) S i = { X k ∣ F ( X k ) < F ( X i ) , k ∈ { 1 , 2 , … , N } , k ≠ i }
where N denotes the population size and F ( ⋅ ) is the objective function. If S i is empty, one individual other than X i is randomly selected from the population as the prey.
Step 2: Select a Prey Position
A prey position, denoted as F P i , is randomly selected from the candidate prey set S i .
Step 3: Update the Position (15) x i , j new , P 1 = x i , j + r i , j ⋅ F P i , j − I i , j ⋅ x i , j , i = 1 , 2 , … , N ; j = 1 , 2 , … , m
where x i , j is the current position of the i -th osprey in the j -th dimension, F P i , j is the corresponding coordinate of the selected prey, r i , j in [0, 1] is a random number, I i , j in {1, 2} is a random integer controlling the movement direction, and m denotes the problem dimension. This update guides the search agent toward a promising region.
Step 4: Greedy Selection
The updated solution is accepted only if it improves the objective value. (16) X i ← X i new , P 1 , if   F ( X i new , P 1 ) < F ( X i ) X i , otherwise

This greedy strategy prevents deterioration of the population fitness.
3.2.2. Local Exploitation Stage (Prey Capture) After locating the prey, the osprey performs fine adjustments before completing the capture. In the optimization process, this behavior is modeled as a local search around the current solution. As the iteration proceeds, the search step gradually decreases, allowing the algorithm to shift from broad exploration to refined exploitation. The position update in the j -th dimension is defined as (17) x i , j new , P 2 = x i , j + r i , j ⋅ ( u b j − l b j ) + l b j t , i = 1 , 2 , … , N ; j = 1 , 2 , … , m
where x i , j new , P 2 is the updated position, l b j and u b j denote the lower and upper bounds of the j -th dimension, r i , j   in   0 , 1 is a random number, and t is the current iteration number. The factor 1 t gradually reduces the perturbation amplitude, thereby strengthening local exploitation in the later search stage. After the update, greedy selection is again applied. (18) X i ← X i new , P 2 , if   F ( X i new , P 2 ) < F ( X i ) X i , otherwise
where X i and X i new , P 2 denote the solution vectors before and after the update, respectively, and F ( ⋅ ) is the objective function. This strategy ensures that the population’s best fitness is preserved during optimization.
Overall, OOA combines global exploration with local exploitation to balance search diversity and convergence. The exploration stage rapidly identifies promising regions, whereas the exploitation stage continuously refines candidate solutions. Despite this balance, the original OOA still has several limitations. Its initialization relies on random sampling, and its search mechanism is mainly designed for continuous optimization. Consequently, its performance may deteriorate in high-dimensional binary feature selection tasks. These limitations motivate the improvements introduced in the proposed optimization algorithm for multimodal feature selection.
3.3. Adaptive Binary Osprey Optimization Algorithm (ABOOA) Although OOA demonstrates strong optimization capability in continuous optimization problems, its direct application to high-dimensional feature selection remains challenging. To improve population quality, search efficiency, and binary feature selection performance, this study proposes an Adaptive Binary Osprey Optimization Algorithm (ABOOA) based on the original OOA. The proposed algorithm incorporates a circle chaotic initialization strategy, an adaptive search strategy, and an adaptive binary mapping mechanism. These improvements enhance global exploration, local exploitation, and binary optimization in discrete feature spaces.
Unlike the original OOA, ABOOA maintains both a continuous search position and a binary feature selection vector for each search agent. The continuous position is updated during the optimization process, whereas the binary vector represents the selected feature subset for fitness evaluation. Let the population size be N , and the original feature dimension be m . The continuous search position of the i -th osprey is defined as (19) X i = x i , 1 , x i , 2 , … , x i , m , x i , j ∈ R
where X i denotes the continuous position vector of the i -th osprey, x i , j is its position in the j -th dimension, and m is the number of original features. The corresponding binary feature selection vector is defined as (20) B i = B i , 1 , B i , 2 , … , B i , m , B i , j ∈ 0 , 1

B i represents the selected feature subset of the i -th osprey. If B i , j = 1 , the j -th feature is selected; otherwise, it is discarded. During optimization, ABOOA first updates the continuous position X i , then converts it into the binary vector B i via a binary mapping, and finally determines whether the new solution should be accepted according to the fitness of B i .
To improve the discriminative capability of the Sigmoid-based binary mapping, the continuous search space is defined over a symmetric interval with l b j = − 6 and u b j = 6 . This setting allows the continuous variable x i , j to span both positive and negative regions. Consequently, the Sigmoid output is not biased toward values greater than 0.5, which would otherwise lead to selecting an excessive number of features when the search space is limited to [0, 1]. The symmetric search boundary provides better control over feature selection probabilities and facilitates the generation of more compact feature subsets.
3.3.1. Circle Chaotic Initialization Strategy The original OOA initializes the population randomly. Although simple, random initialization may produce unevenly distributed individuals, limiting the coverage of promising search regions and reducing the efficiency of subsequent optimization. To address this issue, ABOOA employs a circle chaotic mapping to generate initial continuous positions, thereby improving population diversity and search-space coverage.
The circle chaotic map is defined as (21) z k + 1 = mod ( z k + b − a 2 π s i n ( 2 π z k ) , 1 )
where z k is the chaotic variable generated at the k -th iteration, a and b are control parameters, and mod ( ⋅ ) denotes the modulo operation. In this study, a = 0.5 and b = 0.2 are adopted to improve the ergodicity of the chaotic sequence over the interval [0, 1]. To avoid sequence degeneration, the initial value z 0 is randomly selected from the open interval (0, 1).
Based on the generated chaotic sequence, the initial continuous position of the i -th osprey in the j -th dimension is computed as (22) x i , j 0 = l b j + z i , j ⋅ ( u b j − l b j ) , i = 1 , 2 , … , N ; j = 1 , 2 , … , m
where x i , j 0 denotes the initial position, l b j and u b j are the lower and upper bounds of the j -th dimension, and z i , j ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] is the chaotic variable generated by the circle map. Since the search interval is set to [−6, 6], the initialized positions are distributed symmetrically around zero, providing a suitable basis for the subsequent Sigmoid-based binary mapping.
Because feature selection is a binary optimization problem, the initialized continuous positions must be converted into feature selection probabilities. The Sigmoid function is adopted for this purpose. (23) S ( x i , j 0 ) = 1 1 + e x p ( − x i , j 0 )

S ( x i , j 0 ) denotes the initial probability of selecting the j -th feature for the i -th osprey. According to this probability, the initial binary feature selection state is determined as (24) B i , j 0 = 1 , if   rand < S ( x i , j 0 ) 0 , o t h e r w i s e
where rand ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] is a uniformly distributed random number, and B i , j 0 denotes the initial binary state of the j -th feature. By introducing circle chaotic initialization, ABOOA generates more diverse candidate feature subsets during the early search stage, increases population diversity, and provides higher-quality initial solutions for subsequent global exploration and local exploitation.
3.3.2. Adaptive Search Strategy The original OOA uses relatively fixed position-update rules during both global exploration and local exploitation. As a result, the search intensity cannot be adjusted effectively as the iteration proceeds. For high-dimensional feature selection, larger search steps are needed early to expand the search space and reduce the risk of premature convergence. In later iterations, the perturbation should gradually decrease, allowing the population to refine promising regions more precisely. To achieve this transition, ABOOA introduces an adaptive search factor that varies with each iteration.
Let T denote the maximum number of iterations and t the current iteration, where t = 1 , 2 , … , T . The adaptive search factor is defined as
(25) ω ( t ) = ω m i n + ( ω m a x − ω m i n ) · 1 − t T 2

ω m a x and ω m i n represent the maximum and minimum values of the search factor, respectively. As the iteration number increases, ω ( t ) decreases nonlinearly. A larger value in the early stage promotes broad exploration and helps maintain population diversity. In the later stage, the smaller factor reduces excessive movement and improves the stability and convergence accuracy of local exploitation.
During global exploration, ABOOA constructs a candidate prey set based on the fitness values of binary feature subsets. For the i -th osprey, the candidate prey set is defined as (26) S i = { X k ∣ F ( B k ) < F ( B i ) , k ∈ { 1 , 2 , … , N } , k ≠ i }

S i denotes the candidate prey set of the i -th osprey, and F ( B i ) is the fitness value of its binary feature subset B i . It should be noted that the optimization target of ABOOA is the feature subset instead of the continuous position itself. Therefore, candidate prey are selected based on F ( B k ) < F ( B i ) rather than F ( X k ) < F ( X i ) . If S i is empty, an individual other than X i is randomly selected from the population. One member of S i is then chosen as the prey position of the i -th osprey and denoted by F P i .
Based on the global exploration rule of the original OOA, ABOOA introduces the adaptive search factor into the movement toward the prey position. (27) x i , j new , P 1 = x i , j + ω t ⋅ r i , j ⋅ F P i , j − I i , j ⋅ x i , j , i = 1 , 2 , … , N ; j = 1 , 2 , … , m
where x i , j new , P 1 denotes the updated continuous position of the i -th osprey in the j -th dimension during global exploration, x i , j is the current position, and F P i , j is the corresponding component of the selected prey position F P i . In addition, r i , j ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] is a random number, and I i , j ∈ { 1 , 2 } is a randomly generated integer. Compared with the original global exploration rule, Equation (27) includes ω ( t ) to regulate the movement amplitude. This process allows broader exploration in the early stage and progressively smaller updates near convergence, thereby improving search stability.
During local exploitation, the adaptive search factor is further introduced into the local perturbation term. The updated position is calculated as (28) x i , j new , P 2 = x i , j + ω ( t ) ⋅ l b j + r i , j ⋅ ( u b j − l b j ) t , i = 1 , 2 , … , N ; j = 1 , 2 , … , m
where x i , j new , P 2 is the updated continuous position of the i -th osprey in the j -th dimension during local exploitation. The lower and upper bounds of the j -th dimension are denoted by l b j and u b j , respectively. The random variable r i , j lies in [0, 1], and t is the current iteration number. As shown in Equation (28), the perturbation amplitude is jointly controlled by ω ( t ) and 1 / t . Both terms decrease as the iteration proceeds. Therefore, the search gradually shifts from broad exploration to fine-grained refinement, improving convergence precision in the later stage.
To prevent the updated continuous position from exceeding the feasible search range, a boundary constraint is applied after each update. (29) x i , j new = m i n m a x x i , j new l b j , u b j

x i , j new is obtained from either global exploration or local exploitation. This operation ensures that each coordinate remains within l b j u b j , preventing invalid positions from affecting subsequent binary mapping and fitness evaluation.
After the continuous position is updated, the new vector X i new is converted into a binary feature selection vector B i new through the adaptive binary mapping mechanism. Greedy selection is then performed according to the fitness of the resulting feature subset. (30) X i , B i ← X i new , B i new , if   F B i new < F B i X i , B i , otherwise

Here, X i new denotes the continuous position generated during exploration or exploitation stage, whereas B i new denotes the binary vector obtained from X i new . If the new feature subset achieves a better fitness value, both the continuous position and its binary representation are accepted. Otherwise, the original pair is retained. Unlike the original OOA, which updates only continuous positions, ABOOA maintains X i and B i simultaneously. This design preserves consistency between the continuous search space and the binary feature selection space.
3.3.3. Adaptive Binary Mapping Mechanism Feature selection is essentially a discrete binary optimization problem, whereas OOA generates continuous-valued positions. Therefore, converting continuous search positions into binary feature selection states is a key step in applying ABOOA to feature selection. A fixed Sigmoid function keeps the same mapping intensity throughout the optimization process. This procedure may reduce randomness in the early stage or lead to unstable feature states near convergence. To address this issue, ABOOA introduces an adaptive binary mapping mechanism. A time-varying factor dynamically regulates the selection probability, enabling stronger exploration early on and more stable binary decisions later.
The continuous position x i , j is first transformed into the probability of selecting the j -th feature: (31) P i , j ( t ) = 1 1 + e x p ( − λ ( t ) · x i , j )
where P i , j ( t ) denotes the probability that the i -th osprey selects the j -th feature at iteration t . The adaptive mapping factor λ ( t ) controls the steepness of the Sigmoid function. Since the continuous search interval is symmetric around zero, x i , j can take both positive and negative values. A larger x i , j increases the selection probability, whereas a smaller x i , j increases the likelihood that the feature will be removed.
The adaptive mapping factor is defined as (32) λ ( t ) = λ m i n + ( λ m a x − λ m i n ) ⋅ t T

λ m i n and λ m a x are the minimum and maximum values of the mapping factor, respectively. At the beginning of optimization, λ ( t ) is relatively small, resulting in a smoother Sigmoid curve and more random feature selection probabilities. This process helps maintain population diversity. As the iteration proceeds, λ ( t ) increases and the curve becomes steeper. Continuous positions are therefore more likely to map to stable binary states, improving the consistency of the selected feature subsets.
According to P i , j ( t ) , the binary state of the j -th feature is determined as (33) B i , j = 1 , if   rand < P i , j ( t ) 0 , o t h e r w i s e
where rand ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] is a uniformly distributed random number. If B i , j = 1 , the j -th feature is retained; otherwise, it is discarded. This mapping mechanism links continuous optimization with discrete feature selection. Each osprey can update its position in the continuous space while representing a specific feature subset in binary form.
To evaluate the quality of a candidate feature subset, ABOOA uses a fitness function that balances classification performance and subset size. (34) F ( B i ) = α ⋅ ( 1 − A c c i ) + ( 1 − α ) ⋅ ∣ B i ∣ m
where A c c i denotes the validation accuracy obtained using the i -th binary feature subset B i , ∣ B i ∣ is the number of selected features, and m represents the total number of original features. The parameter α ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] controls the trade-off between classification performance and subset size. In the experiments, α is set to 0.9 to place greater emphasis on classification performance while retaining a penalty on the number of selected features. The first term penalizes classification errors, while the second limits the number of retained features. By minimizing Equation (34), ABOOA removes redundant dimensions while preserving detection performance, yielding a compact, discriminative feature subset. To provide an intuitive illustration of the binary mapping and fitness evaluation process, consider a simplified example with four candidate features. At a given iteration, suppose that the scaled position values entering the Sigmoid function in Equation (31) are λ t x i , 1 ,   λ t x i , 2 ,   λ t x i , 3 ,   λ ( t ) x i , 4 = − 1.2 ,   0.8 ,   2.0 ,   − 0.5 . According to Equation (31), the corresponding feature-selection probabilities are P i , 1 t , P i , 2 t , P i , 3 t , P i , 4 ( t ) = 0.23 ,   0.69 ,   0.88 ,   0.38 . Suppose that the uniformly sampled random values for the four features are 0.40 ,   0.50 ,   0.60 ,   0.70 . According to Equation (33), the resulting binary feature-selection vector is B i = 0 ,   1 ,   1 ,   0 , indicating that the second and third features are retained. If the selected feature subset achieves a validation accuracy of 0.92, then B i = 2 . With α = 0.9 , the fitness value defined in Equation (34) is calculated as F ( B i ) = 0.9 1 − 0.92 + 0.1 × 2 4 = 0.122 . This example illustrates how the adaptive Sigmoid mapping converts continuous search information into feature-selection probabilities, how these probabilities are further transformed into a discrete feature subset, and how classification performance and feature compactness are jointly considered during fitness evaluation.
In summary, ABOOA improves the original OOA in three aspects. First, circle chaotic mapping enhances the diversity of the initial population and expands its coverage of the search space. Second, the adaptive search factor dynamically regulates the search intensity during global exploration and local exploitation. This process enables the algorithm to emphasize broad exploration in early iterations and gradually shift toward local refinement. Third, the adaptive binary mapping mechanism converts continuous positions into binary feature selection vectors, allowing OOA to handle high-dimensional discrete optimization tasks effectively. These improvements make ABOOA better suited to multimodal fake news detection, where features are often high-dimensional, redundant, and strongly correlated. The selected subsets provide a more compact, stable, and discriminative basis for subsequent cross-modal relation modeling and news authenticity classification.
3.4. Cross-Modal Relation Disentanglement Module (CRDM) After ABOOA feature selection, redundant dimensions in both image and text features are removed, leaving representations that are more relevant to the downstream task. However, feature selection alone cannot reveal the semantic relationships between the two modalities. In multimodal fake news detection, the relationship between images and text is more complex than simple similarity or dissimilarity. It usually involves semantic consistency, discrepancy, and complementarity simultaneously. Conventional fusion methods, such as feature concatenation, weighted summation, or standard attention mechanisms, tend to mix these heterogeneous relationships into a single representation space, making it difficult to distinguish semantic consistency, modality-specific characteristics, and cross-modal complementary information.
To address this issue, we propose the Cross-modal Relation Disentanglement Module (CRDM). Using the image and text features selected by ABOOA as inputs, CRDM explicitly decomposes cross-modal relationships into three semantic components: shared, discrepant, and complementary information. Shared information captures semantic evidence that is consistent across the two modalities. Discrepant information preserves modality-specific cues and semantic inconsistencies between images and text. Complementary information models the additional semantics generated through cross-modal interaction. Instead of performing another fusion operation directly, CRDM first establishes a structured representation of different semantic relationships. Each type of cross-modal evidence is modeled independently before being adaptively integrated by the subsequent fusion module.
Let F v and F t denote the image and text features selected by ABOOA, respectively. To reduce the distribution gap between modalities, they are first projected into a common latent space. (35) H v = ϕ ( W v ⋅ F v + b v )
(36) H t = ϕ ( W t ⋅ F t + b t )

H v and H t denote the latent representations of the image and text modalities, respectively. W v and W t are learnable weight matrices, b v and b t are bias vectors, and ϕ ( ⋅ ) is a nonlinear activation function. After projection, both modalities share the same feature dimension, providing a common representation space for subsequent relation disentanglement.
3.4.1. Shared Information Modeling The purpose of shared information modeling is to extract semantic content that is consistent across images and text. In real news, the objects, scenes, or emotional tendencies described in the text are often supported by the accompanying image. In contrast, fake news frequently exhibits image–text mismatches, weak semantic correlations, or partial inconsistencies. Therefore, shared information provides important evidence for evaluating semantic consistency between the two modalities.
A cross-modal interaction vector is first constructed as (37) Q c = [ H v ; H t ; H v ⊙ H t ; ∣ H v − H t ∣ ]
where Q c is the input for shared information modeling, ⊙ denotes element-wise multiplication, [ ; ] represents feature concatenation, and ∣ H v − H t ∣ is the absolute difference between the image and text representations.
