Two observations stand out. First, the unweighted crowd baseline (b) underperforms the content-only classifier, consistent with the CI-theoretic warning that unstructured aggregation over correlated members can be worse than a single competent judge. Second, once reputation and independence weighting are introduced (c → f), the crowd contribution becomes complementary to the content model rather than redundant, and the joint system exceeds either component.
5.6. Ablation Study To isolate the contribution of each CI characteristic, we ablate diversity gating, independence weighting, and reputation-based influence updates while holding the rest of the pipeline fixed. Table 3 reports macro-F1 for each ablation.
Revised Table 3—ablation with variability across five seeds:

- . Independence weighting (Equation (8)): F1 0.804 ± 0.008 | Δ = −0.033 ( p < 0.001).

Independence weighting provides the largest single contribution, consistent with the theoretical prediction that suppressing correlated votes has a stronger effect on aggregate accuracy than tuning who is included. Reputation-based influence update contributes a further, smaller improvement by reducing the effective coupling among users before aggregation. Diversity and decentralization gating produce the smallest incremental gain on GossipCop but are more useful on items with small or highly clustered crowds (see Section 5.7).
5.7. Effect of Collective Size Following the analysis in [7], we examine how the size of the collective—i.e., the number of users associated with a news item—affects performance. We bin news items by collective size and compute macro-F1 within each bin. The CI framework’s advantage over the unweighted crowd + machine baseline is largest in the mid-size range (30 ≤ n ≤ 200) and narrows for very large collectives ( n > 500), where even unweighted aggregation is close to optimal, and for very small collectives ( n < 10), where all crowd-based methods degrade toward the content-only baseline (Figure 2).
5.8. Statistical Significance We apply the paired bootstrap test with 10,000 resamples on the test predictions of the CI framework and each baseline. All pairwise differences in macro-F1 are significant at the 0.01 level ( p < 0.01), including the 5.9-point margin over the unweighted crowd + machine baseline.
5.9. Splitting Strategies and Sensitivity Analysis (New) In response to reviewers, we complement the default news-item-level random split with three additional evaluation protocols and a sensitivity analysis over all key hyperparameters. The purpose is to test whether the reported gains are stable to (i) more adversarial split protocols and (ii) reasonable variation in tuning.
5.9.1. User-Disjoint Split Under this protocol, users are partitioned across train/dev/test such that no user appears in more than one split; news items are assigned to a split according to the majority split of their crowd. This is a strict test of whether reputation and stance signals learned on one population generalize to a disjoint population. Sample sizes are (train, dev, test) = (15,964, 2088, 4088) items after enforcing the disjointness constraint. The proposed CI framework achieves macro-F1 = 0.812 ± 0.008 vs. 0.762 ± 0.010 for the unweighted crowd + machine baseline (e), a gap of +0.050 (paired bootstrap p < 0.001). The absolute F1 is 2.5 pts lower than under the news-item split, as expected under strict user disjointness.
5.9.2. Temporal Split News items are sorted by publication date (available for 21,748 items). The chronologically earliest 80% form the training set, the next 10% the development set, and the most recent 10% the test set. This simulates deployment-time generalization. Under this split, the CI framework achieves macro-F1 = 0.803 ± 0.011 vs. 0.759 ± 0.013 for baseline (e); the gap of +0.044 remains significant ( p < 0.001). The larger absolute drop compared to random splitting is attributable to topic drift between older and newer entertainment news.
5.9.3. Event-Level Split We cluster news items by the entity most frequently mentioned in the title (extracted via SpaCy NER); items sharing an entity are constrained to the same split. This tests whether the model relies on entity-specific stylistic cues. With six 141 entity clusters, the split yields (train, dev, test) sizes (17,512, 2194, 2434). The CI framework achieves macro-F1 = 0.826 ± 0.009 vs. 0.774 ± 0.011 for baseline (e); +0.052, p < 0.001.
5.9.4. Summary of Split Comparisons Macro-F1 across splitting protocols. Split | CI framework | Best baseline (e) | Δ | p -value. News-item (default) | 0.837 ± 0.006 | 0.791 ± 0.007 | +0.046 | < 0.001. User-disjoint | 0.812 ± 0.008 | 0.762 ± 0.010 | +0.050 | < 0.001. Temporal | 0.803 ± 0.011 | 0.759 ± 0.013 | +0.044 | < 0.001. Event-level | 0.826 ± 0.009 | 0.774 ± 0.011 | +0.052 | < 0.001. Across all four protocols, the proposed method maintains a statistically significant advantage of 4–5 macro-F1 points, indicating that the reported gains are not an artifact of the split strategy.

This addresses reviewer concern that the reputation model is oversimplified: while it is indeed simple, the pipeline’s macro-F1 is not brittle to reasonable perturbations of the feature weights.
Summary: Across all four hyperparameters (α, τ_d, τ_c, Δ) and the reputation feature weights, the maximum swing in macro-F1 is ≤0.024, and the framework remains above the strongest baseline throughout the entire tested range. The tuned optima form flat plateaus in parameter space rather than sharp peaks, indicating that the reported gains are not the result of hyperparameter overfitting.
6. Discussion The results support three claims made in the introduction. First, crowd signals on social networks are informative but not additively independent, and treating them as such—by unweighted majority voting—leaves substantial value on the table. Second, the four CI characteristics identified by Surowiecki are not merely a rhetorical checklist but decompose cleanly into measurable quantities on real social-media traces. Third, among those four characteristics, independence is the operationally most consequential on GossipCop: correcting for it produces the largest single accuracy gain in the ablation.
Update (in response to reviewers): The stance classifier is no longer characterized only qualitatively as “another weak link.” Section Standalone Evaluation of the Stance Classifier now reports its standalone macro-F1 (0.69 on an 800-tweet gold set, Cohen’s κ = 0.71 between annotators, and ≈22% distant-supervision noise). Section Standalone Evaluation of the Stance Classifier also reports a controlled perturbation study, demonstrating that the CI framework retains its advantage over the content-only baseline up to a stance noise rate of ~0.30, comfortably above the measured 0.22. Stance inference thus remains the weakest single component of the pipeline, but its error rate lies inside the pipeline’s safety margin.
Two additional robustness checks reinforce the conclusion. First, the sensitivity analyses in Section 5.9.5 show that the framework’s macro-F1 is flat (swing ≤ 0.024) around the tuned optima of all four gating hyperparameters and of the reputation feature weights, indicating that the reported gains are not the result of hyperparameter overfitting. Second, the alternative splitting protocols in Section 5.9.1, Section 5.9.2 and Section 5.9.3 (user-disjoint, temporal, event-level) all preserve the +0.044 to +0.052 macro-F1 advantage over the strongest baseline, indicating the gains are not an artifact of the default random split. Together with the expanded baseline set (RvNN [14], GCNFN [26], UPFD [27], dEFEND [28]) whose strongest member trails the proposed method by 0.027 macro-F1 ( p < 0.001), these checks support the paper’s central empirical claim under a broader set of experimental conditions than in the original submission.
The framework has several limitations. Reputation is computed from four observable features that are gameable by determined adversaries; a coordinated inauthentic-behavior campaign could inflate the reputation of its accounts and thereby their influence weights. A more robust reputation model would incorporate longitudinal behavior signatures and cross-platform identity linkage, both of which are outside the scope of this paper. Stance inference is another weak link: the BiLSTM stance classifier is trained on distant-supervision labels and inherits their noise. On items where the crowd’s stance distribution is nearly uniform, the independence-weighted aggregation approaches the unweighted case, and the CI framework’s advantage narrows accordingly.
Threats to external validity include the domain specificity of GossipCop (entertainment news) and the temporal recency of its crawl. Entertainment news exhibits stance polarization patterns that may not transfer to political news, where partisan alignment strongly biases individual signals. A cross-domain evaluation on the PolitiFact split of FakeNewsNet is a natural next step.
A conceptual point worth stressing is the relationship between the present framework and prior CI work by the same research line. Nguyen and Truong [7] studied independence in a simulation environment with synthetic reputations; here, that measure is instantiated on real social-media data and shown to produce practically useful gains. Dang, Truong, and Nguyen [8] treated consensus as an optimization problem satisfying 1- or 2-Optimality; here, Equation (6) shows that binary-label consensus reduces to independence-weighted majority voting, avoiding the need for the hybrid genetic algorithms required in more general judgment spaces.
7. Conclusions We proposed a Collective Intelligence framework for fake news detection on social networks that treats the crowd around a news item as a formal intelligent collective. The framework represents the crowd as a directed weighted graph, instantiates diversity, independence, decentralization, and aggregation as measurable quantities, and fuses a content-based classifier with independence-weighted crowd signals through a consensus-choice aggregator. On the GossipCop split of FakeNewsNet, the framework improves macro-F1 by 4.6 points over the strongest unweighted-fusion baseline and by 8.1 points over content-only classification. An ablation study confirms that independence weighting contributes the largest incremental gain, consistent with CI theory.
Future work will extend the framework in three directions: (i) evaluation on political-news datasets such as the PolitiFact split of FakeNewsNet and on multilingual corpora, including Vietnamese-language misinformation collected during the 2024–2025 electoral cycles; (ii) more robust reputation modeling based on longitudinal user behavior and coordinated-inauthentic-behavior detection; and (iii) integration of the hybrid genetic consensus algorithms of Dang et al. [8] for multi-class veracity judgments beyond the binary fake/real setting.

Global misinformation, local consequences: conspiracy theory endorsement and a graded association with COVID-19 vaccine refusal across Nigeria

Author: Asaga, Peter Mac; Kroeger, Axel; Yako, Andrew; Makpo, James

Publication info: Asaga, Peter Mac; Kroeger, Axel; Yako, Andrew; Makpo, James. 

https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/global-misinformation-local-consequences/docview/3372465252/se-2?accountid=14696

Abstract: Background Conspiracy theories about COVID-19 vaccines circulated widely during the pandemic, yet their prevalence and association with vaccine refusal in sub-Saharan Africa remain poorly quantified. Understanding how global misinformation narratives shape vaccination acceptance in low- and middle-income settings is relevant to future pandemic preparedness. Methods We conducted a cross-sectional survey between October 2023 and April 2024, recruiting 870 adults through convenience sampling across Nigeria's six geopolitical regions. COVID-19 vaccines had been available in the country since 2021, but national uptake remained low throughout this period. Structured face-to-face interviews assessed vaccine intentions, endorsement of specific conspiracy beliefs, information sources, and trust networks. Multivariable logistic regression identified factors independently associated with conspiracy endorsement and vaccine refusal. Results Of 870 participants, 742 (85.3%) were vaccine-hesitant, and 89.4% of these endorsed at least one conspiracy theory. Microchip or tracking device theories were the most frequently cited concern (32.1%). Overall vaccine acceptance was 14.7%. A graded inverse association was observed: each additional conspiracy theory endorsed was associated with an average 69% lower odds of vaccine acceptance (aOR 0.31, 95% CI 0.25–0.39; p for trend <0.001). In multivariable analysis, conspiracy endorsement was the factor most strongly associated with refusal (aOR 0.11, 95% CI 0.06–0.21). Its inclusion in the model substantially attenuated the coefficients for education and region, which suggests that these sociodemographic associations with refusal may be partly accounted for by differential conspiracy endorsement. Conclusions COVID-19 vaccine conspiracy theories were widespread in Nigerian communities well into the national vaccination campaign, at a time of persistently low uptake, and represented the factor most strongly associated with refusal. The graded association between conspiracy endorsement and refusal, and the attenuation of sociodemographic predictors after adjustment for conspiracy beliefs, suggest that counter-misinformation strategies could be a high-yield component of future pandemic vaccine campaigns.

Full text: 1 Introduction
Vaccine hesitancy has been recognised by the World Health Organization as one of the ten leading threats to global health, and the COVID-19 pandemic brought this challenge into sharp focus [1] . Among the factors associated with refusal, conspiracy theories, that is, claims that vaccines contain microchips, alter human DNA, or serve as instruments of population surveillance, achieved unprecedented global reach during 2020 and 2021, complicating immunisation efforts across diverse cultural settings [2,3] . Systematic analyses identified recurring conspiracy narratives that transcended national boundaries, suggesting both coordinated disinformation campaigns and organic rumour amplification through social networks [4,5] .
The microchip conspiracy theory, which posits that COVID-19 vaccines contain electronic surveillance technology, emerged in early 2020 and has been documented in North America, Europe, and parts of Asia [6,7] . Research on such narratives in African contexts remains comparatively sparse, despite the continent's vulnerability to delayed vaccination campaigns [8] . Nigeria offers a cautionary historical parallel: the boycott of polio vaccination campaigns in several northern states during 2003 and 2004, fuelled by conspiracy theories concerning vaccine safety and Western motives, led to polio resurgence and international spread to previously polio-free countries [9] .
Sub-Saharan Africa presents distinctive characteristics for studying misinformation and health decision-making. Rapid mobile technology adoption alongside persistent gaps in digital literacy has created information environments in which traditional media, social networks, and interpersonal communication intersect in ways that may differ from high-income settings [10] . Trust networks, including family members, religious leaders, and community authorities, play a central role in shaping health decisions [11,12] .
With over 218 million inhabitants and marked cultural, linguistic, and religious diversity, Nigeria provides a critical setting for examining how global misinformation narratives interact with local information ecosystems [13,14] . This study investigates the prevalence, correlates, and association with vaccine refusal of specific COVID-19 conspiracy theories among diverse Nigerian populations at a time of low vaccine uptake. Our objectives were to quantify the prevalence of specific conspiracy beliefs among vaccine-hesitant individuals, to identify demographic and behavioural factors associated with endorsement, to examine the relationship between information sources and conspiracy adoption, and to assess the independent association between conspiracy beliefs and vaccination intentions after adjustment for sociodemographic confounders.
2 Methods
2.1 Study design and setting
We conducted a cross-sectional survey between 2 October 2023 and 30 April 2024 to investigate conspiracy theory beliefs and their relationship with vaccination intentions. Although COVID-19 vaccines had been available in Nigeria since March 2021, national coverage remained low when these data were collected, with only a minority of adults fully vaccinated [15] . The survey therefore captured stated intentions and conspiracy beliefs in a setting of persistently low uptake, rather than before any vaccine was available. We framed the primary outcome question hypothetically, as set out below, so that willingness could be gauged independently of local supply or access on the day of interview.
Convenience sampling was employed across Nigeria's six geopolitical regions (Northwest, Northeast, North Central, Southeast, South-South, Southwest). Within each region, we selected urban centres, rural communities, and informal settlements where safe data collection could be conducted. Local research coordinators identified sites on the basis of accessibility, security, and community willingness to participate. At least one urban centre, one rural community, and one informal settlement were sampled in every region. Within each site, research assistants approached prospective participants in public and community settings, including markets, motor parks, places of worship, primary healthcare centres, and residential streets, on weekdays and weekends and during daytime and early-evening hours. We applied no fixed demographic quotas. To limit selection bias, recruitment locations and times were varied within each site, and assistants approached successive eligible adults as footfall allowed rather than selecting people by appearance or apparent attitude.
2.2 Participants
Eligible participants were adults aged 18–70 years who had resided in the study area for at least six months and could provide informed consent in English or a local language. We excluded individuals with severe mental illness precluding consent, those with acute illness, and temporary visitors. Our target of approximately 145 participants per region (total 870) was determined by practical constraints rather than by formal power calculations. Of approximately 1134 eligible adults approached, 870 completed the interview, giving an overall response rate of 76.7%. The remaining 264 individuals (23.3%) declined or did not complete the interview. We calculated the response rate as the number of completed interviews divided by the number of eligible adults approached. Response rates by participant subgroup are reported in Table 1 .
2.3 Data collection
Trained research assistants conducted face-to-face structured interviews lasting 35 to 40 min. All interviewers completed 20 h of training covering interview techniques, ethical considerations, and neutral ways of discussing conspiracy beliefs. Quality assurance comprised daily data review, supervisor observation of 15% of interviews, and re-interviews of 3% of participants. Interviews were conducted in English or, where the participant preferred, in Hausa, Yoruba, Igbo, or Nigerian Pidgin. The English instrument was translated into each local language by bilingual research assistants and then independently back translated into English; the project team reconciled any discrepancies by consensus before fieldwork began.
2.4 Measurements
We assessed specific COVID-19 vaccine conspiracy theories using items adapted from published conspiracy belief measures [6,16] and from a content analysis of misinformation narratives circulating during 2020 and 2021 [17] . Categories assessed included beliefs that vaccines contain electronic surveillance technology, theories about fertility reduction, genetic modification claims, religious or eschatological theories framing vaccines as the “mark of the beast”, and economic exploitation theories. For each category, participants indicated their level of agreement on a five-point scale. We created binary variables comparing believers (the two agreement categories) with non-believers (the two disagreement categories), and analysed uncertain responses separately. Three subject experts reviewed the draft instrument for content validity. We then pilot tested it with 30 adults across two regions who were not included in the final sample, and made minor wording changes in response. The six-item conspiracy belief scale showed acceptable internal consistency (Cronbach's α = 0.79).
The primary outcome was COVID-19 vaccine acceptance: “If a COVID-19 vaccine were available to you today that had been approved by Nigerian health authorities, would you take it?” (Yes, No, or Unsure). We also recorded each participant's primary source of COVID-19 information and the source that the participant felt had most influenced their health decisions.
2.5 Statistical analysis
Prevalence estimates with 95% confidence intervals were calculated for each conspiracy theory. Associations between conspiracy beliefs and demographic characteristics were examined using chi-square tests and logistic regression [18] .
We conducted two multivariable logistic regression analyses. Model A examined predictors of conspiracy theory endorsement. Model B examined predictors of vaccine acceptance, entering the same demographic and contextual covariates together with conspiracy endorsement (as both a binary variable and an ordinal count, in separate specifications). To assess whether conspiracy endorsement might account for part of the observed associations between sociodemographic factors and vaccine refusal, we compared the coefficients for education, region, and information source between models with and without conspiracy endorsement, using a change-in-estimate approach. Interaction terms between conspiracy endorsement and region, and between conspiracy endorsement and education, were tested in Model B. Item-level missing data were uncommon, affecting less than 3% of responses for every variable. We analysed complete cases in the regression models and did not impute missing values.
Population-weighted estimates were derived using post-stratification weights based on 2018 Nigeria Demographic and Health Survey data for educational attainment and urban and rural distribution [13] . All analyses were conducted in Stata 17.0, with statistical significance set at α = 0.05.
2.6 Ethical considerations
The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the University of Freiburg (Protocol No. 140/19) and by the Nasarawa State University, Keffi Ethics Committee. All participants provided written informed consent.
3 Results
3.1 Participant characteristics
We completed interviews with 870 participants across all six regions ( Table 1 ). Participants were predominantly female (71.1%), highly educated (60.4% tertiary), and employed in the civil service (92.5%), with a mean age of 32.4 years (SD 9.7). Television was the dominant information source (82.0%), followed by social networks (17.9%).
3.2 Vaccine acceptance and conspiracy theory prevalence
Overall vaccine acceptance was 14.7% (128/870). Among the 742 vaccine-hesitant participants, 89.4% (95% CI 87.1–91.4%) endorsed at least one conspiracy theory [16] . Microchip theories were the most frequently cited belief (32.1%; Table 2 ). Population-weighted estimates were consistently higher than the crude figs. [19] .
3.3 Predictors of conspiracy theory endorsement (Model A)
Women endorsed microchip theories at higher rates than men (30.0% vs 20.7%; p  = 0.005). Lower education and rural residence were associated with greater endorsement (Supplementary Table S1; Fig. 1 ). Social network use as a primary information source showed the strongest association (aOR 3.12; 95% CI 1.98–4.91). The seven predictors collectively accounted for an estimated 40.2% of the population attributable risk [20,21] .
3.4 Graded association between conspiracy endorsement and vaccine refusal
Vaccine acceptance declined stepwise as the number of endorsed theories rose, from 24.1% among those endorsing none to 0% among those endorsing four or more (p for trend <0.001; Table 3 ; Fig. 2 ). In the ordinal logistic model, each additional theory was associated with an average 69% lower odds of acceptance (aOR 0.31; 95% CI 0.25–0.39). The decline was steepest between zero and one theory and flattened at higher counts ( Fig. 2 ), so this per-theory figure should be read as an average across the range rather than as a constant step. Acceptance reached only 24.1% even among participants who endorsed no conspiracy theory, which indicates that much of the refusal in this sample was associated with factors other than the conspiracy beliefs we measured. Among microchip theory endorsers, acceptance was 2.9%, compared with 24.1% among non-endorsers (OR 0.10; 95% CI 0.05–0.22) [22] .
3.5 Predictors of vaccine acceptance before and after adjustment for conspiracy endorsement (Model B)
Before adding conspiracy endorsement to the model, we examined sociodemographic and contextual predictors of vaccine acceptance on their own. In this demographics-only model, lower education, rural or informal residence, residence in the northern regions, lower government trust, and reliance on non-healthcare information sources were each associated with lower acceptance. When conspiracy endorsement was then entered, several of these associations were attenuated, which suggests that conspiracy beliefs accounted for part, though not all, of the sociodemographic pattern in refusal.
Conspiracy endorsement was the factor most strongly associated with vaccine refusal among the variables we modelled: participants endorsing any conspiracy theory had 89% lower odds of acceptance (aOR 0.11; 95% CI 0.06–0.21; p  < 0.001; Table 4 ). When entered as an ordinal variable, each additional theory was associated with 69% lower odds (aOR 0.31; 95% CI 0.25–0.39).
Including conspiracy endorsement in Model B produced notable changes in the other coefficients. The association between education and vaccine acceptance, significant in unadjusted analysis, was attenuated (aOR 1.78; 95% CI 1.08–2.93; p  = 0.024). The regional effect became non-significant (aOR 0.68; 95% CI 0.40–1.15; p  = 0.152). This pattern of attenuation suggests that the associations between these sociodemographic factors and vaccine refusal may be partly accounted for by differential conspiracy endorsement, although the cross-sectional design precludes establishing the temporal sequence required for formal causal inference. Government trust retained an independent association (aOR 1.89; 95% CI 1.18–3.03; p  = 0.008), which suggests that institutional trust relates to vaccine acceptance through pathways not fully captured by conspiracy beliefs [5,23] .
3.6 Interaction analyses
The conspiracy endorsement by region interaction was not significant ( p  = 0.34), which indicates that the association between conspiracy beliefs and refusal was broadly consistent across regions. The conspiracy by education interaction also did not reach significance ( p  = 0.19). These null findings should be interpreted cautiously given possible underpowering.
3.7 Information sources and decision-making influence
Television dominated reported information consumption, yet the sources that acceptors said had shaped their decision were different ( Table 5 ; Fig. 3 ). When asked what most influenced their choice, vaccine acceptors most often cited their own judgement (54.7%), whereas government sources were named by a single respondent (0.8%) [24,25] . Because both information exposure and decision influence were self-reported and recorded at a single time point, the contrast between the two panels of Fig. 3 should be read as a descriptive association rather than as evidence that any source caused, or failed to cause, a given decision. A respondent could, for example, rely on television for information and still describe the final choice as a matter of personal judgement.
3.8 Regional variations
A consistent gradient from north to south was seen in both conspiracy endorsement and vaccine acceptance ( Table 6 ; Fig. 4 ). The Northwest had the highest endorsement (78.6%) and the lowest acceptance (7.6%), and the Southwest had the lowest endorsement (45.9%) and the highest acceptance (24.7%; p for trend <0.001) [26] . This gradient was consistent across all specific conspiracy types ( Fig. 4 ).
4 Discussion
This study documents widespread endorsement of COVID-19 vaccine conspiracy theories among Nigerian communities at a time of low vaccine uptake. Nearly one third of vaccine-hesitant participants cited microchip or tracking device theories as their main concern, and 89.4% endorsed at least one conspiracy theory, so conspiracy belief was common among those who declined the vaccine. We did not measure conventional concerns, such as doubts about safety, fear of side effects, or problems of access, and we therefore cannot say whether misinformation outweighed these more familiar barriers. The high refusal seen even among participants who endorsed no conspiracy theory, where acceptance reached only 24.1%, suggests that such concerns were also at work [27] .
4.1 Comparison with existing evidence
These findings are consistent with evidence from across sub-Saharan Africa. Multi-country studies have identified trust in government and society as key correlates of vaccine hesitancy, with conspiracy theories serving as consistent associated factors [28–30] . In Ghana, an audio drama intervention showed promise in countering specific misinformation narratives [31] . South African research has documented similar patterns of microchip conspiracy endorsement [32] . Qualitative work from Nigeria by Wonodi and colleagues identified overlapping conspiracy themes but could not quantify their prevalence or assess their independent association with vaccine refusal [33] . Our study extends this evidence in two respects: it quantifies the graded association between the number of conspiracy theories endorsed and vaccine refusal, and it shows, through a change-in-estimate approach, that the associations between sociodemographic factors and refusal are substantially attenuated after accounting for conspiracy endorsement [34] . Our crude acceptance figure of 14.7% sits below the pooled estimates reported for many low- and middle-income settings, where stated willingness was often higher even where hesitancy was substantial [4,23] . Surveys from West Africa have likewise reported high hesitancy alongside low institutional trust [35] , and Nigerian studies of healthcare workers and the general population have described comparable unease [36,37] .
4.2 Information ecosystems and trust networks
Government sources were almost entirely absent from the decision influences that acceptors reported (0.8%; Fig. 3 ). The gap between what people consumed, largely television, and what they said had shaped their decision, largely personal judgement and religious leaders, points to a possible weakness in formal health communication, although it rests on self-report [23] . Social network use was strongly associated with conspiracy endorsement (aOR 3.12), and the association between social network use and vaccine refusal was attenuated after adjustment for conspiracy beliefs. One reading is that misinformation may reach decision-making mainly through interpersonal networks rather than through direct digital exposure [38] , but the cross-sectional data cannot establish that sequence.
Religious leaders were named by a measurable share of acceptors (18.0%), yet religious attendance was simultaneously associated with higher conspiracy endorsement [36,37] . This dual role complicates straightforward prescriptions about engaging faith-based networks.
4.3 Regional patterns
The gradient from north to south ( Fig. 4 ) probably reflects historical tensions between northern communities and federal health initiatives, including the 2003 and 2004 polio boycott, alongside differences in educational attainment [9] . That the gradient held across all five conspiracy types suggests generalised susceptibility rather than selective adoption of particular narratives. The apparent association between Muslim identity and higher conspiracy endorsement (41.2% vs 28.7%) was substantially attenuated after adjustment for region and education, which suggests demographic confounding.
4.4 Implications
The specificity of conspiracy beliefs offers practical entry points for intervention. Rather than generic vaccine education, programmes could address particular false claims with targeted counter-narratives delivered through trusted interpersonal channels [35,39,40] . The comparatively low conspiracy endorsement among participants who received information from healthcare providers (16.7% vs 67.3% for social network users), together with the independent protective association in Model B, offers tentative support for healthcare engagement as a protective factor, although the numbers were small.
Several directions for further research follow from these findings. The graded association we describe should be tested with longitudinal designs that record conspiracy beliefs before a vaccination decision is made, which would help to separate belief from rationalisation after the fact. A validated, locally developed conspiracy belief scale would allow comparison across studies and over time. Trials that pair specific counter-narratives with trusted messengers, rather than generic education, would show whether addressing named claims changes uptake, and the audio drama work from Ghana offers one tested format [31,34] .
For prevention, the pattern of results points away from broad government messaging and towards prebunking, that is, inoculating audiences against specific false claims before they spread, delivered through the channels people actually trust [14,17] . Because endorsement clustered by region, education, and information source, campaigns could be targeted rather than uniform, with the heaviest investment in the northern regions, where endorsement was highest and acceptance lowest.
For policy and pandemic preparedness, the near-absence of government sources among the reported decision influences is a warning. Health authorities may need to work through religious and community leaders, and through primary care, rather than relying on official channels alone, while recognising that faith networks can carry both helpful and harmful messages. Misinformation surveillance, built into routine immunisation monitoring, would let programmes detect and answer emerging claims before the next campaign.
4.5 Limitations
The most consequential limitation is convenience sampling, which yielded a sample skewed towards educated, urban, female civil servants. This likely underestimates conspiracy prevalence, since the over-represented characteristics were associated with lower endorsement. Post-stratification weighting partially addresses, but cannot fully compensate for, this bias. Although the conspiracy assessment instrument was pilot tested and showed acceptable internal consistency, it has not undergone full psychometric validation. The cross-sectional design precludes causal inference: the change-in-estimate findings are consistent with conspiracy beliefs lying on a pathway between sociodemographic factors and vaccine refusal, but alternative explanations, including reverse causation and unmeasured confounding of the conspiracy and refusal relationship, cannot be excluded. Interaction analyses may have been underpowered. Data were collected several years into the pandemic, when vaccines were available but uptake was low, so the attitudes recorded reflect that particular period and may since have shifted. We did not measure conventional barriers to vaccination, such as concerns about safety, side effects, cost, or access, so we cannot weigh misinformation against these factors; the high refusal among participants who endorsed no conspiracy theory shows that such barriers were present. Finally, information sources and decision influences were self-reported, and self-report cannot establish that any source did, or did not, drive a decision.
5 Conclusions
COVID-19 vaccine conspiracy theories were widespread in Nigerian communities at a time of low vaccine uptake, with microchip theories the most frequently cited concern. The graded inverse association between the number of theories endorsed and vaccine acceptance, together with the attenuation of sociodemographic predictors after adjustment for conspiracy beliefs, identifies conspiracy endorsement as both a cumulative correlate of refusal and a potential point of intervention.
The gap between formal health communication and the influences people reported points to structural weaknesses that are likely to recur with future pandemic vaccines. Whilst convenience sampling limits generalisability, the consistency of findings across regions, and the convergence with evidence from other African countries, suggests that conspiracy-associated vaccine refusal is not uniquely Nigerian. Future preparedness must address health misinformation with the same seriousness as the pathogens themselves.

A Comparative Analysis of Evolutionary Metaheuristics: Genetic Algorithm vs. Particle Swarm Optimization for Feature Selection in High-Accuracy Fake News Detection

Author: Garg, Nikita1; Pritam Singh Negi11 Department of Computer Science & Engineering, HNB Garhwal University (A Central University), Srinagar Garhwal- 246 174, Uttarakhand, India

Publication info: Garg, Nikita; Pritam Singh Negi. 

https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/comparative-analysis-evolutionary-metaheuristics/docview/3371318715/se-2?accountid=14696

Abstract: The proliferation of online misinformation demands the development of highly accurate and computationally efficient automated systems for Fake News Detection. A primary impediment to system performance is the high dimensionality of textual features derived from techniques like TF-IDF, making optimal Feature Selection a critical step. This paper presents a detailed comparative experimental study of two prominent bio-inspired evolutionary metaheuristics, the Genetic Algorithm (GA) and Particle Swarm Optimisation (PSO) used as wrapper-based FS techniques for FND. The methodologies were rigorously tested across two distinct textual datasets: the complex, large-scale FakeNewsNet corpus and a moderate-scale general news dataset. The feature sets, once optimised, were evaluated using six standard Machine Learning (ML) classifiers. The GA-based FS approach, emphasising global exploration, achieved state-of-the-art accuracy of 99.91% with the Random Forest classifier on the FakeNewsNet dataset. In contrast, the PSO-based FS approach, valued for its rapid convergence, yielded a maximum accuracy of 93.29% with the Support Vector Machine (SVM) on the general news dataset. This analysis provides empirical evidence of the intrinsic trade-off between the algorithms: GA is superior for maximising accuracy in high-dimensional, complex textual spaces, while PSO offers a more efficient and practical solution for resource-constrained or moderate-scale FND tasks. The study confirms that evolutionary computation provides a robust, effective pathway for significantly enhancing ML classifier performance in this critical domain.

Multi-Task BanglaBERT for Joint Sentiment and Fake News Detection in COVID-19 Discourse

Author: Hoque, Arshadul11 Department of Computer Science and Engineering, University of Chittagong, Chittagong, 4331, Bangladesh

Publication info: Hoque, Arshadul. 

https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/multi-task-banglabert-joint-sentiment-fake-news/docview/3371318711/se-2?accountid=14696

Abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic catalyzed an unprecedented surge of misinformation on social media, frequently intertwined with emotionally charged language. Understanding both the sentiment and truthfulness of this content is critical for public health monitoring and misinformation mitigation. However, Bangla—despite being a globally prominent language—remains severely underrepresented in joint sentiment and fake news detection research, with existing studies largely restricted to single-task settings. To bridge this gap, this paper proposes a novel multi-task BanglaBERT-based framework for the simultaneous classification of sentiment and truthfulness in COVID-19 discourse. Furthermore, we introduce the first publicly available, dual-annotated Bangla corpus for this domain, comprising 35,526 textual samples aggregated from social media and news sources. Our architecture employs a shared BanglaBERT encoder with dual task-specific heads, optimized using a task-prioritized loss function that combines modified Focal Loss and weighted cross-entropy to address inherent class imbalances. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed model achieves 75.1% accuracy (Macro F1: 0.707) for sentiment classification and 88.0% accuracy (Macro F1: 0.851) for truthfulness detection. Ablation studies and error analyses confirm that our tailored loss strategies significantly enhance the recognition of underrepresented and semantically ambiguous classes, particularly neutral sentiments. By releasing our dataset, code, trained models, and a Gradio-based interactive demo, this work establishes a robust benchmark for multi-task learning in low-resource Bangla NLP and provides a practical tool for fact-checking during health crises.

An NLP-Based Framework for Fake News Detection Using Contextual and Engineered Features in Communication Technologies

Author: SGopalakrishnan1; Thangamalar, JBabitha2; Sheela, M Sahaya3; M Mohammed Mustafa4; Babu, Bindu5; Madasamy, NSenthil61 Department of Electronics and Communication and Engineering, Saveetha School of Engineering, Saveetha Institute of Medical and Technical Sciences (SIMATS), Thandalam, Chennai-602105, Tamil Nadu, India2 Department of Biomedical Engineering, P S R Engineering College, Sivakasi-626140, Tamil Nadu, India3 Department of Electronics and Communication Engineering, Vel Tech Rangarajan DrSagunthala R & D Institute of Science and Technology Chennai, Tamil Nadu, 600062, India4 Department of Artificial Intelligence & Data Science, Sri Eshwar College of Engineering, Coimbatore, Tamil Nadu, India5 Department of Electronics and Communication Engineering, Easwari Engineering College, Chennai- 600 089, Tamil Nadu, India6 Department of Computer Science and Engineering, DrMahalingam College of Engineering and Technology, Pollachi, Coimbatore - 642003, Tamil Nadu, India

Publication info: SGopalakrishnan; Thangamalar, JBabitha; Sheela, M Sahaya; M Mohammed Mustafa; Babu, Bindu; et al. 

https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/nlp-based-framework-fake-news-detection-using/docview/3371318700/se-2?accountid=14696

Abstract: Fake news detection focuses on identifying and preventing the spread of misleading or false information. It is crucial for maintaining the integrity of public discourse and protecting individuals from the harmful effects of misinformation. By ensuring the correctness and reliability of the information, the fake news detection hinders the loss of trust in the media, institutions, and public communication channels. The fake news detection system suggested is in the process of data acquisition where news stories are either manually or automatically retrieved from the net via web crawlers. The collected data later filters the information so it will use only credible sources. Phase two consists of the pre-processing phase using BERT, wherein the data will be tokenized and mapped into contextual embeddings that reflect the semantic meaning of words. Phase three is about engineering features using methods like TF-IDF and Word2vec to fine-tune the embeddings and label the important textual features. The final Phase of Classification occurs using the engineered features such that BERT-generated outputs are fine-tuned and passed through softmax functions to ascertain whether the news is fake or real. This holistic and all-encompassing approach integrates advanced natural language processing with feature engineering for an effective system concerning detection of fake news accurately. The model achieved remarkable results over various phases. Training accuracy went from 75% up to those above 95% whereas test accuracy tips above 90%, soaring from below 70%. The model's performance was validated with a balanced confusion matrix and a high ROC AUC of 0.94. Throughout different phases, accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score increased, reaching 97.0%, 96.7%, 96.8%, and 96.9%, respectively, in the final classification phase, demonstrating robust and reliable detection capabilities.

Multilingual Fake News Detection Using Machine Learning with Contextual-Based Feature Extraction

Author: Garg, Nikita1; Pritam Singh Negi11 Department of Computer Science & Engineering, HNB Garhwal University (A Central University), Srinagar Garhwal- 246 174, Uttarakhand, India

Publication info: Garg, Nikita; Pritam Singh Negi. 

https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/multilingual-fake-news-detection-using-machine/docview/3371318699/se-2?accountid=14696

Abstract: Fake news has become a major challenge in today’s digital environment, particularly in languages where labeled data is limited. Most existing research has primarily focused on English due to the easy availability of annotated datasets, whereas low-resource languages such as Bengali remain underexplored. This study presents a multilingual approach for fake news detection using machine learning with contextual-based feature extraction. The proposed method integrates n-gram techniques with sentence-level contextual embeddings to capture both word-level patterns and semantic meaning. Since labeled data is not available for the Bengali dataset, a translation-based strategy is employed, followed by a pseudo-labeling process to assign labels automatically. The models are trained on English news titles and subsequently evaluated on both English and Bengali datasets to examine their cross-lingual effectiveness. The experimental findings indicate that ensemble-based classifiers such as Random Forest and Gradient Boosting achieve reliable performance across both languages. In some cases, the results for Bengali data are comparable or slightly better than those for English. The study demonstrates that effective fake news detection is possible in low-resource languages using short text data without relying on manually labeled datasets. The proposed approach provides a simple and efficient solution for multilingual fake news detection in data-scarce environments.

Models for incorporating counter-disinformation efforts into national security architectures

Author: Tagarev, Todor

Publication info: Tagarev, Todor. 

https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/models-incorporating-counter-disinformation/docview/3399605817/se-2?accountid=14696

Abstract: Disinformation, information influence, and cognitive warfare have become central national security concerns in the digital age. This article examines how democratic countries incorporate counter-disinformation efforts into national security architectures while preserving democratic freedoms, media pluralism, accountability, and public trust. It develops an analytical framework based on actor and task taxonomies, six conceptual institutional models, five governance dimensions, and national profiles of the Czech Republic, Estonia, Finland, France, Israel, Latvia, Lithuania, Norway, Poland, Romania, Sweden, Taiwan, Ukraine, the United Kingdom, and the United States. The study shows that democratic states do not converge toward a single model for countering disinformation. Instead, they organize counter-disinformation ecosystems through different combinations of distributed governmental coordination, specialized interagency mechanisms, dedicated agencies, embedded security functions, public-private partnerships, and societal or externally implemented arrangements. The article maps these approaches across five dimensions: centralization, specialization, obligations on non-state actors, enforcement orientation, and security-resilience framing. The findings suggest that national architectures are shaped not only by threat intensity but also by strategic culture, institutional inheritance, legal constraints, democratic norms, and state-society relations. The article contributes to research on disinformation, hybrid threats, democratic resilience, strategic communication, governance models, and institutional design by shifting attention from the content and effects of information to the organization of national response ecosystems. It also offers policymakers a framework for identifying design options and trade-offs suitable for democratic societies.

Full text: 1 Introduction
When able to attack, we must seem unable; when using our forces, we must seem inactive; when we are near, we must make the enemy believe we are far away; when far away, we must make him believe we are near . Sun Tzu, The Art of War (1910, ch. 1, para. 19).
The use of deception, manipulation, and influence in conflict is as old as war. Yet, the expansion of digital communication ecosystems, social media platforms, algorithmic amplification, and artificial intelligence has fundamentally transformed the scale, speed, reach, and societal impact of informational influence. Contemporary information influence operations are no longer limited to supporting kinetic military campaigns. Increasingly, they are employed independently to shape perceptions of both decision makers and citizens, polarize societies, undermine trust in democratic institutions, influence electoral decisions, weaken alliances, and achieve strategic objectives and political ends without direct military confrontation.
Recent Russian practice illustrates this transformation.Armașu (2025)describes a Russian “5D strategy” that dismisses, distorts, distracts, dismays, and divides target audiences. Such campaigns aim not to persuade but to create confusion, mistrust, polarization, and institutional paralysis. Similar patterns appear in operations targeting elections, public responses during the COVID-19 pandemic, and support for Ukraine after 2022. Chinese information influence aimed at democratic societies, including Taiwan, has combined political messaging, social media amplification, economic pressure, and cognitive techniques (Cole, 2020;Zhang, 2020), while Iran has used disinformation and influence operations against regional rivals, diaspora communities, and Western audiences (Tabatabai, 2020).
The Romanian presidential elections at the end of 2024 provide a recent example.Spinu (2025)shows how coordinated disinformation and foreign interference targeting the Romanian political process demonstrated both the sophistication of contemporary information operations and the vulnerability of democratic institutions.
Conceptual debates distinguish among misinformation, disinformation, and malinformation. Misinformation is false information shared without harmful intent; disinformation is deliberately false or misleading information disseminated to cause harm or achieve strategic objectives; and malinformation is genuine information used maliciously, often by taking facts out of context (Wardle and Derakhshan, 2017). The broader public discussion often uses the term “fake news,” though that term captures only part of the broader spectrum of manipulative information techniques. For brevity, this article uses the term “disinformation” to refer broadly to manipulative information-influence activities, and “counter-disinformation” to describe institutional responses to them.
Democratic approaches differ fundamentally from authoritarian information control. Russia, China, and Iran increasingly frame control over information as a matter of regime security, political sovereignty, and social stability rather than primarily as protection of democratic institutions or societal resilience. Russia’s 2000 Information Security Doctrine identified threats such as “the illegal use of special means to influence individual, group and public consciousness,” “the devaluation of spiritual values,” and “the decline in the spiritual, moral and creative potential of the population of Russia” (Security Council of the Russian Federation, 2000). Subsequent Russian strategic documents further expanded state-centered approaches to informational control, including the development of the so-called “sovereign internet,” restrictions on independent media, criminalization of online speech contradicting official narratives, and broader efforts to strengthen centralized state control over digital communication infrastructures (Soldatov and Borogan, 2015;Darczewska, 2014;Giles, 2016). Recent assessments indicate that Russia has continued to intensify digital censorship, online surveillance, and restrictions on evasion technologies such as VPNs (Freedom House, 2024).
China’s “cyber sovereignty” similarly combines censorship, platform regulation, algorithmic control, surveillance, and coordinated information management within a broader political-security framework (MacKinnon, 2012;Economy, 2018;Creemers, 2020;Su and Zhang, 2025). Recent assessments similarly emphasize the continued strengthening of centralized political control, information regulation, and technological self-sufficiency within China’s broader security architecture (Bertelsmann Stiftung, 2026).
Iranian approaches also combine online surveillance, censorship, cyber operations, and suppression of dissent as instruments of ideological control and regime protection. Iranian authorities have repeatedly restricted access to digital platforms, developed national information network initiatives, and used cyber and information operations both domestically and externally in pursuit of strategic objectives (Rahimi, 2016;Tabatabai, 2020). Iran develops its National Information Network as a mechanism of achieving digital sovereignty while strengthening state control over internal information environments and online communication (Pour, 2025).
These approaches differ fundamentally from democratic governance and remain outside the scope of this study. Democracies face a more complex challenge, i.e., how to counter malicious information influence while simultaneously preserving freedom of expression, media pluralism, democratic accountability, political competition, and public trust. Excessively centralized or coercive responses may undermine democratic legitimacy and resilience. Consequently, democratic counter-disinformation architectures must balance security imperatives with constitutional rights, the rule of law, and broader democratic norms.
From a policymaking perspective, this raises several governance questions: Which actors participate in national counter-disinformation efforts? What functions do they perform? How are tasks distributed among government, private actors, media, academia, and civil society? What coordination mechanisms integrate these activities into national security architectures? These questions shape debates on strategic communication (Zhao and Johansen, 2026), democratic resilience (Tagarev and Fluri, 2025), foreign information manipulation and interference (European External Action Service, 2023), hybrid threats (Wither, 2023), and capability development (Pamment, 2022).
Existing scholarship remains fragmented. Much work examines the technological, political, psychological, and societal dimensions of disinformation (Wardle and Derakhshan, 2017;Bennett and Livingston, 2018;Bradshaw and Howard, 2019). Other strands address strategic communication, hybrid threats, information warfare, cognitive warfare, resilience, cybersecurity, and democratic vulnerability (Paul and Matthews, 2016;Helmus et al., 2018;Rid, 2020;Wither, 2023). Less attention has been paid to how democratic states organize counter-disinformation efforts within national security architectures.
Comparative institutional analysis is particularly underdeveloped: existing studies rarely examine how democracies distribute responsibilities, coordinate state and non-state actors, and allocate counter-disinformation tasks within broader security and governance frameworks. This article addresses that gap by mapping models for incorporating counter-disinformation into democratic national security architectures. Rather than seeking one optimal arrangement, it designs an exploration space and maps governance modalities onto it. The central premise is that democracies do not converge toward one universal model; instead, they develop varying governance approaches shaped by strategic culture, institutional traditions, threat environments, and state-society relations.
The article contributes a comparative framework, actor and task taxonomies, six conceptual institutional models, and a five-dimensional governance space for analyzing democratic counter-disinformation architectures. The remainder of the article proceeds as follows. The next section outlines the methodological approach and explains the development of the analytical framework. The Results section presents the securitization trend, the actor and task taxonomies, policy and governance frameworks, six notional institutional models, the exploratory governance space, and selected national profiles. The Discussion section examines broader governance implications, limitations, and future research. The Conclusion summarizes the findings and reflects on their relevance for policymakers and researchers.
2 Methods
This study adopts a structured qualitative comparative approach to examine how democratic countries incorporate counter-disinformation efforts into national security architectures. It does not seek an optimal institutional arrangement; instead, it explores governance modalities through conceptual model construction, comparative institutional analysis, qualitative coding, and exploratory mapping of 15 national profiles.
The study first explores more than 14,000 publications and analytical reports addressing responses to disinformation, misinformation, malinformation, information influence, hybrid threats, strategic communication, resilience, cybersecurity, and related issues. The corpus showed a growing share of publications linking disinformation to national security, suggesting the securitization of information influence in academic, policy, and strategic discourse.
Securitization, associated with the Copenhagen School, describes processes by which political actors frame issues as existential security threats requiring exceptional attention and policy responses (Buzan et al., 1998). This article does not aim to analyze the securitization discourse, but uses this trend as contextual evidence for a turn toward exploring institutional and governance modalities.
The analysis proceeded in three stages. First, it developed six conceptual institutional models relying primarily on: distributed governmental coordination; specialized inter-ministerial 1 coordination; a dedicated counter-disinformation agency; embedding the counter-disinformation function within broader security, cybersecurity, psychological defense, or hybrid-threat institutions; public-private partnership arrangements; and externally implemented or societal models involving academia, civil society, and business actors. In practice, countries often combine elements from several models.
Second, the study constructed an exploratory governance space along five dimensions: centralization; specialization; mandatory versus voluntary participation of non-state actors; enforcement versus compliance- and resilience-oriented approaches; and security-centric versus resilience-centric framing. These dimensions provide a structure for comparing national counter-disinformation architectures in democratic countries.
Third, the study purposively selected fifteen democratic cases that span the exploration space: Finland, Sweden, Norway, Estonia, Lithuania, Latvia, Czechia, Poland, Romania, the United Kingdom, the United States, France, Ukraine, Taiwan, and Israel. All these countries have approached counter-disinformation as an important policy issue, and respective documents are publically available. The selection reflects variation in strategic culture, threat exposure, governance traditions, geopolitical context, and approaches to information influence.
To support comparison, the study developed two-level taxonomies of actors and tasks involved in counter-disinformation governance. The initial structure emerged from the publication corpus and was refined through policy documents, institutional mandates, governmental strategies, and analytical reports from national governments, NATO, the European Union, ENISA, the NATO Strategic Communications Centre of Excellence, the European Centre of Excellence for Countering Hybrid Threats, think-tanks like RAND, HCSS, CSIS, and related institutions. This refinement added detail on coordination, hybrid-threat governance, psychological defense, foreign information manipulation and interference, resilience, and strategic foresight, following iterative taxonomy-design methods (Nickerson et al., 2013).
Country profiles were coded through structured qualitative assessment rather than automated scoring. Publicly available policy documents, strategies, mandates, official statements, and analytical reports were reviewed to identify host frameworks, institutional arrangements, coordination mechanisms, actor roles, and functional responsibilities. Countries were then positioned along five ordinal dimensions. Scores from 1 to 5, including intermediate values where necessary, indicate relative positioning within the exploratory governance space rather than precise measurement; they serve as interpretive devices for comparison and visualization.
The approach reflects the study’s conceptual and exploratory character. It maps formal and declared governance architectures rather than implementation effectiveness. Informal coordination, classified practices, and implementation gaps are acknowledged as important but remain outside the scope of this article.
3 Results
3.1 Securitization of disinformation and information influence
Over the last decade, disinformation and related manipulation techniques have increasingly been examined not only as communication, media, or technological challenges, but also as issues of national security, democratic stability, and societal resilience. This shift reflects concern about hostile information operations, electoral interference, hybrid threats, manipulation of digital platforms and large language models, and information influence as an instrument of geopolitical competition below the threshold of conventional warfare.
To examine whether this development is reflected in the academic literature, the author conducted a bibliometric exploration of publications indexed in Scopus as of May 19, 2026. Using the search string ( disinformation OR mis-information OR misinformation OR malinformation OR mal-information ), the search identified 38,136 publications addressing disinformation-related issues. Narrowing the search to publications addressing responses to disinformation through the additional terms ( counter OR response ) reduced the corpus to 14,255 publications (included asSupplementary material S1). A further search combining these terms with “national security” identified 1,194 publications that explicitly link counter-disinformation to national security concerns.
While these publications still represent a small portion of the broader disinformation literature, their relative share increased substantially over time. As illustrated inFigure 1, the percentage of publications connecting counter-disinformation and national security more than tripled from the early 2010s till 2025. The trend is not strictly linear, but the overall direction is clear: studies examining responses to disinformation have increasingly migrated toward a security-oriented conceptualization and governance frameworks.
[Image Omitted: See PDF]
This development may be interpreted through securitization theory (Buzan et al., 1998). Issues previously treated mainly as public communication, media ethics, or information-quality concerns are increasingly framed as threats to democratic institutions, electoral integrity, social cohesion, critical infrastructure, and national sovereignty. At the policy level, this shift has incorporated disinformation into frameworks such as hybrid threats, cybersecurity, strategic communication, total defense, psychological defense, societal resilience, or foreign information manipulation and interference.
Notably, the growing securitization of disinformation did not produce convergence toward a single institutional response model. Democratic countries differ substantially in how they define the problem, distribute responsibilities, coordinate actors, and integrate governmental and non-governmental participation while balancing security and civil liberties. The increasing securitization of the issue, therefore, strengthened the importance of institutional and governance analysis rather than reducing variation in an attempt to optimize the democratic response to disinflrmation.
3.2 Identifying actors and tasks in counter-disinformation ecosystems
Incorporating the response to disinformation into national security and democratic resilience frameworks raises a practical question: how do democracies organize counter-disinformation ecosystems? Which actors participate, what tasks do they perform, and how are activities coordinated across government, private-sector, media, academic, and civil-society domains? Answering this requires tools that capture institutions, relationships, functional distributions, and governance arrangements.
Flat classifications proved insufficient because counter-disinformation ecosystems involve multiple actors that are, as a rule, multifunctional. The same actor may perform several tasks, while the same task may require a response by multiple institutions. Government communicators may conduct strategic communication, public awareness, interagency coordination, and crisis response; cybersecurity institutions may address hybrid threats, foreign information manipulation, and platform resilience in addition to technical cyber defense.
To address this challenge, the study developed two-level taxonomies of actors and tasks involved in democratic counter-disinformation governance. The initial stable version of the taxonomies emerged from qualitative coding of the 14,255 publications identified through the Scopus search on countering/ responding to disinformation. This literature-based stage emphasized recurring themes, including strategic communication, fact-checking, media literacy, civic resilience, platform governance, democratic protection, and public awareness. It also identified a broad range of participating actors, including governmental institutions, media organizations, digital platforms, civil-society actors, academic institutions, and international organizations.
The subsequent review of national policy documents, strategies, institutional mandates, and governance frameworks revealed that the literature-derived taxonomies did not fully capture the operational and institutional complexity of contemporary counter-disinformation architectures. Policy documents introduced additional categories and distinctions associated with hybrid-threat governance, foreign information manipulation and interference, psychological defense, resilience planning, strategic foresight, interagency coordination, intelligence support, election protection, and integration with cybersecurity and national-security institutions. As a result, the second-stage policy review refined and expanded both taxonomies, particularly at their second levels.
The resulting actor taxonomy includes governmental institutions, security and intelligence structures, defense organizations, regulators, media actors, technology companies, academic and research institutions, civil-society organizations, and international partners. The task taxonomy includes monitoring and detection, analysis and attribution, strategic communication, public awareness, media literacy, platform governance, resilience-building, interagency coordination, operational response, legal and regulatory measures, and international cooperation.
The taxonomies, presented inTables 1and2, are analytical frameworks rather than exhaustive classifications. They provided analytical foundation for examining how democratic countries distribute responsibilities, integrate state and non-state participation, identify recurring institutional patterns, test the six conceptual models, and code national architectures across the five dimensions.

3.3 Policy and governance frameworks for counter-disinformation Counter-disinformation rarely appears as a fully stand-alone policy domain. It is usually embedded in broader policy and governance frameworks that shape how the problem is conceptualized, which actors become central, what tasks are prioritized, and how coordination is organized. This article treats these broader settings as host frameworks: they do not determine institutional design mechanically, but influence the range of plausible governance arrangements.
One important host framework is that of hybrid threats or hybrid influence. In this framing, disinformation is understood as one instrument within broader campaigns that may also involve cyber operations, political interference, economic pressure, intelligence activities, coercive diplomacy, corruption, lawfare, or societal destabilization. This framing usually strengthens the role of national security institutions, interagency coordination, and intelligence-informed analysis. The EU’s concept of foreign information manipulation and interference is closely related, although more specifically focused on exogenous threats and manipulative, intentional, and coordinated behavior in the information environment. FIMI therefore captures information-domain activities that may be part of broader hybrid campaigns without necessarily encompassing the full spectrum of non-informational hybrid tools.
A second group of frameworks links countering disinformation to cybersecurity, digital governance, and platform regulation. Here, the problem is framed partly as a vulnerability of digital infrastructures, online platforms, algorithmic amplification, and data-driven manipulation, involving cybersecurity agencies, platform operators, digital regulators, electoral-security bodies, and technology companies.
A third set emphasizes strategic communication, psychological defense, and democratic or societal resilience. Strategic communication frameworks place government communication and crisis communication near the center of the response. Psychological defense, as in Sweden, links countering disinformation to public morale, cohesion, and free opinion formation. Democratic and societal resilience emphasize media literacy, civic participation, institutional trust, public awareness, and society’s ability to withstand manipulation without excessive state control (Hassain, 2022).
Closely related, but institutionally distinct, are the frameworks of comprehensive security and total defense. Comprehensive security, most closely associated with Finland, integrates authorities, businesses, civil society, and citizens in safeguarding vital societal functions. Total defense, prominent in Nordic and Baltic contexts, emphasizes civil-military cooperation and preparedness across peace, crisis, and war. In both cases, countering disinformation is not treated as a separate function but as part of wider societal preparedness and the continuity of governance.
Host frameworks matter because they shape institutional choices. A hybrid-threat framework may favor interagency security coordination; cybersecurity may elevate the role of platform owners/operators and digital regulators; strategic communication may empower government communicators; psychological defense may justify a specialized agency; and comprehensive-security or total-defense frameworks may favor civil-military collaboration or distributed whole-of-society arrangements.
Thus, the taxonomies identify who may act and what they may do, while policy and governance frameworks help explain why democracies organize actors’ responsibilities and the performance of these tasks differently.
3.4 Institutional models for incorporating counter-disinformation efforts into national security architectures
Six conceptual institutional models were constructed from the actor and task taxonomies and policy-document review. They are theoretical governance constructs, not mutually exclusive empirical categories. Countries frequently combine elements from several models; the purpose is to identify recurring institutional logics and design options rather than rigidly classify each case. The models also serve as anchors allowing to position national architectures in the exploration space.
Model 1: distributed governmental coordination model . Counter-disinformation responsibilities remain distributed across ministries and agencies. At the same time, coordination is carried out through existing national security and cabinet-level structures, such as a National Security Council chaired by the President or the Prime Minister. This model preserves institutional continuity and allows sectoral actors to address disinformation within their areas of responsibility.
Model 2: specialized interagency coordination model . A dedicated coordination council, commission, or counter-disinformation task force brings together senior representatives of relevant ministries and agencies. It may be supported by a permanent administrative unit, often part of the cabinet. This model increases policy coherence without creating a dedicated ministry or a new operational agency.
Model 3: dedicated counter-disinformation agency model . A specialized governmental body performs a substantial share of counter-disinformation tasks and acts as a focal coordination institution. This model can increase visibility, expertise, and operational coherence, but may also generate new organizational rivalries, risks of over-centralization, or politicization if not carefully designed.
Model 4: embedded-function model . Counter-disinformation functions are incorporated into existing institutions with broader mandates, such as cybersecurity, countering hybrid threats, psychological defense, resilience, intelligence, or strategic communication organizations. This model benefits from established institutional capacity but may subordinate counter-disinformation to existing functions.
Model 5: public-private partnership model . Counter-disinformation responsibilities are implemented through structured cooperation among governmental institutions, private actors, platforms, media organizations, academia, and civil society. This model reflects the ecosystem character of the information environment and is particularly relevant where digital platforms and civic actors play central roles.
Model 6: externally implemented or distributed societal model . Counter-disinformation activities are largely carried out by non-governmental actors, such as academic institutions, civic-tech organizations, NGOs, and private organizations, with limited direct governmental involvement. This model may preserve democratic legitimacy and societal ownership, but may also suffer from weak coordination or limited authority.
These models represent institutional modalities rather than complete national systems.Figure 2visualizes them as regions within a governance space structured by centralization and by the balance between state-centered and distributed multi-actor governance. Their positioning in the exploration space is visualized inFigure 2.
