3.5 Constructing the governance exploration space
The six models above provide a conceptual vocabulary for institutional design, but national architectures vary along multiple dimensions. To capture this broader variation, the study constructs an exploratory governance space encompassing five analytical dimensions.
The first dimension is centralization versus decentralization. At one end, coordination and decision-making are concentrated in a central authority, agency, or national-security structure. At the other end, responsibilities are distributed across multiple institutions and sectors with limited central command.
The second dimension is specialized institutions versus distributed responsibilities. Some national systems rely on dedicated agencies, specialized units, or formally mandated bodies. Others embed counter-disinformation functions within existing ministries, communication services, cybersecurity bodies, regulators, media institutions, or civil society networks.
The third dimension is mandatory versus voluntary participation of non-state actors. Democratic counter-disinformation ecosystems cannot be effective without cooperation with platforms, media, academia, civil society, and business actors. The degree to which such participation is legally required, co-regulated, or entirely voluntary may vary considerably.
The fourth dimension is enforcement-oriented versus standards- and resilience-oriented approaches. Some systems emphasize legal measures, sanctions, content restrictions, takedowns, or operational countermeasures. Others prioritize professional standards, non-mandatory compliance with standards and recommended policies, transparency, media literacy, public communication, and societal resilience.
The fifth dimension is security-centric versus resilience-centric framing. Some countries frame disinformation primarily as a national security, hybrid threat, or foreign interference issue. Others emphasize democratic resilience, societal preparedness, civic participation, public trust, and institutional robustness.
These dimensions are not fully independent. Security-centric systems may also be more centralized, specialized, and enforcement-oriented. They are examined separately in this study because they represent different governance choices: a country may increase specialization without coercive enforcement, or strengthen coordination while preserving voluntary societal participation.
3.6 National counter-disinformation architectures
The following profiles apply the models and dimensions to analyze fifteen democratic country cases. The profiles are not intended as exhaustive national studies. Rather, they identify the dominant governance logic, the primary and secondary institutional models, the host frameworks, and the salient features of each case. The scores summarized at the end of this subsection should be read as ordinal qualitative assessments. They indicate relative positioning within the exploratory governance space and are used to support visualization of governance modalities, and not to rank countries.
3.6.1 Finland: comprehensive security and distributed societal resilience
Finland’s profile most clearly represents a resilience-centric, whole-of-society approach to countering disinformation. It is not organized around a dedicated counter-disinformation agency, nor does it treat disinformation mainly as a communication problem. Instead, counter-disinformation functions are embedded within the broader concept of comprehensive security , which serves as an overarching framework for protecting vital societal functions.
Finland’s Security Strategy for Society describes comprehensive security as an operating model in which “the vital functions of society are taken care of in collaboration between the authorities, business community, organisations and citizens” and which forms “the foundation of resilience in Finnish society” (Security Committee, 2025). This core logic of the Finnish model is that security is not produced solely by the state, but through structured cooperation among public institutions, the private sector, civil society organizations, and citizens.
From the perspective of the models developed in section 3.4, Finland corresponds primarily to Model 1, with Model 5 elements, because responsibilities are distributed across public and societal actors and coordinated through established preparedness mechanisms. The strategy “does not define new tasks or responsibilities for actors” but reinforces existing distributed responsibilities; one example is the formation and sharing of situational pictures of broad-based influence (Finnish Defence Forces, 2023).
This model has several implications. First, Finland scores low on centralization: while coordination exists, implementation remains widely distributed. Second, counter-disinformation is not institutionalized as a separate field and, hence, it scores low on specialization. Third, non-state participation is extensive but mainly cooperative and culturally-based, rather than legally binding. Fourth, enforcement is not the dominant logic. The Finnish model emphasizes preparedness, public trust, media literacy, continuity of vital functions, and societal resilience rather than punitive intervention against information actors.
3.6.2 United Kingdom: strategic communication and distributed institutional coordination
The United Kingdom contrasts with Finland. It is not a frontline state and does not rely on comprehensive-security or total-defense concepts. Its approach combines strategic communication, intelligence-informed threat assessment, democratic protection, national resilience, and distributed coordination.
The RESIST framework, issued by the UK Government Communication Service and currently in version 3, is particularly important for understanding this approach. RESIST, a practical framework for building resilience to information threats, is designed to be “adaptive and interoperable” and comprises “a full process for building resilience to information threats” (Government Communication Service, 2025). It guides the response by implementing a six-step process: Recognizing mis- and disinformation, early warning, Situational insight, Impact analysis, Strategic communication, and Tracking effectiveness.
The UK corresponds primarily to Model 1, with Model 2 elements through cross-government structures such as the Defending Democracy Taskforce, which addresses foreign interference, disinformation, and threats to democratic institutions (UK Government, 2022). Its distinctive feature is structured distributed capability under parliamentary oversight: more operationally organized than Finland, but less centralized and specialized than France or Ukraine.
3.6.3 Sweden: psychological defense and democratic resilience
Sweden combines societal resilience, psychological defense, and renewed security awareness after 2014 and especially after Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine. The re-established Swedish Psychological Defence Agency aims to “identify, analyse and counter undue information influence” while safeguarding “the open and democratic society and the free formation of opinion” (Swedish Psychological Defence Agency, 2024).
Sweden corresponds primarily to Model 4, because counter-disinformation functions are embedded within a broader psychological-defense and societal-resilience framework. At the same time, important Model 1 elements remain through distributed responsibilities and interagency coordination. Sweden, therefore, occupies an intermediate position between resilience-oriented Nordic models and more explicitly security-operational approaches. The Swedish model is more specialized than Finland’s because psychological defense is institutionalized, but remains more decentralized and resilience-oriented than France or Ukraine.
3.6.4 Norway: total defense and societal preparedness
Norway incorporates counter-disinformation into total defense and societal preparedness, influenced by NATO membership, Arctic security concerns, and renewed attention to hybrid threats. Total defense emphasizes “mutual support and cooperation between the civil and military sectors” in managing crises and security threats (Norwegian Government Security and Service Organisation, 2018). Counter-disinformation functions are therefore distributed across security institutions, strategic communication structures, civil preparedness mechanisms, media actors, and educational initiatives rather than concentrated within a single specialized body.
Norway corresponds primarily to Model 1, with Model 5 characteristics through whole-of-society cooperation. Information resilience is embedded in civil preparedness and total defense rather than a dedicated counter-disinformation structure. The model remains decentralized, moderately specialized, cooperative rather than coercive, and close to the resilience-oriented region of the governance space.
3.6.5 Estonia: digital resilience and hybrid-threat governance
Estonia combines strong digital capabilities with a growing emphasis on hybrid threats, cybersecurity, and societal resilience. Its approach to counter-disinformation reflects both its experience with Russian information influence campaigns and its broader strategic orientation toward digital governance and cyber resilience.
The Estonian National Security Concept identifies information influence as part of a broader spectrum of hybrid threats directed against democratic institutions and societal cohesion (Government of Estonia, 2023). Counter-disinformation functions are distributed across governmental communication structures, cybersecurity institutions, strategic communication capabilities, media initiatives, and civil society actors.
Estonia, therefore, corresponds primarily to Model 1, with secondary Model 4 characteristics due to the close integration of counter-disinformation with cybersecurity and hybrid-threat governance. Compared with Finland and Norway, Estonia places greater emphasis on security considerations and hostile foreign influence, reflecting its geopolitical exposure and experience with Russian information operations.
Its distinctive feature is the integration of digital governance, cyber resilience (Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications of Estonia, 2024), and resilience to hostile information influence within a relatively agile state architecture. Estonia demonstrates the importance of technological competence and digital capacity, and while resilience remains important, it is more security-aware and operationally oriented than Finland.
3.6.6 Lithuania: strategic communication and frontline hybrid-threat governance
Lithuania frames disinformation mainly through hybrid threats, strategic competition, and national security. Its threat assessments repeatedly emphasize Russian and Belarusian information operations as components of broader hostile influence activities (State Security Department of Lithuania, 2024). Responsibilities are distributed across strategic communication, security institutions, defense organizations, media-monitoring capabilities, and public-awareness initiatives.
Lithuania corresponds primarily to Model 1, with Model 2 characteristics through cross-government coordination. Compared with Nordic resilience models, it places greater emphasis on threat attribution, strategic coordination, and operational response while remaining within democratic governance constraints. Thus, Lithuania occupies the more security-centric part of the governance space without moving toward highly centralized or coercive approaches.
3.6.7 Latvia: resilience under conditions of persistent information pressure
Latvia combines resilience-building with strong awareness of Russian information pressure. Historical experience, linguistic diversity, and proximity to Russia shape its approach. The National Security Concept emphasizes strengthening societal resilience against hostile propaganda, information and psychological influence, and protecting the democratic information environment (Saeima of Latvia, 2023). Counter-disinformation functions are distributed among governmental communication structures, media regulators, security institutions, and civil-society actors.
Latvia corresponds primarily to Model 1, with Model 2 elements through strategic communication and interagency coordination. It is close to Lithuania and Estonia, but places somewhat greater emphasis on societal cohesion and media policy, positioning it between resilience-oriented and security-centric approaches.
3.6.8 Poland: strategic-security coordination and resilience building
Poland has increasingly incorporated counter-disinformation into broader national security, cybersecurity, and strategic communication frameworks, particularly following Russia’s aggression against Ukraine. Polish approaches emphasize both operational response to hostile information activities and strengthening societal resilience against foreign influence.
The National Security Strategy identifies information activities and disinformation as elements of hybrid threats directed against state institutions and social stability (National Security Bureau of Poland, 2020). Poland corresponds primarily to Model 1, while also displaying significant Model 4 characteristics through the integration of counter-disinformation with cybersecurity and strategic security structures.
Compared with the Baltic states, Poland combines strong security framing with somewhat broader institutional distribution of responsibilities. Thus, Poland occupies a relatively security-oriented position in the governance space, while remaining institutionally plural rather than strongly centralized.
3.6.9 Romania: democratic resilience and emerging institutional adaptation
Romania’s approach remains less institutionalized than those of several frontline states, but concerns regarding foreign influence and information manipulation have clearly been on the rise in recent years. The Romanian presidential elections at the end of 2024 reinforced perceptions of disinformation as a national security challenge and a threat to democratic institutions.
Strategic documents increasingly link information influence to hybrid threats, cybersecurity, and democratic resilience. The architecture combines governmental communication, cybersecurity structures, intelligence institutions, media regulation, and European and NATO cooperation, but coordination appears less consolidated than in Lithuania or Poland.
Romania corresponds primarily to Model 1, with emerging Model 2 characteristics as coordination among security and governmental institutions increases. Romania appears to be moving from a relatively fragmented approach toward more structured coordination in the account of its growing awareness of foreign information influence, and occupies an intermediate position as awareness and coordination gradually increase.
3.6.10 Czechia: hybrid-threat coordination and institutional pragmatism
Czechia has developed a pragmatic, coordination-oriented approach shaped by hybrid threats, foreign influence, and democratic resilience. The centre against terrorism and hybrid threats, established within the Ministry of the Interior, was among the earliest European governmental structures explicitly addressing hybrid threats and disinformation. Czech strategic documents frame hostile information activities within broader hybrid-threat and democratic-security contexts (Ministry of Defence of the Czech Republic, 2021).
Czechia corresponds primarily to Model 2, because of the importance of specialized coordination mechanisms, while also retaining strong Model 1 characteristics through distributed institutional responsibilities. Compared with the Baltic States, the Czech approach appears somewhat less securitized and more administratively pragmatic.
3.6.11 France: state-centered coordination and information sovereignty
France approaches counter-disinformation through national security, information sovereignty, cybersecurity, and strategic state coordination. The General Secretariat for Defence and National Security, under the authority of the Prime Minister while related to the Presidency, coordinates inter-ministerial security and resilience policies, while the VIGINUM agency identifies and analyzes foreign digital interference operations.
France corresponds primarily to Model 4, because counter-disinformation is embedded within broader national-security and state-coordination structures, with Model 1 and selected Model 5 elements through distributed implementation and regulatory bodies such as VIGINUM and Arcom. 2 Compared with the UK, France is more centralized and state-centric. Compared with Ukraine, however, it remains less operationalized and less wartime-oriented. Its distinctive feature is the integration of counter-disinformation into strategic autonomy and information sovereignty.
3.6.12 Ukraine: wartime coordination and operational counter-disinformation
Ukraine represents the most security-oriented case among the democratic countries examined in this study. Since 2014, and especially following Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, Ukraine has treated information influence and disinformation as integral components of ongoing hybrid war and closely aligned with kinetic warfare.
The Center for Countering Disinformation (CCD), established under the National Security and Defence Council of Ukraine, plays a core institutional role. CCD’s mission includes “countering disinformation, information terrorism and information manipulation” directed against Ukraine (Center for Countering Disinformation, 2024). The institutional placement of the CCD under the National Security and Defence Council, chaired by the President, is significant because it embeds counter-disinformation within the highest level of wartime national security coordination.
Ukraine corresponds primarily to a combination of Model 1 and Model 3. The CCD provides a focal institutional capability for operational coordination, analysis, and strategic communication. Yet, multiple governmental and societal actors remain involved, cooperating through formal and informal mechanisms. The Security Service of Ukraine and the Cyber Police under the Ministry of Interior are responsible for exposing bot farms and networks and terminating their activities, including by blocking hostile Telegram channels and websites that spread hostile narratives. The Center for Strategic Communication 3 under the Ministry of Culture and Strategic Communications is tasked with debunking myths, monitoring the information domain, and implementing counter-disinformation campaigns. All major TV channels have regular dedicated counter-disinformation programs. Numerous individual bloggers, professors, and former ambassadors actively reveal and debunk Russian disinformation. Accounting for the role of civil society actors, such as the Center for Democracy and Rule of Law 4 and university-related organizations like StopFake 5 makes the Ukraine case, already heavily securitized, also representative of the whole-of-society approach.
Ukraine demonstrates the strongest integration of counter-disinformation into wartime national security governance and, thus, it occupies the most security-centric position in the governance space, although important resilience and civil-society components remain visible.
3.6.13 Taiwan: civic resilience and distributed democratic defense
Taiwan combines national security awareness with civic participation, digital democracy, and societal resilience under sustained pressure from Chinese information operations. Its approach relies on cooperation among government, civic-tech communities, fact-checkers, digital platforms, and civil society. Rather than emphasizing centralized information control, Taiwan promotes rapid public communication, transparency, and participatory governance; Audrey Tang has described this as building immunity against disinformation rather than censorship (Tang, 2025).
Taiwan corresponds primarily to Model 5, with important Models 1 and 6 characteristics through governmental coordination mechanisms and autonomous civic actors. Compared with European frontline states, Taiwan places a stronger emphasis on civic-tech ecosystems, participatory governance, and distributed societal resilience. By integrating democratic participation and technological innovation into national resilience against information influence, Taiwan occupies a unique position in the governance space: strongly security-aware, yet simultaneously highly distributed and resilience-oriented.
3.6.14 Israel: security integration and strategic information management
Israel approaches disinformation and information influence primarily through broader national security, strategic communication, and information management frameworks shaped by persistent conflict conditions and high threat awareness. Compared with most European democracies, Israeli approaches are more strongly integrated with national security institutions with strategic, national-level coordination.
Capabilities are distributed across, cybersecurity, intelligence, and strategic communication structures. The country’s extensive experience with information operations, strategic messaging, and digital influence in conflict environments has contributed to a comparatively operational understanding of the information domain. After October 7, 2023, civic-tech initiatives contributed to the timely response to disinformation. 6
Israel corresponds primarily to Model 6 because much of the visible counter-disinformation response is voluntary and informally coordinated among civil society and business actors, with Model 1 characteristics through distributed state implementation. It is a high-security case, less institutionally formalized than Ukraine but similarly reflects persistent security-oriented framing. Israel, therefore, occupies a relatively centralized, security-centric position within the democratic governance space while maintaining significant technological and societal innovation capacity.
3.6.15 United States: pluralistic governance and platform-centered coordination
The United States is the most plural and politically contested case. Responsibilities are distributed across federal institutions, cybersecurity agencies, intelligence organizations, election-protection mechanisms, local actors, platforms, civil society, and universities. The scale and diversity of the American information ecosystem make centralized approaches both politically difficult and institutionally fragmented.
The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency describes strengthening resilience against foreign influence and disinformation targeting democratic institutions and elections as a core goal (CISA, 2024), this is just one institutional example, while American debates on countering disinformation remain highly sensitive due to constitutional protections of free speech, political polarization, and concerns about governmental overreach.
The United States corresponds primarily to Model 5, with substantial Model 1 characteristics: decentralized, platform-centered, operationally capable, and shaped by constitutional limits on centralized information governance. Its distinctive feature is the coexistence of strong operational capabilities, especially in regard to the physical control of networks, with fragmented governance and extensive reliance on non-state actors.
3.7 Emerging governance modalities
The country profiles and dimensional scores reveal broad governance modalities without rigid classification. A resilience-oriented modality appears in Finland, Norway, and partly Sweden, where countering disinformation is embedded in societal preparedness, comprehensive security, total defense, or psychological defense frameworks.
A hybrid-threat and strategic-security modality is visible in Lithuania, Latvia, Poland, Romania, Czechia, and Estonia. These cases emphasize foreign interference, cyber vulnerabilities, and interagency coordination while remaining largely distributed rather than fully centralized.
An embedded state-security modality appears in France and Ukraine, with Israel as a related but more distributed high-security case. Expectedly, Ukraine is the strongest case of wartime operationalization, while France represents institutionalized state coordination and information sovereignty.
Pluralistic distributed governance is illustrated by the United Kingdom and the United States. Both combine government coordination, communication structures, regulatory mechanisms, platform governance, contributions by civil-society, and constitutional constraints. Still, the response of the United Kingdom appears more coordinated, while that of the United States is more decentralized and platform-centered.
Taiwan remains distinctive because it combines high threat exposure with low coercion, civic-tech participation, and distributed resilience. Its position shows that severe external pressure does not necessarily lead to centralized or enforcement-heavy design.
Figures 3,4,5visualize national profiles in the exploration space and support the central claim: democratic counter-disinformation architectures occupy different regions of a multidimensional governance space, with choices being shaped by threat perception, institutional inheritance, and strategic culture.

4 Discussion
4.1 Democratic diversity rather than institutional convergence
The analysis suggests that democracies do not follow or converge towards a single institutional model for countering disinformation. Even as information influence is increasingly framed as a national security concern, responses remain diverse. Countries differ in threat framing, institutional empowerment, the creation of new bodies, roles of non-state actors, and ways of balancing security concerns with societal freedom and personal initiative.
This matters because securitization might be expected to produce convergence toward centralized, security-oriented models. The profiles suggest otherwise. Finland, Norway, and Taiwan combine high threat awareness with distributed and resilience-oriented governance. France, Ukraine, and Israel illustrate more security-centric approaches. The United Kingdom and the United States show pluralistic architectures, while Baltic and Central European cases occupy intermediate positions shaped primarily by hybrid-threat framing and proximity to Russia.
The implication is that democratic counter-disinformation architectures are contingent. They reflect threat severity, but also strategic culture, administrative tradition, legal constraints, political history, trust in formal institutions, and state-society relations. Policymakers from other countries should, therefore, ask not which institutional model is worth transferring, but which combination of arrangements fits the national security architecture and context while preserving democratic legitimacy.
4.2 Governance trade-offs and policy implications
The five dimensions represent governance trade-offs. Centralization can facilitate capacity building and improve coordination and accountability but may reduce flexibility and local initiative. Decentralized systems can mobilize societal resources and expertise, but require trust, mature formal and informal coordination mechanisms, and clear responsibilities.
Specialization can strengthen expertise and visibility, especially where hostile information influence is persistent or tied to broader security threats. Yet, it can also create silos, intensify institutional rivalries, and diminish the role of wider resilience or communication systems. Distributed responsibility better reflects the ecosystem nature of the problem, but risks fragmentation if coordination is weak.
Obligations on non-state actors are another trade-off. Stronger legal duties for platforms, media actors, and private entities may increase accountability, but can raise legitimacy concerns, encourage defensive compliance, or stifle legitimate expression. Voluntary and partnership-based models preserve pluralism while depending on the level of trust and incentives.
Enforcement-oriented approaches may be necessary against coordinated foreign interference, illegal content, or wartime information operations, but they cannot substitute for public trust, media literacy, transparency, and resilient institutions. Security-centric framing mobilizes resources but may over-securitize debate. Resilience-centric framing, on the other hand, protects legitimacy but may be slow under acute pressure.
Some dimensions may correlate: security-centric systems often display higher centralization, specialization, and enforcement. Nevertheless, they remained analytically distinct in this study because they represent different design choices. A country may specialize without coercive enforcement, or coordinate more strongly without alienating civil society and business actors.
4.3 Limitations
Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the country profiles rely on publicly available policy documents, strategies, mandates, official statements, and analytical studies. These sources reveal formal architectures and declared priorities, but may miss informal coordination, classified arrangements, operational practices, institutional rivalries, or political bargaining.
A related limitation concerns the distinction between formal design and implementation. This article captures how countries formally conceptualize, organize, and justify counter-disinformation efforts. It does not systematically assess whether policies are implemented effectively, coordination works in practice, or mandates are adequately resourced. Operational practice may not fully correspond to declared strategies. Hence, the profiles should be read as assessments of formal architectures rather than actual practice and implementation performance (seeTable 3).

Third, documentation varies across countries. Some cases are supported by accessible strategies and mandates, while others, including Israel and some rapidly evolving Central and Eastern European cases, are harder to assess solely from public sources.
Finally, the field is changing rapidly. Russia’s war against Ukraine, generative artificial intelligence, platform regulation, electoral interference, and shifting attitudes toward state intervention may alter national architectures quickly, as in the Romania case. The profiles should therefore be read as provisional current assessments of evolving systems.
4.4 Future research The exploratory governance space developed here may support future quantitative and comparative clustering analysis of democratic counter-disinformation architectures. Ordinal country assessments could be used for clustering, dimensionality reduction, or other exploratory techniques to test whether the qualitatively identified modalities correspond to more stable empirical groupings.
Future studies could also examine institutional trajectories over time. For example, Ukraine, Taiwan, and Israel are especially relevant for studying wartime operationalization, civic-tech resilience, and democratic information governance under chronic security conditions.
Other scholars could complement this document-based analysis by reflecting on parliamentary inquiries, investigative reports, and conducting expert assessments of how formal architectures operate in practice, identifying implementation gaps, studying informal coordination mechanisms, and assessing institutional effectiveness.
Finally, research should examine how generative artificial intelligence, platform regulation, foreign information manipulation, and cognitive influence may reshape national architectures, and how democratic models differ from authoritarian information control systems without treating the latter as transferable alternative designs.
5 Conclusion
This article examined how democracies integrate counter-disinformation into national security architectures. It shifted attention from information content and effects to the institutional question of how response ecosystems are organized.
The article developed actor and task taxonomies, six conceptual institutional models, five governance dimensions, and fifteen national profiles. The models capture distributed governmental coordination, specialized inter-ministerial coordination, a dedicated agency, embedded functions, public-private partnerships, and externally implemented or societal arrangements. The five dimensions map variation in centralization, specialization, non-state obligations, enforcement orientation, and security-resilience framing.
The main finding is that democracies do not converge toward a single model. Their architectures reflect combinations of strategic culture, threat perception, institutional inheritance, legal constraints, democratic norms, and state-society relations. Finland, Sweden, France, Ukraine, Taiwan, the United Kingdom, and the United States illustrate different governance pathways, showing that democratic adaptation is not determined solely by threat intensity.
For policymakers, the framework identifies institutional design options and trade-offs rather than prescribing a universal solution. Centralization, specialization, enforcement, and non-state obligations can improve coordination but may also create risks for flexibility, legitimacy, civil liberties, and trust. Resilience-oriented and distributed models preserve democratic legitimacy but require coordination, trust, and sustained societal participation.
For researchers, the study offers conceptual infrastructure for comparative analysis of formal architectures, implementation gaps, longitudinal trajectories, and possible clustering of democratic responses.
The future architecture of democratic national security will depend not only on countering disinformation, but on designing governance systems that protect democratic societies without undermining the principles they defend.

Document 16 of 55

Weaponizing “fake news” as agenda cutting: a content analysis of partisan media discourse in the U.S., 2020–2024

Author: Rashid, Mamunor

Publication info: Rashid, Mamunor. 

https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/weaponizing-fake-news-as-agenda-cutting-content/docview/3399605695/se-2?accountid=14696

Abstract: This study investigates the rhetorical and agenda-setting functions of the term “fake news” in U.S. partisan and centrist media from 2020 to 2024. Originally denoting fabricated information, “fake news” has evolved into a politically charged label used to challenge the credibility of journalists, media organizations, political actors, and public institutions. Using quantitative content analysis of 1,972 news items from nine outlets, the study examines differences across left-leaning, centrist, and right-leaning media in usage type, targets, tone, evidentiary support, and political context. Findings reveal that left-leaning outlets primarily employ an analytical approach to “fake news,” discussing misinformation, democratic risk, and media trust. In contrast, centrist outlets focus on platforms, technology companies, and governance. Right-leaning outlets, particularly Fox News, use the term predominantly as an accusatory label targeting mainstream or center-left media. Across all ideological categories, election and voting politics dominate the context of use. The study contributes to understanding agenda manipulation in a platformized attention economy by showing that “fake news” functions not only as a marker of misinformation but also as a tool for framing, agenda cutting, agenda steering, and credibility contestation in polarized media environments. These insights have implications for journalism, media literacy, and democratic communication in the contemporary information ecosystem.

Full text: 1 Introduction
Since 2016, the term “fake news” has undergone a notable transformation. In a dictionary sense, it refers to false or fabricated news reporting, but in contemporary political discourse it has increasingly become a politically charged label used to challenge the credibility of journalists, media organizations, political opponents, and public institutions (see also Oxford English Dictionary, 2026;Egelhofer and Lecheler, 2019;Tandoc et al., 2018;Waisbord, 2018a,2018b). In contemporary media discourse, “fake news” no longer functions solely as a neutral descriptor of false information; it also operates as a rhetorical weapon through which actors seek to delegitimize competing narratives, weaken trust in rival sources, and shape how audiences interpret political information (Benkler et al., 2018;Egelhofer and Lecheler, 2019;Waisbord, 2018a,2018b).
This transformation is particularly relevant in the polarized U.S. media environment, where partisan media systems, social media platforms, and countermedia outlets contribute to the fragmentation of public discourse by encouraging audiences to consume information that confirms existing political identities (Benkler et al., 2018;Guess et al., 2020a,2020b;Stroud, 2011). Accusations of “fake news” serve as symbolic cues that direct audiences toward distrust of opposing outlets while reinforcing loyalty to ideologically aligned sources (Hameleers and van der Meer, 2020;Pennycook and Rand, 2021). The period from 2020 to 2024, encompassing the COVID-19 pandemic, the 2020 and 2024 presidential elections (Matthews, 2024), the 2022 midterm elections, and ongoing debates over platform moderation, misinformation, and media legitimacy, provides a critical context for examining these dynamics (Newman et al., 2025;Pew Research Center, 2026).
Although prior scholarship has extensively studied misinformation, disinformation, and public trust, comparatively little systematic attention has been paid to how news outlets themselves strategically employ the label “fake news” in their discourse (Egelhofer and Lecheler, 2019;Tandoc et al., 2018). Existing evidence suggests that the term may function differently across ideological contexts, yet systematic comparative research is limited. Understanding these differences is important because the political effect of the term depends not only on the truth of specific claims but also on how the label is used to frame actors, suppress rival narratives, and shape public judgments of credibility (Benkler et al., 2018;Fletcher and Nielsen, 2019;Waisbord, 2018a,2018b;Egelhofer and Lecheler, 2019).
This study conceptualizes weaponized “fake news” rhetoric as a form of agenda manipulation, encompassing agenda cutting, agenda building, and agenda steering (Amazeen and Vargo, 2021;Balles et al., 2026;Vargo and Amazeen, 2021). At the level of interpretation, framing theory explains why the label is rhetorically powerful: by emphasizing selected aspects of reality, “fake news” encourages audiences to read a target as unreliable, deceptive, or politically motivated rather than simply factually incorrect (Entman, 1993;Egelhofer and Lecheler, 2019). At the audience level, agenda-melding theory helps explain why such labels matter in high-choice media environments, where individuals combine cues from multiple sources to build personally and politically meaningful agendas; in this context, “fake news” accusations can steer audiences toward identity-consistent sources and away from rival ones (Shaw et al., 1999a,1999b,1999c;Vera-Revilla et al., 2025). Countermedia scholarship further clarifies how antagonistic outlets, particularly those positioned against mainstream journalism, may use “fake news” rhetoric to contest institutional authority and strengthen alternative epistemic communities (Heft et al., 2020;Loosen, 2018;Rone, 2022).
Guided by these theoretical perspectives and prior research on fake news rhetoric, partisan media, and countermedia dynamics (see Sections 2.1–2.5), this study addresses two research questions: how do left-leaning, centrist, and right-leaning outlets differ in the frequency and functional use of “fake news,” including accusatory, defensive, analytical, and meta-commentary uses?; and who or what is most often labeled as “fake news” across ideological categories, and to what extent does verifiable evidence support such claims? Building on prior work suggesting that right-leaning and countermedia outlets are more likely to use delegitimizing rhetoric against mainstream journalism, while left-leaning and centrist outlets more often frame fake news in analytical, corrective, or procedural terms, the study hypothesizes that right-leaning outlets will use the term more frequently and accusatorily, left-leaning outlets will employ it more analytically, conservative outlets will target mainstream media, liberal outlets will target right-wing sources, and centrist outlets will provide comparatively stronger evidentiary support. To examine these questions, the study conducts a comparative content analysis of nine prominent U.S. news outlets representing left-leaning, centrist, and right-leaning categories during 2020–2024, analyzing usage type, target, tone, evidence provision, and political context to provide an operational framework for understanding how “fake news” functions as agenda cutting, agenda building, and agenda steering in polarized media discourse (Benkler et al., 2018;Egelhofer and Lecheler, 2019;Newman et al., 2025).
2 Literature review
2.1 “Fake news” as a strategic rhetorical tool
The term “fake news” initially referred to deliberately fabricated information presented as legitimate news. Since the 2016 U.S. presidential election, the meaning of “fake news” has expanded beyond false or misleading content (Tandoc et al., 2018;Egelhofer and Lecheler, 2019). In contemporary political communication, “fake news” functions as a rhetorical label used by media actors, politicians, and audiences to challenge the credibility of opposing sources. Rather than being solely descriptive, the term has become a contested political signifier, whose meaning depends on the user, the target, and the political context (Bennett and Livingston, 2020;Lazer et al., 2018).
Accusations of “fake news” operate as tools of delegitimization. Labeling a journalist, outlet, political actor, or public claim as “fake news” not only calls into question factual accuracy but can also undermine the authority of the source itself (Bernecker et al., 2021;Scardigno and Mininni, 2020;Waisbord, 2018a,2018b). The term may close down debate rather than encourage verification, working hegemonically to frame opponents’ claims as untrustworthy before evidence is considered (Zompetti, 2019). Audience reception is shaped by political identity: accusations targeting out-group sources are more likely to be accepted, whereas accusations involving ideologically aligned actors are often rejected (Pennycook and Rand, 2021;Hameleers and Van Der Meer, 2020). This dynamic highlights the power of “fake news” rhetoric in polarized environments, linking misinformation to rhetorical influence, institutional trust, and political identity (Benkler et al., 2018;Lazer et al., 2018).
2.2 Framing mechanisms in “fake news” interpretation
Framing theory explains how “fake news” shapes public interpretation. Framing involves selecting certain aspects of reality to define problems, diagnose causes, make moral judgments, and suggest remedies (Entman, 1993;Deaville and Lemire, 2021). Describing a story, institution, or actor as “fake news” frames the target as biased, deceptive, or politically motivated (Sample et al., 2020;Ramirez-Salina et al., 2025). Embedding the term in broader political messaging renders selective interpretations cognitively accessible, transforming the label into a mechanism of strategic persuasion (Deaville and Lemire, 2021;Ramirez-Salina et al., 2025).
Ideological differences in framing appear in the literature, although the exact pattern varies by context and outlet type. Left-leaning outlets have been shown in some studies to frame “fake news” as a threat to democratic institutions, electoral integrity, or public health, particularly when the term is discussed in relation to misinformation or systemic risk (Zhou and Shen, 2024; see alsoEgelhofer and Lecheler, 2019;Bennett and Livingston, 2020). Right-leaning outlets, especially in studies of partisan or countermedia environments, have been found to use the label to emphasize mainstream media bias and to reinforce distrust of established journalism, although such patterns may differ across national and outlet-specific settings (Benkler et al., 2018;Heft et al., 2020;Rone, 2022). Centrist or institutional outlets more often adopt procedural, verification-oriented, or platform-governance frames, but this, too, appears to depend on the media system and the issue context under study (Sample et al., 2020;Fletcher and Nielsen, 2019;Sarmento, 2025). Taken together, these framing differences may shape how audiences evaluate information legitimacy and may contribute to broader mistrust, though the magnitude of this effect likely varies across political and media environments (Zapata et al., 2025;Hameleers and van der Meer, 2020;Zhou and Shen, 2024).
Functional uses of the term include accusatory frames, defensive frames, analytical usage, and meta-commentary (Boudana and Segev, 2026;Ramirez-Salina et al., 2025;Scherling, 2026;Sarmento, 2025). These distinctions allow the study to move beyond frequency counts to examine how “fake news” performs rhetorical and communicative work in partisan media discourse (Sample et al., 2020).
2.3 Agenda manipulation: cutting, building, steering, and melding
Agenda manipulation extends analysis beyond framing to consider how media influence issue visibility, legitimacy, and salience (Vargo and Minooie, 2025). Agenda building highlights the promotion of preferred narratives (Vargo et al., 2018), whereas agenda cutting strategically reduces the visibility or legitimacy of competing narratives (Amazeen and Vargo, 2021). Weaponized “fake news” rhetoric exemplifies agenda-cutting by discrediting rival claims without engaging with evidence (Amazeen and Vargo, 2021;Vargo and Minooie, 2025).
Agenda cutting is linked to agenda steering, which is particularly useful for analyzing the present study because the label “fake news” does more than dismiss a claim: it can direct audiences toward preferred interpretations and ideologically aligned sources in a fragmented media environment (Vargo et al., 2018). Accusations of “fake news” therefore serve as cognitive shortcuts, signaling which outlets, actors, or stories to trust or reject, especially in a polarized context where audiences rely on partisan cues to navigate competing information streams (Nazar, 2024;Rone, 2022). Agenda-melding theory is likewise well suited to this study because it explains how audiences combine information from multiple sources to form personalized agendas, making them especially vulnerable to repeated “fake news” cues that reinforce ideological silos and sharpen partisan divisions (Shaw et al., 1999a,1999b,1999c;Vera-Revilla et al., 2025). In this sense, the “fake news” label is effective not only because it discredits opponents but also because it helps organize the ways audiences sort, prioritize, and integrate media messages within the broader agenda structure of high-choice media systems.
This theoretical alignment makes agenda-setting, agenda-steering, and agenda-melding perspectives uniquely suited for analyzing the contemporary “fake news” discourse. Rather than operating merely as a tool for fact-checking or descriptive media criticism, the strategic deployment of the “fake news” label functions as a powerful cognitive shortcut for audiences navigating a high-choice media environment. By weaponizing the phrase to attack political opponents or rival media outlets, elite actors and partisan outlets engage in a form of agenda-setting that actively diminishes the visibility and perceived legitimacy of competing narratives. Concurrently, this rhetoric performs agenda steering by providing strong identity-consistent cues that guide audiences away from out-group information channels and deeply entrench them within alternative, ideologically isolated epistemic communities, a process that directly drives the mechanics of modern agenda-melding. It is from this theoretical synthesis of attention redirection and source delegitimation that the core predictions of this study are derived.
2.4 Countermedia dynamics and asymmetric polarization
Countermedia outlets position themselves against mainstream journalism, presenting themselves as necessary alternatives (Frischlich et al., 2023;Hopp et al., 2020;Loosen, 2018). Many prominent U.S. countermedia outlets are right-leaning, where distrust of mainstream media is central to political identity and audience engagement (Blassnig et al., 2019;Rone, 2022). The term “fake news” in these outlets poses a systemic challenge to journalistic authority and normative legitimacy (Heft et al., 2020;Loosen, 2018).
Countermedia outlets position themselves against mainstream journalism, presenting themselves as necessary alternatives (Frischlich et al., 2023;Hopp et al., 2020;Loosen, 2018). Prior research suggests that many prominent U.S. countermedia outlets are right-leaning and that distrust of mainstream media is often central to their political identity and audience engagement (Blassnig et al., 2019;Rone, 2022). These insights are directly relevant to the present study because they suggest that “fake news” rhetoric may function differently depending on whether an outlet is reporting on misinformation, defending its own legitimacy, or actively delegitimizing mainstream journalism. In right-leaning countermedia, the term is especially likely to operate as a challenge to journalistic authority and normative legitimacy, whereas left-leaning and centrist outlets may use it more often to discuss misinformation, electoral integrity, public health, or platform governance (Heft et al., 2020;Loosen, 2018;Scherling, 2026;Fletcher and Nielsen, 2019). Prior work on asymmetric polarization further informs the present study by suggesting that ideological sectors do not engage with “fake news” in the same way: right-leaning outlets are more likely to use accusatory rhetoric, left-leaning outlets tend to frame structural or institutional threats, and centrist outlets emphasize procedural verification (Blassnig et al., 2019;Scherling, 2026). Taken together, these findings justify the study’s comparative design and help explain why the analysis expects distinct patterns in agenda-setting, agenda-building, agenda-cutting, and audience distrust across ideological categories (Benkler et al., 2018;Kaiser et al., 2025;Hopp et al., 2025).
2.5 Research gap and contribution
Despite extensive research on misinformation, disinformation, and media trust, important gaps remain in the literature. Prior work has often concentrated on false content, audience exposure, or single-outlet or single-sector contexts, rather than on how media organizations themselves strategically use the label “fake news” across ideological environments (for example, seeEgelhofer and Lecheler, 2019;Tandoc et al., 2018;Bennett and Livingston, 2020). This study addresses that gap by conducting a comparative analysis of nine U.S. outlets across left-leaning, centrist, and right-leaning categories over the 2020–2024 period, allowing us to examine how rhetorical use varies across ideological settings rather than only within a single sector or event cycle. By integrating framing theory, agenda-melding, agenda-cutting logic, and countermedia scholarship, the study conceptualizes “fake news” as a mechanism for agenda-cutting, agenda-building, and agenda-steering. It operationalizes this through coding categories such as usage type, target, tone, evidence provision, and political context. In doing so, the study provides a systematic empirical basis for understanding the politics of credibility in contemporary U.S. media systems.
2.6 Research questions and hypotheses
RQ1 : How do left-leaning, centrist, and right-leaning outlets differ in the frequency and function of “fake news” use?
RQ2 : Who or what is most often labeled as “fake news,” and how often does factual evidence across ideological camps support such claims?
H1 : Right-leaning outlets will use “fake news” more frequently and more accusatorily than centrist or left-leaning outlets. In contrast, left-leaning outlets will use it more often in analytical or meta-commentary ways.
H2 : Conservative outlets will more often label mainstream media as “fake news,” liberal outlets will more often target right-wing sources, and centrist outlets will be more likely to provide explicit factual evidence when invoking the term.
3 Materials and methods
3.1 Study design
This study employed quantitative content analysis complemented by qualitative thematic illustration to examine how U.S. news outlets used the term “fake news” from January 1, 2020, to December 31, 2024. Content analysis enables systematic, replicable, theory-guided examination of media texts (Krippendorff, 2018;Neuendorf, 2017). The study conceptualized “fake news” as a mechanism of agenda manipulation, encompassing agenda cutting, agenda building, and agenda steering, consistent with prior research on its function as a politically charged label used to delegitimize opponents and shape credibility judgments (Tandoc et al., 2018;Egelhofer and Lecheler, 2019). The design was informed by framing theory and agenda-melding theory (Entman, 1993;Shaw et al., 1999a,1999b,1999c).
3.2 Sampling frame and outlet selection
The sampling frame included news reports, analyses, opinion columns, editorials, and relevant broadcast or online transcripts from nine major U.S. news outlets, grouped into left-leaning, centrist, and right-leaning categories. This structure facilitated comparisons of how “fake news” rhetoric varied across media environments shaped by partisan credibility cues and distrust of opposing sources (Benkler et al., 2018). The outlet grouping was based on a combination of external media-bias assessments and established scholarly precedent, with the classification used here serving as an analytical rather than absolute ideological designation. Specifically, CNN, MSNBC, and The New York Times were treated as left-leaning; Associated Press, Politico, and USA Today Online were treated as centrist/institutional outlets; and Fox News, The Daily Caller, and Conservative Daily News were treated as right-leaning. Because some rating systems place certain outlets near the boundary between center and left-of-center, we interpret these categories comparatively and transparently rather than as fixed labels. The unit of analysis was the individual article or transcript, coded once according to the dominant use of “fake news” in the text (Krippendorff, 2018;Neuendorf, 2017).Table 1presents the final coded sample by outlet and ideological category.

To ensure analytical rigor and minimize subjectivity, the categorization of these nine outlets into left-leaning, centrist, and right-leaning blocks was cross-validated using prominent independent media-bias tracking frameworks (specifically, AllSides and the Ad Fontes Media Bias Chart) alongside established scholarly precedents in political communication research. Outlets such as The New York Times, CNN, and MSNBC are consistently classified within these frameworks as left-of-center or liberal-leaning due to their editorial orientations and audience profiles. Conversely, Fox News, The Daily Caller, and Conservative Daily News are structurally categorized as right-leaning due to their explicit conservative framing, countermedia positioning, and systemic reliance on anti-mainstream media rhetoric. The Associated Press, Politico, and USA Today Online serve as institutional, centrist anchor points, characterized by an operational focus on procedural reporting and factual verification, and by a lack of explicit, consistent alignment with either major political party (seeTables 2,3).

3.3 Article identification and inclusion criteria Articles were identified through systematic keyword searches in Nexis Uni, an academic research database that provides access to news articles, broadcast transcripts, and related legal and business sources. Searches were conducted separately for each of the nine selected U.S. news outlets and focused on the rhetorical use of the term rather than on broader categories such as misinformation or disinformation (Wardle and Derakhshan, 2017;Egelhofer and Lecheler, 2019). Retrieved items were screened and coded according to the study’s coding scheme, including usage type, target, tone, evidence provision, and political context. Items were excluded if they were duplicates, automated updates, letters to the editor, republications without original framing, or incidental mentions lacking sufficient context for coding. Only items published within the study period, appearing in one of the nine selected outlets, and containing the exact phrase “fake news” in the headline or body text were retained for analysis (Krippendorff, 2018). 3.4 Sampling procedure
A stratified sampling strategy ensured comparability across outlets and ideological categories. Eligible items were collected separately for each outlet, with manageable samples retained when volumes were large and all retrievable items included when fewer were available (Neuendorf, 2017). The final dataset consisted of 1,972 coded items: left-leaning ( n = 614), centrist ( n = 690), and right-leaning ( n = 668). Duplicates were removed based on headline, date, author, outlet, URL, or database identifier.
3.5 Coding categories and measures
A structured codebook captured five variables: usage type, target of labeling, tone, evidence provision, and political context. The coding scheme was developed through a hybrid approach, drawing first on prior typologies of fake news rhetoric, framing, delegitimation, and information disorder, and then refined during pilot coding to ensure that the categories captured the range of uses observed in the dataset (Krippendorff, 2018;Neuendorf, 2017). More specifically, the categories were informed by prior work on the rhetorical and delegitimizing functions of “fake news” (Tandoc et al., 2018;Egelhofer and Lecheler, 2019;Zompetti, 2019), by framing and information-disorder scholarship (Entman, 1993;Wardle and Derakhshan, 2017;Lazer et al., 2018;Allcott and Gentzkow, 2017), and were adjusted during coding to ensure that the codebook remained exhaustive and practically applicable to the texts analyzed. Each item received one code per variable based on the dominant function of “fake news” in the text. Usage types were accusatory, defensive, analytical, or meta-commentary. Target categories included mainstream/center-left media, right-leaning media, political actors or parties, platforms/technology companies, foreign actors/state media, specific stories or claims, or no identifiable target. Tone was coded as alarmist/hostile, neutral/analytical, dismissive/satirical, or mixed. Evidence provision measured reliance on strong evidence, formal fact-checks, expert or official sources, non-expert/partisan sources, no evidence, or undetermined. Political context included electoral politics, public health, immigration, economic policy, race and policing, platform governance, media trust, crime/legal issues, and other general criticism.
To ensure strict transparency and allow for systematic replication, variables were operationalized using explicit criteria and textual anchors developed during the pilot phase. “Usage type” was classified based on the text’s primary communicative intent. “Accusatory” use was coded when the label functioned as a direct delegitimizing attack aimed at undermining a specific target’s credibility (e.g., Fox News stating, “The mainstream media continues to push fake news to protect their preferred political candidates”). “Analytical” use was coded when the term was embedded in a descriptive, conceptual, or systemic discussion of information ecosystems (e.g., an AP report noting, “Researchers are investigating how algorithmic amplification accelerates the spread of fake news during election cycles”). Tone of coverage was explicitly differentiated between “alarmist/hostile” and “neutral/analytical.” Texts were coded as “alarmist/hostile” when they relied on emotionally charged language, hyperbole, or threat-oriented framing to instill urgency or outrage (e.g., using terms such as “assault on democracy,” “dangerous lies,” or “corrupt deception”). Texts were coded as “neutral/analytical” when they maintained a detached, matter-of-fact expository style, relying on objective reporting verbs and legal or academic framing. Evidence provision measured the explicit presence of verifiable grounding. Strong evidence required the inclusion of explicit text anchors, such as direct references to official public records, named institutional experts, or established non-partisan fact-checking organizations (e.g., “According to verified data from PolitiFact.”). Items were coded as “no explicit evidence” when an assertion of falseness was made as a bald narrative claim without any accompanying external source verification or systemic contextual support.”
3.6 Coder training and reliability
A single coder applied the codebook after a pilot phase to refine categories and reduce ambiguity, coding ambiguous items as “cannot determine” when appropriate (Krippendorff, 2018;Neuendorf, 2017). Consistency was assessed by recoding 10% of the sample ( n = 197) after 4 weeks without reference to the original coding. Cohen’s kappa values exceeded 0.80, indicating high reliability (Cohen, 1960). To ensure high reliability of quantitative data and address the limitations of single-coder analysis, an inter-coder reliability test was conducted. A second independent communication researcher was trained on the structured codebook using an independent pilot dataset. Following the training phase, this second coder independently evaluated a randomly selected 10% sub-sample of the primary dataset ( n = 197). Inter-coder agreement was calculated using Cohen’s kappa, yielding values ranging from 0.81 to 0.87 across the five primary variables (usage type, target, tone, evidence provision, and political context). These metrics exceed the standard threshold of 0.80, demonstrating strong inter-coder reliability and confirming the replicability of the coding instrument.
3.7 Data analysis
Analysis proceeded in two stages. First, descriptive statistics summarized the distribution of usage type, target, tone, evidence provision, and political context across outlets and ideological categories (Neuendorf, 2017). Second, chi-square tests of independence examined associations between ideology and the categorical variables, with Cramér’s V reported as an effect size to assess the strength of the relationships and standardized residuals used to identify which cells contributed most to statistically significant patterns. Where expected cell counts were low, categories were combined with appropriate caution or interpreted with caution. Statistical significance was set at α = 0.05.
3.8 Qualitative thematic illustration
High-salience patterns were contextualized using qualitative thematic illustration to demonstrate how accusatory, defensive, analytical, and meta-commentary uses appeared in practice, providing interpretive support for quantitative findings (Krippendorff, 2018).
3.9 Ethical considerations
The study analyzed publicly available news content, without human participants, private data, interviews, surveys, or experiments. Formal ethics approval was therefore not required. Illustrative excerpts adhered to copyright standards and were appropriately attributed.
3.10 Data availability
The author retained the coded dataset, codebook, and analysis materials. Shared datasets should include metadata, outlet name, publication date, URL or database identifier, and coding variables rather than full text. Availability is subject to copyright and institutional requirements.
4 Results
4.1 Sample overview
The sample was relatively balanced across ideological categories, although the centrist group contained the most coded items. Because some outlets contained more single-mention or low-context cases, several items were coded as “cannot determine.” Accordingly, the interpretation of rhetorical function focuses primarily on clearly codable cases. The initial stratified sample yielded 1,972 items retrieved via keyword searches (left-leaning: n = 614; centrist: n = 690; right-leaning: n = 668). However, during the structured coding process, a subset of items ( n = 676) was identified as containing single-mention, incidental, or low-context references to the keyword, lacking sufficient text to determine a dominant rhetorical function. To preserve data integrity and prevent skewing of inferential statistics, these uncodable items were systematically excluded from subsequent cross-tabulations. This resulted in a final analytical sample of 1,296 clearly codable cases for the chi-square tests of independence across usage type, target identity, and tone.
4.2 Usage type of “fake news”
The results show clear ideological differences in how the phrase “fake news” was used. Among clearly codable items, left-leaning outlets used the term mainly in an analytical way. Of the 604 codable left-leaning items, 414 articles or transcripts (68.5%) used “fake news” to discuss misinformation, disinformation, media systems, political communication, or democratic risk, while 12.4% used the term in a directly accusatory way.
This pattern is illustrated by cases in which left-leaning outlets framed “fake news” as a broader democratic or informational problem, for example, in discussions of misinformation ecosystems, election integrity, and public trust. In contrast, accusatory cases were coded when the label was directed at a specific political actor, outlet, or claim as a delegitimizing accusation rather than a descriptive or analytical reference.
For example, an item discussing the spread of misinformation during an election cycle was coded as analytical because “fake news” was used to describe a broader information problem rather than to attack a specific opponent. By contrast, an item criticizing a misleading claim from a political actor was coded as accusatory because the phrase was used to challenge the credibility of a specific target. Similarly, a centrist item explaining how social media platforms amplify false claims was coded as analytical because the emphasis was on verification, platform governance, and information systems, whereas a right-leaning segment referring to mainstream media as “fake news” was coded as accusatory because the label functioned as a direct delegitimizing attack on an institutional source.
Centrist outlets also used the term mostly analytically, although the pattern was weaker than in left-leaning outlets. Among 334 codable centrist items, 195 (58.4%) were analytical and 99 (29.6%) were accusatory. Analytical cases were typically characterized by explanatory or contextual language, such as references to misinformation systems, platform governance, fact-checking, election integrity, or public trust, where “fake news” was used to describe a broader information problem rather than to attack a specific target. By contrast, accusatory cases were coded when the label was used to challenge the credibility of a named actor, outlet, or claim, often signaled by delegitimizing verbs and adjectives or by direct attribution of deception. This suggests that centrist outlets often used the term to explain or contextualize misinformation, while also reporting cases in which actors accused others of producing or spreading “fake news”.
Right-leaning outlets showed the strongest accusatory pattern. Among 358 codable right-leaning items, 188 items (52.5%) used “fake news” accusatorily. This was substantially higher than in the left-leaning and centrist categories. Accusatory cases were commonly marked by direct attacks on mainstream media, journalists, or opposing political actors, with the phrase functioning as a delegitimizing label rather than as a descriptive reference. Fox News was especially influential in this pattern, with 187 of 250 codable Fox items (74.8%) coded as accusatory. This finding supports the expectation that right-leaning outlets would use “fake news” more frequently as a delegitimizing label.Figure 1shows A chi-square test showed a statistically significant association between outlet ideology and usage type, χ 2 ( 6 , N = 1 , 296 ) = 195.12 , p < .001 , Cramér’s V = 0.274. This indicates that ideological category was meaningfully related to the rhetorical function of “fake news”.
[Image Omitted: See PDF]
As visualized inFigure 1, the rhetorical function of “fake news” varied drastically based on the outlet’s ideology. A chi-square test confirmed a statistically significant association between outlet ideology and usage type, χ 2 ( 6 , N = 1 , 296 ) = 194.28 , p < 0.001 , Cramér’s V = 0.274 . Right-leaning outlets adopted a predominantly accusatory stance, while left-leaning and centrist outlets used the term more analytically.
4.3 Target of the “fake news” label
The target analysis also revealed substantial ideological differences. In right-leaning outlets, the most common target was mainstream or center-left media. Among codable right-leaning items, 208 items (58.1%) targeted mainstream or center-left outlets. This pattern was driven primarily by Fox News, where attacks on mainstream journalism were the dominant form of the label. For example, items were coded as targeting mainstream or center-left media when “fake news” was used to dismiss established news organizations or to present them as politically biased or untrustworthy.
Left-leaning outlets showed a more distributed target pattern. Their most common target was also mainstream or center-left media, but this accounted for only 24.4% of left-leaning items. In these cases, the label often appeared in discussion of attacks on mainstream outlets rather than as a direct attack by the outlet itself. For example, items were coded in this category when they discussed accusations that mainstream journalism was misleading, biased, or manipulative. Left-leaning outlets also frequently targeted political actors, platforms, specific stories or claims, and foreign actors.
Centrist outlets showed a different pattern again. Among codable centrist items, the most common target was platforms or technology companies, which appeared in 123 items (36.8%). These cases typically situated “fake news” in relation to social media, platform moderation, online information systems, and technology governance (Lu et al., 2026). For example, items were coded in this category when the label was linked to platform responsibility for the circulation of false claims.
This distinct targeting asymmetry is further illustrated inFigure 2. The association between ideology and target was statistically significant, χ 2 ( 16 , N = 1 , 306 ) = 312.33 , p < 0.001 , Cramér’s V = 0.346 . This suggests a moderate relationship between ideological category and the entity or phenomenon that was strategically labeled as “fake news”.
