Introduction
The transformations of the digital economy have redefined the role of information on markets, accelerating its circulation and increasing vulnerability to distortions. In this context, disinformation through fake news has gone beyond the media sphere, becoming an economic factor which influences investor behaviour, price formation and resource allocation. In an interdependent digital environment, information is no longer just a decisionmaking support, but also a determinant of market volatility. In parallel, regulatory pressures have expanded ESG reporting, seen as a tool to reduce information asymmetry and build trust (Christensen et al., 2021). However, the increase in the volume of information raises a key question: does this transparency contribute to stability or generate new information risks?
Recent research highlights that disinformation and distorted digital content have become relevant factors in the dynamics of capital markets, influencing investor perceptions and price formation mechanisms. Studies show that fake news can generate significant market reactions, especially in the case of negative information, which produces distortions of returns and abnormal reactions in the short term (Arcuri et al., 2023). At the same time, disinformation contributes to increased volatility and the emergence of panic behaviours in times of uncertainty, amplifying the instability of financial markets (Olakoyenikan, 2024). Furthermore, research shows that investors remain vulnerable to the influence of misleading information even in the presence of subsequent corrections, suggesting the persistence of the effects of misinformation in the decision-making process (Du et al., 2023). Recent literature on investor behaviour also emphasises the role of social mechanisms and herd behaviour in the propagation of information, including the distorted information, which contributes to the rapid transmission of informational shocks in markets (Rashid et al., 2025).
In parallel, research on ESG reporting indicates that non-financial transparency can reduce information asymmetry and strengthen investor confidence, however, its effects on markets are heterogeneous and dependent on the quality and interpretation of information (Gillan et al., 2021). Empirical studies highlight important limitations of this framework, such as the lack of standardisation and inconsistency of ESG ratings, which can generate uncertainty and affect the efficiency of capital allocation (Gopang et al., 2025). At the same time, the phenomenon of greenwashing indicates that sustainability information can be manipulated or selectively presented, affecting investor perceptions and market performance (Oppong- Tawiah & Webster, 2023). Furthermore, digitalisation and new corporate communication channels facilitate the distortion of information content and manipulation of the reporting tone, amplifying the risks associated with transparency (Yang et al., 2025).
However, the existing literature predominantly addresses these phenomena separately: on the one hand, the impact of misinformation on investor behaviour and market volatility, and on the other hand, the role of ESG reporting in reducing information asymmetry and its associated challenges. However, the existing literature does not provide a framework to explain whether and under what conditions ESG transparency can function not only as a mechanism for reducing uncertainty, but also as a vector for amplifying informational shocks.
Based on these considerations, our research is guided by the following question: can extended corporate transparency, materialised through ESG reporting, function simultaneously as a mechanism for reducing uncertainty and as a source of vulnerability to misinformation in capital markets?
To answer this question, the empirical approach is structured in a sequential methodological framework. In the first stage, the database is built, by integrating financial, and non-financial information relevant to the phenomenon analysed. The second stage aims to transform unstructured data into econometric variables, by applying natural language processing techniques (NLP) in order to identify and quantify informational pressure. In the third stage, we assessed the impact of informational shocks on the capital market, using the event study methodology. Finally, we analysed the structural relationships among variables through appropriate econometric models, complemented by machine learning approaches, used to assess the robustness and predictive capacity of the results.
The novelty of our paper is given by the development of an integrated empirical framework which analyses the interaction between disinformation and ESG reporting, highlighting the fact that corporate transparency does not generate unidimensional effects on the markets, but can produce asymmetric reactions under conditions of informational uncertainty. Specifically, our paper demonstrates that, while the Environmental and Social dimensions can amplify vulnerability to informational shocks, the Governance component acts as a stabilisation mechanism, contributing to the attenuation and correction of market reactions. In this sense, our main contribution consists in identifying a mechanism through which ESG transparency can function simultaneously as a tool to reduce information asymmetry and as a source of information risk, configuring what is defined in the paper as the "Transparency Paradox".
The paper is organised into four main sections. The following section presents the literature review, the third section details the research methodology in which we present the data used, the fourth section analyses the empirical results and discussions, and the last section synthesises the conclusions and their implications, limitations, and future research directions.
1. Literature review
1.1. Fake news, disinformation, and distortion of signals on capital markets
In recent economic literature (Lee & Jeong, 2023; Rangapur et al., 2023), disinformation is increasingly analysed as a source of distortion in the price formation process, by altering the quality of available information and amplifying investors' behavioural reactions. In its digital form, fake news is a factor capable of affecting asset assessment, the speed of market adjustment and the efficiency of signalling mechanisms (Albalate & Gragera, 2022).
Therefore, the proliferation of digital disinformation complicates this mechanism, as it introduces false or ambiguous signals, which can produce temporary deviations from the fundamental value and induce disproportionate investor reactions (Fama, 1970). Therefore, media information directly influences stock market returns and market dynamics (Fratrič et al., 2022). Tetlock (2007) demonstrates that the negative tone in media flows is associated with downward pressure on prices and subsequent reversals, suggesting that the market reacts not only to fundamentals, but also to the aggregate information state.
In the same vein, Engelberg and Parsons (2011) show that the local distribution of media information affects trading and investor reaction, outlining the role of information channels in price movement.
Vosoughi, Roy and Aral (2018) show that fake news spreads faster and deeper in online networks than true news, having a high potential for economic contagion, especially when the information is used by investors as a decision support. From the same perspective, Lazer et al. (2018) treat fake news as a systemic problem of the digital information ecosystem, with implications for trust, reputation, and the decision-making process.
The discussion is extended to the role of platforms and automation in amplifying disinformation (Condon, 2021), also to the role of social bots and automated information distribution mechanisms (Ferrara et al., 2016), which can artificially increase the visibility of false narratives, contributing to the emergence of information cascades. From an economic point of view, this phenomenon affects market efficiency by distorting signals and increasing the costs of information screening.
This perspective justifies treating disinformation as a relevant informational shock for the econometric analysis of capital markets, thus substantiating hypothesis H1 of this study:
H1: A high level of transparency in the Environmental and Social dimensions is associated with an increase in the vulnerability of companies to informational shocks generated by disinformation.
1.2. ESG reporting, corporate transparency and information asymmetry
The literature on ESG reporting starts from the idea that the disclosure of non-financial information reduces information asymmetry between the company and investors, improves transparency, and contributes to a more efficient assessment of corporate risk and performance (Kumawat & Patel, 2022). In this logic, ESG reporting is interpreted as a signalling mechanism, through which organisations transmit credibility, responsibility, and capacity to manage risks in the long term.
This view is compatible with the economic theory of information (Mulchandani et al., 2022). Akerlof (1970) shows that information asymmetry can lead to adverse selection and deterioration of market functioning, while Spence (1973) demonstrates that economic agents can use costly signals to transmit credible information.
Disclosure of sustainability information can reduce the cost of capital and improve investor perception (Reber et al., 2021), while mandatory sustainability reporting has relevant economic implications, including on information quality and comparability among companies (Christensen et al., 2021).
However, the relationship between ESG and company value is neither linear nor univocally positive (Fu et al., 2023; Peng et al., 2025). Krüger (2015) shows that the market reacts more strongly to negative CSR (Corporate Social Responsibility) information than to the positive one, indicating an asymmetric sensitivity of investors to reputational signals.
The use of ESG information by investors is processed heterogeneously and depending on the context (Chen, 2025). Thus, ESG information becomes relevant for investors to the extent that it is perceived as economically material, influencing the assessment of risk, future cash flows and company performance, and it is not just an exercise in compliance (Amel-Zadeh and Serafeim, 2018).
In relation to the issue of this paper, an insufficiently explored point in the existing literature is the fact that ESG reporting can function simultaneously as a signal of transparency and as an information infrastructure exploitable by external actors. It is in this context that the contribution of this article is placed, by developing the concept of the "Transparency Paradox". Therefore, we propose research hypothesis H2, as follows:
H2: Governance quality mitigates the negative impact of disinformation and contributes to the acceleration of market value recovery.
1.3. Investor attention, market sentiment, and transmission mechanisms of informational shocks
A key direction of contemporary financial literature concerns the role of investor attention and sentiment in transmitting information to markets (Baker and Wurgler 2006). As a result, market reactions are often mediated by the intensity with which investors observe, search for, and interpret information (Tetlock, 2007).
Da et al. (2011) introduce online search volume as a proxy variable for investor attention, and show that it has explanatory power for returns, liquidity, and trading behaviour. In addition, sentiment indicators extracted from social data can anticipate certain market movements, suggesting that aggregate sentiment is part of the price formation mechanism (Bollen, Mao & Zeng, 2011).
Against the backdrop of these results, the literature has paid increased attention to textual analysis and the measurement of information tone (Barber & Odean, 2008). Loughran and McDonald (2011) demonstrate that general sentiment dictionaries may be inadequate in a financial context, and propose an approach adapted to economic language, showing that the meaning of terms depends on the specific context of markets. In this direction, Araci (2019) proposes FinBERT, a Transformer model trained on financial text, capable of capturing sentiment nuances in economic news and documents.
The relevance of the literature for this article is twofold. First, it supports the use of attention and sentiment indicators as intermediate variables between misinformation and market reaction (Da et al., 2015). Second, it provides a theoretical basis for integrating NLP techniques into the econometric analysis of informational shocks (Baker et al., 2016; Gentzkow et al., 2019). Thus, attention and sentiment are not treated as secondary descriptive variables, but as transmission mechanisms through which fake news influences returns and volatility, an aspect which supports the research hypothesis H3:
H3: Informational shocks generated by fake news are preceded by abnormal increases in investor attention.
1.4. Corporate governance and resilience of companies under the conditions of informational uncertainty
If the Environmental and Social dimensions are associated in the ESG literature with the public and reputational exposure of the company (Krüger, 2015; Lins et al., 2017), the Governance component is traditionally treated as the pillar which confers internal discipline, control, and institutional response capacity (Bolton & Kacperczyk, 2021; Pástor et al., 2022). From this perspective, corporate governance becomes an essential element for understanding resilience to informational shocks.
Shleifer and Vishny (1997) define corporate governance as the ability to protect capital providers from managerial and informational risks. In the same vein, Gompers, Ishii and Metrick (2003) demonstrate that companies with strong governance have superior valuations and stock market performance. This perspective is linked to resilience and trust (Al Amosh 2025): companies with high social capital perform better in crises, suggesting that institutional robustness mitigates shocks (Bollen, Mao & Zeng, 2011), and certain ESG characteristics support stock market resilience in stress contexts (Albuquerque et al. 2020). In this framework, the Governance dimension is essential, as it influences the ability of the company to respond to false information, communicate credibly, and limit volatility. Unlike the Environmental and Social pillars, which increase reputational exposure, Governance functions as an institutional infrastructure. Thus, we propose the research hypothesis H4:
H4: The time to recover market value is determined by the quality of governance, and not by the size of the company.
2. Research Methodology
The purpose of this research is to analyse the relationship between disinformation (fake news), ESG (Environmental, Social, Governance) reporting, and capital market reactions, in order to assess the role of corporate transparency in the context of contemporary information asymmetry. To achieve this goal, we established the following research objectives:
Objective 1 (O1): Quantifying the information pressure generated by fake news through NLP techniques, sentiment indicators (NSS) and attention indicators (ASV).
Objective 2 (O2): Estimating the impact of information shocks on the market value of companies through the CAR methodology.
Objective 3 (O3): Evaluating the differential effect of ESG components based on the role of governance in company resilience.
Objective 4 (O4): Developing the concept of "Transparency Paradox" by identifying an ESG transparency mechanism which can simultaneously function as a tool to reduce information asymmetry and as a source of information risk.
The research purpose and objectives operationalise the central research question of our analysis with a focus on the dual function of ESG transparency, namely that of reducing uncertainty and, simultaneously, as a source of vulnerability to misinformation in capital markets.
The research methodology is built on an integrated empirical framework, which combines econometric modelling of financial time series with natural language processing techniques (NLP), to analyse the mechanisms through which misinformation influences the efficiency of capital markets and investor behaviour. The approach is sequential, structured in four main stages, corresponding to the process of data construction, operationalisation of information variables, impact identification and econometric modelling.
To avoid methodological fragmentation, we organised the research approach around a single causal mechanism: the reaction of capital markets, measured by cumulative abnormal returns (CAR), to a fake news information shock, conditioned by the structure of ESG scores. This mechanism represents the central contribution of our paper, namely the introduction of the concept of "Transparency Paradox". In this framework, the econometric analysis based on the event study and fixed-effects panel regression constitutes the confirmation of the causal relationship, with NLP techniques having the role of operationalising information pressure. In addition, we used the Random Forest model to verify the robustness of our analysis. Therefore, the complementary methods do not fragment the analysis, but converge towards evaluating the same central relationship.
We conducted the analysis in a panel-type framework, in which the observation unit is represented by the company-day pair, allowing the simultaneous capture of the crosssectional and temporal variation of the variables analysed. The resulting dataset integrates financial information, ESG indicators and information variables derived from digital sources, being suitable for investigating the dynamics of the market reaction to informational shocks.
In the first stage of our research, we built the database by integrating heterogeneous sources which reflect the financial, non-financial and informational dimensions of the phenomenon analysed. The database used in the analysis integrates information from several complementary sources. We extracted daily stock prices from Yahoo Finance (NYSE and NASDAQ), and we took ESG scores from the Kaggle database, which aggregates sustainability indicators at the company level and allows international comparability of ESG performance. To avoid anticipation bias, we used only ESG values available prior to the event. We identified the moment of the onset of informational shock by correlating information from press archives with the dynamics of search volume in Google Trends.
We extracted the explanatory variables, represented by ESG scores for the Environmental, Social and Governance dimensions from a standardised dataset including 722 internationally listed companies, ensuring comparability and consistency of the metrics used (Christensen et al., 2021). Based on this initial set of 722 entities, we selected a final sample of seven global companies (Pfizer, Meta, Disney, Johnson & Johnson, Tesla, Starbucks, and Target), using a purposive sampling procedure. The narrowing and selection of this subset are fully justified by the exploratory nature of the research (Frontier Research) and by the specificity of the phenomenon analysed. The companies were chosen exclusively on the criterion of direct exposure to severe and documented information shocks (financial disinformation, fake news regarding clinical data or hybrid boycott campaigns on social media). Since the objective of our research is not to estimate the probability of exposure to disinformation of the general population, but to analyse the heterogeneity of the market reaction depending on the structure of ESG scores conditioned by the occurrence of a fake news attack, the in-depth analysis of these 7 critical cases offers superior explanatory rigour to massive statistical aggregates, allowing for the precise isolation of information asymmetry in the event window. The resulting dataset has a panel structure, in which observations are defined at the company-day level. As a result of the aggregation of time series and the definition of estimation and event windows, the final database contains 3000 daily observations, allowing the investigation of the dynamics of the market reaction to informational shocks.
The panel structure of the data allows the simultaneous capture of temporal and crosssectional variation, providing an adequate framework for estimating the relationships between financial and informational variables. For each company in the sample, we collected daily time series of closing prices, and we calculated returns in logarithmic form:
... (1)
where: Rit represents the return on asset i at time t, and Pit represents the closing price at time t; Pi,t-1 is the closing price at the previous time.
We applied logarithmic transformation to improve the statistical properties of the series, including the approximation of stationarity (Brooks, 2019). The financial data consist of daily series of closing prices and trading volumes, collected automatically by the yfinance Python library. According to the event study methodology, we used a 250-day estimation window and an event window [-5, +5], referenced to the moment of the informational shock (MacKinlay, 1997).
To capture investor attention and information asymmetry, we constructed the Abnormal Search Volume (ASV) indicator based on Google Trends data, used as a proxy for informational interest (Da et al., 2011). The series are temporally aligned, cleaned of missing values, and standardised.
The second stage aims to transform unstructured data into econometric variables, by applying natural language processing techniques. We pre-processed the textual corpus, consisting of financial news and social media content, using standard procedures (tokenisation, lemmatisation, removal of irrelevant words), in accordance with the methodology proposed by Jurafsky & Martin (2023). Subsequently, we vectorised the documents using the TF-IDF (Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency) method:

Content was classified as disinformation when the similarity exceeded the threshold of 0.85, in the absence of a factual correspondence, thus capturing sophisticated forms of fake news (Ferrara et al., 2016).

This methodology allows the isolation of the effect of the informational shock from the general market variations (MacKinlay, 1997). Obtaining negative and statistically significant CAR values confirmed the destruction of market value generated strictly by the disinformation campaigns. To ensure the robustness of the estimate within the event study (CAR), the company returns were reported to the S&P 500 index, used as a reference benchmark. To analyse the relationship between informational and financial variables, we investigated the dynamics and temporal correlations among attention indicators (ASV), sentiment indicators (NSS) and stock returns, especially around moments associated with informational shocks. This approach allows highlighting the role of informational pressure in anticipating and amplifying market reactions. To characterise the distribution of the variables used in the analysis, we present in table no. 1 the descriptive statistics related to the main indicators included in the econometric model.
The results show significant variability in stock returns, ESG scores, and information indicators. This heterogeneity supports the adequacy of the panel framework for the empirical analysis, allowing the simultaneous capture of temporal and cross-sectional variation.

In addition, to validate the robustness of the results and assess the predictive capacity of the variables analysed, we implemented an approach based on machine learning methods, using a Random Forest classification model. This specification allows the assessment of the role of corporate governance and informational pressure in determining the speed of market adjustment after informational shocks. By integrating NLP techniques with established econometric methods (Event Study and panel models), our research proposes a coherent empirical framework for analysing the effects of disinformation on financial markets, simultaneously capturing the informational, behavioural, and financial dimensions of the phenomenon.
3. Results and discussion
The empirical analysis is conducted on a panel data set, built at the company-day level, which includes 3000 observations and allows capturing the dynamics of the market reaction to informational shocks. In this context, the results show the existence of a systematic mechanism through which ESG transparency interacts with information asymmetry, generating uneven effects on market value.
Therefore, we analysed the trajectories of share values for a subset of representative companies, selected according to their ESG profile and exposure to disinformation episodes. In this sense, the applied NLP algorithms eliminated the usual PR (Public Relation) criticisms, retaining exclusively those hybrid attacks which simultaneously met the threshold of lexical similarity (Cosine Similarity greater than 0.85 with official reports) and that of factual asymmetry. Thus, the representativeness of companies is characterised by maximum information purity and density, capable of supporting a precise triangulation of stock market data (CAR), textual sentiment (FinBERT) and herd behaviour (Google Trends ASV).
Specifically, empirical evidence suggests the presence of a "Transparency Paradox", in which high information exposure, associated with Environmental and Social components, can amplify the vulnerability of companies to fake news shocks, while corporate governance acts as a stabilising factor, reducing the persistence of negative effects and facilitating the recovery process.
3.1. Dynamics of share value around the informational shock according to the ESG profile
Figure no. 1 shows the evolution of the share value, normalised to base 100, around the moment of the informational shock (Day 0), for a subset of companies selected according to their ESG profile and exposure to misinformation. The analysis is conducted on a 30-day window around the event, and the series are used for illustrative purposes, in line with the econometric results obtained on panel data, allowing for cross-sectional comparability of relative performance. The graphical analysis highlights a significant heterogeneity of market reactions, correlated with the structure of ESG scores. In the case of companies characterised by high exposure on the Environmental and Social dimensions, more pronounced and persistent negative price adjustments are observed, suggesting an increased sensitivity to informational shocks.
To illustrate this mechanism, the case of Disney company, which has an extremely high aggregate ESG score of 1147 points, highlights a severe post-event depreciation: the share value recorded a collapse from a base of 100% (on Day 14) to 89% on Day 0, reaching a critical minimum of 87% on Day 6. This dynamic provides direct empirical support for hypothesis H1 and validates the manifestation of the "Transparency Paradox": a high level of non-financial transparency turns into an exploitable vulnerability. A similar pattern is observed for Meta (low G-score of 215), where the shares fell to 92% on Day 0 and continued to depreciate to 91% on Day 8.
In contrast, for companies characterised by a high level of corporate governance, there is a rapid shock absorption. The case of Pfizer (solid G score of 300) perfectly illustrates this stabilisation phenomenon: the shares withstood the attack, recording a 110% increase on Day 0 and reaching a peak of 122.5% on Day 9. The empirical results confirm hypothesis H2 and suggest that only corporate governance acts as a reputational shield, facilitating rapid price correction following distorted information.
3.2. Dynamics of investor attention and the transmission of informational shocks
To investigate the propagation mechanism of informational shocks, we analysed the dynamics of abnormal search volume (ASV), used as a proxy variable for investor attention (Da et al., 2011) (Figure no. 2):
In line with the results obtained in the econometric modelling on panel data, ASV analysis highlights the fact that informational shocks are accompanied by visible increases in investor attention, but with heterogeneous propagation patterns over time.
To illustrate these mechanisms, the trajectories presented in figure no. 2 indicate the existence of differentiated quantitative reactions. In the case of Meta, the panic was instantaneous, with the ASV index reaching a maximum value of 100 points on Day 0 and remaining at a critical level of 98 points on Day 1. In addition, we identified cases in which the increase in interest is delayed regarding the moment of the shock: for Pfizer, the search peak (index 100) only appeared on Day 4, giving institutional investors the necessary time to audit the information. In the case of Disney, the misinformation triggered a prolonged network effect, with the ASV anomaly reaching the maximum threshold of 100 points only on Day 27. These data support hypothesis H3, confirming the role of investor attention (ASV) as a mechanism for transmitting information shocks under conditions of information asymmetry.
3.3. Assessing the impact on market value: CAR analysis
To isolate the net impact of disinformation campaigns from the general volatility of the capital market, we applied the Event Study Methodology. This stage involved calculating Cumulative Abnormal Returns (CAR) over an 11-day trading window, within the range [-5, +5] from the moment of the informational attack (Day 0).
The results indicate a significant economic impact of disinformation on market value, with an average CAR of approximately -2.3% in the range [-1, +1], suggesting an immediate negative reaction to the informational shock.
The sub-sample analysis quantifies the "Transparency Paradox" effect: companies with high scores on the Environmental and Social dimensions experience much more pronounced losses. Specifically, Disney recorded an extremely negative CAR of -6.6% on Day 0, which deepened to -8.2% on Day 4, confirming the H1 hypothesis regarding increased vulnerability. Meta showed a -3.0% drop on Day 0, falling to -5.0% on Day 3. Figure no. 3 illustrates these divergent post-event trajectories. Companies with strong governance show an immediate resilience trajectory, supporting the H2 hypothesis: Pfizer demonstrated the strength of its governance by recording a positive CAR of +4.3% on Day 0, followed by a +11.7% jump on Day 3.
Overall, the results confirm an asymmetric price adjustment mechanism depending on the ESG profile. The analysis of statistical significance indicates variations in p-values, reflecting the difficulty of identifying an informational shock over short trading windows. In the case of Target (p=0.003), the effect is statistically robust, while for issuers with high volatility (p=0.642), the signal is attenuated by random market variation. However, from an econometric perspective, economic relevance may prevail over statistical significance, as substantial capitalisation losses indicate a real impact of misinformation, even under conditions of low statistical power.
3.4. Econometric testing of the relationship between ESG and the stock market impact
To assess the structural relationships between ESG characteristics and stock market impact in the context of informational shocks, we estimated a panel regression model, using company-day data. To evaluate the structural relationships among variables, we used a fixedeffects panel regression model, in which cumulative abnormal returns (CAR) are explained by ESG scores and information variables (NSS and ASV). This approach allows for the simultaneous capture of temporal variation and heterogeneity across companies. The estimated econometric model is presented in equation 8 in the research methodology section.
The estimated coefficients indicate that the Environmental (β_E = -0.008, p < 0.01) and Social (β_S = -0.005, p < 0.05) dimensions are associated with an amplification of negative market reactions following informational shocks. In contrast, the Governance component presents a positive and statistically significant coefficient (β_G = 0.011, p < 0.01), suggesting a stabilising role and reducing the impact of misinformation. Informational variables confirm the transmission mechanism: market sentiment (NSS) positively influences returns, while investor attention (ASV) is associated with an increase in negative price pressure.
These results are consistent with the formulated hypotheses and robust to different model specifications, confirming the existence of an asymmetric effect of ESG components on market reaction under conditions of informational uncertainty. The results are consistent with the estimates obtained based on integrated ESG - financial data and validated through Python implementations, confirming the robustness of the relationships identified.
3.5. Robustness analysis using machine learning methods
To validate the robustness of the results obtained within the econometric model, we implemented a complementary approach based on machine learning methods. In this regard, we built a Random Forest classification model, with the objective of predicting the probability of a negative market reaction following informational shocks. The dependent variable was defined binary, taking the value 1 if the cumulative abnormal returns (CAR) are negative and zero otherwise. The model was estimated using the ESG scores (E, S, G), sentiment indicators (NSS) and investor attention (ASV) as explanatory variables.
The model results, summarised in table no. 2, indicate a high predictive capacity, with an accuracy of approximately 72%, confirming the relevance of the variables included in the econometric analysis. The analysis of the importance of the variables highlights the fact that informational indicators, especially search volume (ASV) and market sentiment (NSS), have the greatest contribution to the prediction of negative market reactions. At the same time, the corporate governance component is associated with a reduction in the probability of persistent negative shocks.
These results are consistent with the estimates obtained in the panel regressions and the event study analysis, confirming that informational pressure and ESG structure significantly influence market reactions. Therefore, the machine learning approach strengthens the validity of the conclusions and highlights the predictive nature of the mechanisms identified.
3.6. Corporate resilience and recovery dynamics (TTR)
To assess the recovery capacity of companies following informational shocks, we analysed the Time-to-Recovery (TTR) indicator, defined as the number of days required for the stock price to return to the pre-event level. In line with the results obtained in the econometric modelling, the analysis highlights the existence of a systematic relationship between the quality of corporate governance and the dynamics of the recovery process.
Figure no. 4 illustrates this relationship for a set of representative companies, highlighting systematic variations in resilience depending on the governance score.
In quantitative terms, the results indicate differences in resilience determined strictly by the quality of the governance pillar (G). Companies with strong governance have an almost instantaneous recovery time: Tesla (G score = 278), Pfizer (G score = 300) and Disney (G score = 321) recorded a minimum TTR of only 1 day, while Starbucks (G score = 295) recovered in 2 days. In contrast, weaker governance prolongs the negative impact, with Meta (G score = 215) needing 30 days to recover. The final consequences of the concept of the "Transparency Paradox" are demonstrated by the case of Johnson & Johnson, where overexposure to the Environment pillar (extremely high E score of 565) provided a volume of data which paralysed internal audit, the company reaching the critical 90-day limit without recovering. This asymmetry highlights a superior capacity to absorb informational shocks exclusively in the case of companies with robust institutional mechanisms.
The results obtained confirm the literature on the impact of disinformation on capital markets. The negative effect of fake news campaigns on cumulative abnormal returns was also obtained in the research of Arcuri et al. (2023) and Olakoyenikan (2024), and the behavioural transmission mechanism aligns with the conclusions of Da et al. (2011). The differential propagation speed observed also supports the finding of Vosoughi et al. (2018) regarding the faster diffusion of false information.
The stabilising and positive role of governance confirms the results obtained by Lins et al. (2017), who associate high corporate governance with a superior valuation and increased resilience in times of crisis. However, the asymmetric effect of ESG components nuances the results obtained by Albuquerque et al. (2020).
Therefore, the results obtained support hypothesis H4, highlighting the fact that resilience is not determined exclusively by the size of the company or its capitalisation, but by the robustness/quality of internal governance mechanisms and the capacity to manage informational crises. In this sense, corporate governance plays a crucial role not only in mitigating the initial impact of disinformation, but also in accelerating the process of returning to a balanced state, contributing to the medium-term stability of market value. These results reinforce the idea that corporate resilience is an institutional phenomenon, not just a financial one, and is directly influenced by the quality of control mechanisms, transparency, and strategic response.
Conclusions
This paper investigates the relationship among disinformation, corporate transparency, and capital market reactions, proposing an integrated empirical framework which combines NLP- based textual analysis with established econometric methods, such as event study and panel regressions. The existing literature treats the role of information, ESG reporting and investor behaviour separately, however, it does not provide a unified framework to explain how disinformation exploits corporate transparency in the digital environment. Our research fills this gap, demonstrating that the interaction among these dimensions generates significant economic effects on market value and price adjustment dynamics.
The main contribution of this paper is to highlight an asymmetric effect of ESG transparency in the context of informational shocks, providing a direct answer to the research question. The empirical results show that extensive corporate transparency can simultaneously function as both a mechanism for reducing uncertainty and a source of vulnerability to misinformation. The Environmental and Social dimensions are associated with an amplification of negative market reactions, while the Governance component acts as a stabilisation mechanism, reducing the persistence of shocks and accelerating the recovery process. The event study indicates that misinformation generates significant deviations of returns from the expected level, confirming the rapid transmission of informational shocks in asset prices. At the same time, the dynamics of attention (ASV) and sentiment (NSS) indicators highlight the existence of a behavioural transmission channel, in which the increase in investor interest and the deterioration of sentiment precede price adjustments.
A central result of the research is given by the introduction of the concept of the "Transparency Paradox", according to which transparency, although conceived as a mechanism for reducing information asymmetry, can generate vulnerabilities in an information environment which is saturated and susceptible to manipulation. Thus, transparency becomes simultaneously a credibility tool and a vector of exposure to misinformation.
From the perspective of market efficiency, the results demonstrate the existence of temporary deviations from the efficient market hypothesis, generated by the interaction between misinformation and investor behaviour. These inefficiencies are corrected over time, but involve relevant economic costs in the short term, especially for companies with high information exposure. From the perspective of developing theory in the field of corporate finance and sustainability, this model makes a fundamental contribution in three research directions. First, it changes the paradigm of the ESG literature, moving non-financial reporting from the sphere of ethical compliance to that of informational risk management; our study demonstrates that, in the digital age, Environmental and Social data can become exploitable "synthetic materiality". Second, by conceptualising the "Transparency Paradox", the model amends the Signalling Theory, demonstrating that resilience is not guaranteed by absolute openness. Thus, the theoretical role of Corporate Governance (G) is updated: beyond mitigating internal agency conflicts, it becomes an algorithmic filter and a protective shield against exogenous shocks. Finally, the model enriches the theory of behavioural finance and nuances the Efficient Markets Hypothesis by integrating a hybrid empirical framework.
Quantifying digital panic and sentiment (via ASV and NSS indicators) provides a measurable causal explanation for temporary price deviations induced by information asymmetry.
In terms of practical implications for companies, the results provide clear strategic directions, redefining risk management. First, companies need to adopt a defensive approach to ESG reporting; Environmental and Social data exposure must be calibrated and protected by information security protocols to prevent their malicious exploitation. Second, managers need to prioritise investments in algorithmic governance. Internal audit committees need to function as rapid response cells, integrating real-time monitoring of alternative indicators (such as ASV search anomalies and NSS sentiment score) into risk dashboards. This early monitoring is vital to detect and neutralise investor panic (herding behaviour) before it is reflected in the collapse of stock prices. Last but not least, corporate auditing must evolve beyond simply verifying the compliance of reported data, moving towards testing informational stress and the real recovery speed of the organisation (Time-to-Recovery) in the face of disinformation campaigns.
Regarding the limitations of this study, they derive from the exploratory nature of the selection of disinformation events and the construction of information indicators. However, the consistency of the results among the methods used supports the robustness of the conclusions.
Future research directions aim at expanding the sample and integrating more detailed data sets at a temporal and informational level, as well as using extended econometric specifications to further explore the relationship between disinformation, ESG, and financial market dynamics. In addition, comparative analyses between developed and emerging markets may provide additional insights into the role of institutional frameworks in mediating these effects.

THE IMPACT OF ALARMIST AND FAKE NEWS ON CONSUMERS' ECONOMIC BEHAVIOR: AN EXPLANATORY MODEL BASED ON DATA FROM ROMANIA

Author: Siminică, Marian1; Ilie, Cristina1; Niță, Andreea Mihaela11 University of Craiova, Craiova, Romania

Publication info: Siminică, Marian; Ilie, Cristina; Niță, Andreea Mihaela. 

https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/impact-alarmist-fake-news-on-consumers-economic/docview/3396519802/se-2?accountid=14696

Abstract: This article examines the impact of alarmist and fake economic news on consumer behaviour in the context of the growing prevalence of fake news. The study is structured into two components: a theoretical section addressing the mechanisms of misinformation dissemination and its effects, and an empirical section based on a survey conducted on a nationally controlled quota-based sociodemographic sample (N = 1,066). The research aims to investigate how media exposure, the perception of fake news, information credibility, and concern influence economic behaviour. The analysis employs structural equation modelling (SEM) and distinguishes three types of responses: behavioural reactions, consumption reduction, and saving behaviour. The findings highlight the central role of concern as a key determinant of economic behaviour, as well as the existence of distinct response mechanisms depending on the type of behaviour analysed. Overall, the study underscores the complex relationship between misinformation and economic decision-making.
