Introduction
Fake news has increasingly become a critical external shock disrupting corporate operations. Against the backdrop of social media and algorithmic recommendations accelerating information diffusion, listed companies frequently encounter unverified market rumours. These range from allegations of financial fraud and product defects to rumours of major technological breakthroughs and substantial orders. While the veracity of such content is difficult to discern, its rapid propagation creates a distinct form of high-attention information noise. Although firms can respond by issuing clarification announcements, such disclosures often fail to fully eliminate market skepticism (Shi et al., 2023). This phenomenon raises a core question: how do firms adjust their internal resource allocation to cope with the resulting external belief uncertainty when the information environment is polluted by noise?
This paper aims to reconceptualise corporate responses to fake news not as passive adaptation to distorted market signals, but as proactive strategic crisis management. We argue that firms deploy observable, costly, and irreversible investments-specifically research and development (R&D) and capital expenditures (CAPEX)-as credible signals to restore trust with external stakeholders. Unlike prior literature that interprets investment shifts under information shocks through the lens of either catering to market sentiment (Baker & Wurgler, 2004; Dessaint et al., 2019; Polk & Sapienza, 2008) or defensive retrenchment (Barker & Mone, 1994; Czarnitzki & Giebel, 2025; Grieser et al., 2026; Wang & Zhu, 2025), we propose that these decisions serve a distinct strategic function: they constitute multidimensional crisis responses, calibrated to the specific cognitive dimension disturbed by the fake news.
The significance of this study lies in its theoretical reframing of investment behaviour under misinformation. Existing frameworks struggle to explain counter-cyclical expansion observed in practice. For instance, after clarifying data fraud allegations in 2022, GoodWe (688390) significantly increased R&D expenditure, hired more technical staff, and expanded R&D infrastructure. Similarly, after denying rumours of operational suspension in 2023, RichInfo (300634) substantially raised its R&D investment. These firms did not retrench in the face of negative shocks; instead, they intensified long-term commitments - a pattern inconsistent with both defensive retrenchment and catering logic. We resolve this puzzle by introducing external belief uncertainty as a core construct and showing that when verbal clarifications lack credibility, firms resort to tangible actions to repair the broken trust contract.
Using data from Chinese A-share listed companies between 2012 and 2024, we employ corporate clarification announcements as an identification strategy for fake news shocks. Our empirical results show that firms issuing clarification announcements significantly increase both R&D investment and capital expenditure overall. Upon further distinguishing the direction of rumours, we find that firms clarifying negative news primarily exhibit a significant rise in R&D, while those clarifying positive news are dominated by a significant increase in capital expenditure. This strategic response is more pronounced in firms with lower governance quality and poorer information disclosure, which suggests that investment functions as a credible signalling tool when verbal clarifications alone are insufficient to restore market trust.
This study makes three contributions. First, it moves beyond the traditional dichotomy of defensive versus catering investment by reframing corporate behaviour under fake news as strategic belief management, emphasising the signalling function of real investment. Second, it introduces and operationalises the concept of external belief uncertainty, offering a novel lens to assess how information noise translates into real economic consequences. Third, it demonstrates that a firm's pre-existing credibility conditions its reliance on costly signals, providing actionable insights for regulators aiming to mitigate market distortions during public opinion crises.
The remainder of the paper is structured as follows. Section 1 reviews the literature and develops the hypotheses. Section 2 describes the research methodology. Section 3 reports the empirical results, along with some discussion. Section 4 offers a broader discussion of the findings. We then conclude.
1. Literature review and hypothesis development
1.1. Corporate responses to information shocks: from passive adaptation to strategic crisis management
This study centres on the concept of external belief uncertainty - a state where stakeholders' collective perceptions about a firm's fundamentals become volatile and unreliable due to exogenous information shocks. Strategic crisis management posits that crises are not merely operational disruptions but profound threats to an organisation's strategic legitimacy and stakeholder trust (Bundy et al., 2017). Within this framework, information shocks - particularly fake news - act as catalysts of strategic crises by generating high-attention noise that undermines the implicit trust contract between firms and stakeholders. Unlike traditional market frictions, fake news creates a cognitive distortion that requires active strategic intervention rather than passive financial adaptation. Signalling theory complements this by explaining how firms can resolve information asymmetry under such uncertainty: because verbal denials are often deemed "cheap talk", observable, costly, and irreversible actions serve as credible signals to restore strategic legitimacy (Connelly et al., 2011; Spence, 1973). Thus, the core challenge for firms is to actively manage this external belief uncertainty to prevent transient noise from crystallising into lasting operational damage.
The literature on corporate responses to external information shocks has largely converged on two canonical frameworks, which traditionally treat investment behaviour as a passive adaptation to distorted market beliefs (Baker et al., 2003). Under the defensive retrenchment hypothesis, negative shocks trigger reductions in long-term investment due to weakened customer demand or tightened credit conditions (e.g., Coviello et al., 2022; Danso et al., 2019; Stein, 1989; Zabavnik & Verbič, 2024). Conversely, the catering expansion hypothesis posits that positive shocks generate excessive optimism, prompting managers to undertake inefficient investments to sustain high valuations (Baker et al., 2003; Du & Hu, 2020; Mrad et al., 2024; Polk & Sapienza, 2008).
While these frameworks successfully explain investment distortions when market beliefs deviate from equilibrium, they share a critical limitation: they portray firms as constrained actors unable to effectively correct market misjudgements. In our view, this premise fails to capture the essence of fake news. When the shock source is falsifiable misinformation, firms are not entirely helpless; they possess immediate channels to clarify the situation. Therefore, we argue that corporate responses to fake news should be conceptualised through the lens of strategic crisis management rather than mere market adaptation. Under this paradigm, the objective of corporate behaviour shifts from adapting to a distorted equilibrium toward actively managing external belief uncertainty. Investment decisions thus transcend their traditional economic functions and become deliberate instruments of strategic communication aimed at repairing damaged stakeholder trust.
1.2. Strategic signalling under fake news shocks: a multidimensional crisis response
Building upon the strategic crisis management perspective, the core challenge during a fake news shock is restoring deep trust. Although firms can issue clarification announcements, verbal statements are frequently perceived as self-serving defences and fail to restore strategic legitimacy (Nazari & Poursoleyman, 2025). In this context, observable, costly, and irreversible long-term investment behaviours serve as highly effective strategic signals (Bafera et al., 2026). Firms do not view R&D and capital expenditure as mutually exclusive alternatives; rather, they deploy them as complementary components of a signalling portfolio. Depending on whether the market's perception of long-term value or short-term operational capability is threatened, firms dynamically allocate resources to the relevant signal.
This strategic division of labour implies that, in a pooled sample encompassing both positive and negative fake news events, the aggregate response manifests as a concurrent rise in both investment types. We therefore hypothesise:
H1: Firms that issue clarifications in response to fake news exhibit significant increases in both R&D investment and capital expenditure on average across the full sample.
In the face of false news propagation, the specific allocation of a firm's R&D investment and capital expenditure largely depends on the cognitive dimensions disrupted by the false news.
the face of negative fake news (e.g., allegations of financial fraud or product defects), the strategic crisis primarily targets a firm's long-term value, technical reliability, and moral reputation. Under these circumstances, CAPEX, being strongly associated with short-term operations, might be interpreted as a distraction or misappropriation of funds, thereby possessing lower signalling credibility for trust restoration (Stein, 1989). Conversely, R&D investment is highly aligned with narratives of technological innovation and long-termism. It effectively signals a steadfast focus on core competencies rather than short-term crisis management, thus repairing damaged long-term trust (Nelson & Brown, 2024; Piñeiro- Chousa et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025). Therefore, negative fake news is more likely to drive a significant increase in R&D.
H2: Firms issuing clarification announcements due to negative fake news exhibit a significant increase in R&D investment.
In contrast, positive fake news (e.g., rumours of major contracts or technological breakthroughs) generates market expectations for the firm to validate favourable prospects and demonstrate fulfilment capabilities. Merely denying such rumours may be perceived as forfeiting a strategic opportunity, while silence risks a credibility deficit. In this context, capital expenditure serves as the most tangible demonstration of strategic readiness. It signals to customers, suppliers, and investors that the firm is operationally prepared for potential growth. R&D investment, despite its long-term value, lacks signalling efficiency in scenarios demanding immediate fulfilment validation (Lev & Sougiannis, 1996). Consequently, positive fake news is more likely to drive a significant increase in capital expenditure.
H3: Firms issuing clarification announcements due to positive fake news exhibit a significant increase in capital expenditure.
Prior to a crisis, corporate governance quality and disclosure transparency shape stakeholders' baseline trust in a firm's public statements, thereby influencing how effectively a clarifying announcement can restore credibility. Firms with weak governance or opaque information environments lack an established reputation for reliability, making their verbal denials less persuasive. For such firms, the marginal benefit of costly investment signals is higher, because they need to work harder to rebuild trust. In contrast, firms with strong governance and high transparency enjoy greater baseline trust and may rely less on high-cost signalling mechanisms.
H4: The positive association between clarification announcements and the combined increase in R&D and capital expenditures is stronger for firms with lower corporate governance quality and poorer information disclosure transparency.
2. Research methodology
2.1. Data
This study uses A-share listed firms in China from 2012 to 2024 as the baseline sample. Clarification announcements are sourced from the Chinese Research Data Services (CNRDS) database, while all other firm-level financial and governance data are obtained from the China Stock Market & Accounting Research Database (CSMAR). The sample is constructed following standard empirical practices in corporate finance research (Song et al., 2024). We first exclude financial firms due to their distinct regulatory and operational characteristics. Second, we remove observations for firms designated as ·ST or ST, as these firms face heightened distress and delisting risk that may confound our identification. Third, to ensure clean identification of rumour sentiment, we exclude all firm-year observations for companies that issue both positive and negative clarifications during the sample period. Fourth, we drop observations with missing values for key variables. Finally, we winsorise all continuous variables at the 1% and 99% percentiles to mitigate the influence of outliers. After these procedures, the final sample consists of 25,749 firm-year observations from 3,878 unique firms.
2.2. Modelling and variable definition
To examine how firms strategically deploy investment as a signalling instrument in response to fake news, this study uses the issuance of clarification announcements as the primary identification strategy. We estimate the following baseline specification:
... (1)
where i and t denote firm and year, respectively. The dependent variable INVit captures corporate investment behaviour along two dimensions: capital expenditure (CAPEX) and research and development (R&D). Following standard practice in the investment literature (e.g., Coles & Li, 2023), CAPEX is measured as net cash outflows for the acquisition of property, plant, and equipment (and other long-term assets), scaled by total assets at yearend. This measure reflects tangible commitments to operational capacity and is widely interpreted as a signal of short-term business continuity. R&D intensity is captured by the natural logarithm of R&D expenses, consistent with prior work on innovation signalling (e.g., Rahman & Howlader, 2022), as it conveys long-term technological commitment and credibility. The key explanatory variable, PUBit, equals one if firm i issues a clarification announcement in year t, and zero otherwise. Clarification announcements are typically issued in direct response to high-attention but unverified market rumours, allowing us to isolate corporate responses to information noise rather than fundamental shocks.
To account for confounding determinants of investment, we include a set of firm-level control variables drawn from the finance and governance literature (Biddle et al., 2009; Chen & Chen, 2012). Financial controls comprise firm size (SIZE), return on equity (ROE), leverage (LEV), cash holdings (CASH), and asset tangibility (PPE). Governance controls include supervisory board size (SUP), the proportion of independent directors (IND), and ownership balance, measured as the ratio of shares held by the second through tenth largest shareholders to those held by the largest shareholder (BALANCE). Firm and year fixed effects are included to absorb time-invariant heterogeneity and common macroeconomic or market-wide shocks, respectively. Full variable definitions are provided in table no. 1.
3. Results
3.1. Summary statistics
Table no. 2 reports the descriptive statistics for the main variables. The mean of capital expenditure (CAPEX) is 0.049, with a maximum of 0.212 and a minimum of -0.007, reflecting considerable cross-firm heterogeneity in net investment intensity after accounting for asset disposals. R&D expenditure has a mean of 18.215 (in natural logarithm), ranging from 14.285 to 22.223, reflecting considerable heterogeneity in firms' innovation efforts. The variable PUB, which indicates the issuance of a clarification announcement, has a mean of 0.02, suggesting that approximately 2% of firm-year observations involve a public clarification in response to market rumours. The distributions of the control variables are consistent with those documented in the existing literature.
3.2. Baseline findings
Table no. 3 columns (1) and (2) report the baseline results for the full sample. In column (1), with R&D investment as the dependent variable, the coefficient on the clarification dummy (PUB) is positive and significant at the 1% level. In column (2), using capital expenditure (CAPEX) as the dependent variable, the PUB coefficient is also positive and significant at the 5% level. Thus, across the full sample, both R&D and CAPEX increase on average after firms issue clarifications.
This aggregate pattern differs from what prior work has documented under conventional negative shocks. During credit crunches or demand downturns, firms typically cut back on both R&D and physical investment (Campello et al., 2010; Stein, 1989). Here, despite the disruptive nature of fake news, firms do not retrench on average. Nor do they simply cater to short-run sentiment as suggested by the catering hypothesis (B aker et al., 2003). T he average rise in both investment types is consistent with Hypothesis 1, which predicts broad-based increases across the full sample that pools positive and negative fake news events.
3.3. Strategic investment adjustments by fake news valence
To examine whether investment responses differ by fake news valence, we estimate the model (1) separately for negative and positive events. The results, reported in table no. 4, reveal a sophisticated, state-contingent investment strategy.
For negative fake news, column (1) shows that the coefficient on PUB for R&D investment is positive and statistically significant at the 5% level. In contrast, the coefficient on PUB for CAPEX in column (2) is not significant. This suggests that firms facing negative fake news do not significantly increase their capital expenditures but instead significantly boost their R&D investments. This selective increase in R&D differs from the broad-based cuts documented in conventional negative shocks (e.g., Campello et al., 2010; Stein, 1989). Here, firms do not retrench; they use R&D to signal continued technological capability, thereby repairing long-term credibility. This finding supports Hypothesis 2.
In the case of positive fake news, column (3) table no. 4 shows that the coefficient on PUB for R&D investment is not significant, while column (4) reveals that the coefficient for CAPEX is positive and statistically significant at the 5% level. Firms thus increase capital expenditure on average after clarifying a positive rumour, with no corresponding rise in R&D. Catering theories (Baker et al., 2003) predict general overinvestment following positive sentiment, yet we observe a targeted CAPEX response rather than a broad increase across both investment types. This selective tangible investment helps substantiate the optimistic narrative (e.g., major orders, policy benefits) through visible, near-term actions, consistent with Hypothesis 3.
Together, these results challenge a monolithic view of managerial reactions to information noise. Firms do not adopt a uniform "catering" posture; instead, they deploy contextcontingent signalling strategies: leveraging long-term, hard-to-reverse R&D investments to rebuild credibility after negative shocks, and employing short-term, observable CAPEX to substantiate - and capitalise on - positive misperceptions. By calibrating their investment to the specific nature of the fake news event, firms actively manage external belief uncertainty in a way that preserves both strategic flexibility and market trust.
3.4. The role of pre-existing credibility in strategic signalling
We examine whether firms' investment responses to fake news vary with their pre-existing credibility, measured by corporate governance quality and information disclosure transparency. These dimensions reflect the extent to which stakeholders trust a firm's public statements prior to a crisis, thereby shaping the effectiveness of verbal clarifications.
We first examine whether governance structures shape firms' reliance on investment-based signalling. Following Ammann et al. (2011), we construct a composite governance index via principal component analysis using eight variables: CEO-chair duality, proportion of independent directors, board and executive ownership, top-1 shareholder concentration, board size, supervisory board size, and total compensation of the top three executives. A higher index indicates stronger governance and greater institutional credibility.
As shown in table no. 5, among firms with low governance quality, clarification of negative fake news is associated with a significant increase in R&D investment. Similarly, after positive fake news, these firms significantly raise capital expenditure. In contrast, highgovernance firms show no statistically significant investment changes in either case.
We next assess how information transparency moderates signalling behaviour. We measure disclosure quality using the KV index from Kim and Verrecchia (2001), where a higher value indicates lower transparency and greater information asymmetry. Firms are split at the industry-year median of this index.
Table no. 6 reveals a parallel moderation effect: only firms with poor disclosure quality exhibit significant investment responses. Specifically, they increase R&D following negative fake news and raise CAPEX after positive fake news. In contrast, firms with high transparency show no statistically meaningful adjustments in either investment type.
Together, these results indicate that strategic signalling is contingent on pre-existing credibility. Firms with weaker institutional trust are more likely to use investment as a tool to manage external belief uncertainty, while those with stronger credibility can rely more on verbal communication. These heterogeneous effects align with the costly signalling principle (Connelly et al., 2011): when external monitoring is weak, firms must invest more heavily to make their clarifications credible.
3.5. Robustness checks
Corporate investment involves implementation lags, particularly for physical assets which require planning and construction cycles. We re-estimate the baseline model using investment outcomes in period t+1. Due to space constraints, table no. 7 reports only the t+1 results. Additional tests using t+2 and t+3 outcomes yield qualitatively similar but weaker results, suggesting that the primary strategic response occurs contemporaneously and gradually dissipates over time.
As shown in table no. 7, the positive effect of fake news on R&D remains significant in the aggregate sample (Column (1)) and is driven primarily by negative rumours (Column (3)). This persistence confirms that firms' R&D increases are substantive strategic signals rather than transient reactions. Conversely, the coefficient for CAPEX becomes insignificant in the t+1 specification (Columns (2), (4), and (6)). Given that our CAPEX measure captures actual cash outflows for long-term assets, this result likely reflects the extended execution cycle of physical investments; while the strategic decision to expand is made immediately upon positive news (as evidenced by the significant t period results), the corresponding cash disbursements are often smoothed over subsequent periods or delayed by project implementation phases.
To ensure the reliability of our main findings, we conduct a series of robustness checks addressing potential estimation biases and measurement issues. The results are summarised in table no. 8, which is structured into three distinct panels corresponding to different identification strategies.
Columns (1) and (2) address potential sample selection bias using Propensity Score Matching (PSM). Since firms issuing clarifications may differ systematically from those that do not, we estimate propensity scores based on all baseline controls and perform 1:1 nearestneighbour matching. Re-estimating our regressions on this matched sample, we find that the coefficient on PUB remains positive and significant for both R&D and CAPEX. This suggests that our baseline results are not driven by non-random treatment assignment or observable firm characteristics.
Columns (3) and (4) tackle concerns regarding reverse causality and cumulative signalling effects. We restrict the treatment group to observations corresponding to a firm's first clarification announcement during the sample period, assigning all subsequent announcements to the control group. This design isolates the initial strategic response to an information shock. As shown in these columns, the PUB coefficient remains significantly positive, supporting the interpretation that clarification announcements trigger investment adjustments rather than merely reflecting pre-existing innovation capabilities.
Finally, Columns (5) and (6) assess sensitivity to the choice of dependent variables. We replace absolute investment values with scaled measures: R&D expenditure-to-total assets and cash paid for long-term assets-to-total assets. The coefficients on PUB remain positive and statistically significant across both specifications, confirming that our findings are robust to alternative measurement choices.
Collectively, these tests reinforce the validity of our core finding: firms strategically adjust their investment behaviour in response to fake news to manage external belief uncertainty, regardless of sample composition or variable definition.
4. Discussion
Our results show that, on average, firms respond to fake news clarification announcements by increasing both R&D and capital expenditure. But this aggregate pattern masks an interesting asymmetry. When we separate negative versus positive misinformation, a clearer picture emerges: firms facing negative rumours raise R&D, while those responding to positive fake news tend to boost CAPEX. These effects are strongest in firms with weaker governance and lower transparency.
This pattern is hard to reconcile with the idea that investment simply tracks market valuation or passively absorbs noise. Instead, it aligns with strategic crisis management. When verbal denial alone is unlikely to be trusted, especially under high information asymmetry, firms put money into tangible, hard-to-fake actions. R&D signals a commitment to long-term legitimacy under attack; CAPEX signals growth credibility when the hype is overly positive.
The existing literature has largely converged on two frameworks. One is the defensive retrenchment hypothesis, which predicts investment cuts in response to tightened credit or demand constraints (Danso et al., 2019; Stein, 1989). The other is the catering expansion hypothesis, where managers over-invest to cater to inflated sentiment (Baker et al. , 2003; Polk & Sapienza, 2008). Both explain behaviour during genuine economic fluctuations reasonably well, but they fall short when it comes to fake news. Unlike standard market frictions, fake news generates a distinct form of external belief uncertainty that demands active correction. Our results show that rather than retrenching following negative rumours or simply catering to positive ones, firms use investment, R&D to rebuild legitimacy and capital expenditure to signal growth, as a strategic tool to back up their clarifications. This extends the work of Baker et al. (2003) by showing that when the distortion is identifiable and falsifiable, firms do not merely adapt to a distorted equilibrium; they try to repair it through visible, irreversible actions.
Our analysis also speaks to signalling theory in a crisis context. Consistent with Spence (1973) and Connelly et al. (2011), cheap talk - here, verbal clarifications - is often met with skepticism. The fact that firms with weaker governance and lower transparency exhibit stronger investment responses provides direct evidence of costly signalling. When trust is already fragile, the signal needs to be more expensive to be credible. Hence the observed increases in R&D and CAPEX are not just operational adjustments; they represent a "credibility premium" that firms pay to counter the cognitive distortion caused by fake news. This insight distinguishes our study from earlier work that treats investment distortions primarily as agency problems or market inefficiencies, highlighting instead their deliberate use as a tool for restoring strategic legitimacy.
Conclusions
This study contributes to the literature by establishing that corporate investment, in the face of fake news, functions as a strategic instrument of belief management rather than a mere economic response. Our analysis of Chinese A-share firms reveals a novel mechanism: clarifications issued in response to fake news are systematically followed by targeted increases in R&D (for negative rumours) and capital expenditure (for positive rumours). This finding introduces external belief uncertainty - the credibility gap between a firm's private truth and public perception - as a critical driver of real decisions, thereby reframing investment under information shocks through the lens of strategic crisis management.
The core novelty of our work lies in demonstrating this active, signalling-based response. It departs from conventional frameworks that view firms as passive adapters to market noise (e.g., defensive retrenchment or catering hypotheses). Instead, we show that managers proactively deploy costly, observable actions to validate their narratives when verbal denials are insufficient.
From a managerial standpoint, our findings underscore that in environments where public information is prone to distortion, credibility must be substantiated through action, not just words. When firms issue clarifications - especially in response to damaging rumours - their subsequent investment choices send powerful signals about their underlying health and strategic intent. Managers should recognise that R&D spending can serve as a credible commitment to long-term technological capability in the face of reputational threats, while capital expenditure can demonstrate operational capacity to meet market expectations inflated by positive misinformation.
Importantly, this signalling imperative is not uniform across firms. Our evidence shows that organisations with weaker governance structures or less transparent disclosure practices face greater skepticism from stakeholders. For these firms, verbal rebuttals alone are insufficient; they must incur higher "credibility costs" through tangible resource commitments to restore trust. Conversely, firms with strong institutional credibility may rely more on communication alone, reserving costly investments for genuine strategic opportunities rather than defensive signalling. This insight offers practical guidance for corporate communication and capital budgeting strategies under conditions of high information uncertainty.
Our study has several limitations that point to fruitful avenues for future research. First, while our use of official clarification announcements provides a clean identification strategy, it may overlook unaddressed rumours. Future work could leverage advanced textual analysis to directly measure rumour characteristics from news or social media. Second, our context is an emerging market with high information asymmetry; it remains an open question whether these signalling dynamics persist in more institutionally robust settings. Third, we document the immediate investment response but not its long-term payoff. Future studies should examine whether such strategic investments successfully restore market valuation, customer relationships, or innovation pipelines over time.

THE EFFECTS OF FAKE NEWS ON BUSINESS ORGANIZATIONS: EVIDENCE FROM AN EVENT STUDY ON US LISTED COMPANIES

Author: Kamer-Ainur, Aivaz1; Mastac, Lavinia21 Ovidius University of Constanta, Romania2 Bucharest University of Economic Studies, Bucharest, Romania

Publication info: Kamer-Ainur, Aivaz; Mastac, Lavinia. 

https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/effects-fake-news-on-business-organizations/docview/3396519139/se-2?accountid=14696

Abstract: This study examines the market impact of fake news on publicly traded companies in the U.S., using an event study analysis applied to a sample of 30 confirmed cases of misinformation that affected U.S. companies between 2020 and 2025. From the perspective of the economy of information, fake news constitutes a major source of information asymmetry, with direct effects on market value, company reputation, and the rationality of investor decisions. Using a single-factor market model estimated over a 252-day period, with the SandP 500 index as the benchmark, events are classified into five categories: companyspecific (A), contagion (B), market-wide systemic (C), null/control cases (D), and SEC- documented pump-and-dump schemes (E). The results show that fake news generally generates significant abnormal returns on the day of the event, with a predominantly negative directional trend, suggesting that disinformation rapidly erodes investor confidence in the targeted organisations. Contagion effects prove to be the most systematic and powerful, indicating that disinformation can extend beyond the target company and affect entire sectors. The inclusion of null cases validates the methodology, confirming that in the absence of an active disinformation mechanism, no measurable effects are recorded. The proposed multicategory framework demonstrates that aggregating heterogeneous types of disinformation can mask relevant specific effects, with important methodological implications for future research. For business organisations, investors, and regulators, the findings underscore that information risk is not uniform and requires differentiated management strategies depending on the mechanism and context of disinformation.

Full text: Abstract
This study examines the market impact of fake news on publicly traded companies in the U.S., using an event study analysis applied to a sample of 30 confirmed cases of misinformation that affected U.S. companies between 2020 and 2025. From the perspective of the economy of information, fake news constitutes a major source of information asymmetry, with direct effects on market value, company reputation, and the rationality of investor decisions. Using a single-factor market model estimated over a 252-day period, with the SandP 500 index as the benchmark, events are classified into five categories: companyspecific (A), contagion (B), market-wide systemic (C), null/control cases (D), and SEC- documented pump-and-dump schemes (E). The results show that fake news generally generates significant abnormal returns on the day of the event, with a predominantly negative directional trend, suggesting that disinformation rapidly erodes investor confidence in the targeted organisations. Contagion effects prove to be the most systematic and powerful, indicating that disinformation can extend beyond the target company and affect entire sectors. The inclusion of null cases validates the methodology, confirming that in the absence of an active disinformation mechanism, no measurable effects are recorded. The proposed multicategory framework demonstrates that aggregating heterogeneous types of disinformation can mask relevant specific effects, with important methodological implications for future research. For business organisations, investors, and regulators, the findings underscore that information risk is not uniform and requires differentiated management strategies depending on the mechanism and context of disinformation.
Keywords: fake news, event study, abnormal returns, capital market, contagion, business organisations, information asymmetry.
JEL Classification: G14, G12, G18, D83, L82.
(ProQuest: ... denotes formulae omitted.)
Introduction
The proliferation of false information in financial markets represents a major challenge to market integrity, investor protection, and the effectiveness of regulatory mechanisms. From fabricated corporate announcements to AI-generated deepfake images, the ways in which misinformation influences asset prices have diversified significantly in the age of social media. At the same time, the implications of this phenomenon extend beyond the strictly financial sphere, affecting business organisations through reputational damage, the erosion of stakeholder trust, and increased costs associated with managing information risk. The World Economic Forum (2024) has identified misinformation as one of the most severe global risks, while the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has intensified its actions against market manipulation through false online content.
Despite growing concerns among regulators, the academic literature on the impact of fake news on financial markets remains limited. Arcuri et al. (2023) conduct the first comprehensive event study on the effects of fake news on U.S. and EU markets (2007-2019), analysing 19 events. Clarke et al. (2021) investigated pump-and-dump schemes documented by the SEC on the Seeking Alpha platform. Louchez (2025) provided a detailed analysis of a single event highlighting contagion effects within the pharmaceutical oligopoly.
However, several relevant gaps persist. First, the post-2019 period remains insufficiently investigated, although it is characterised by the emergence of new forms of misinformation, including impersonation facilitated by digital platforms and content generated by artificial intelligence. Second, the existing literature frequently treats fake news as a homogeneous phenomenon, without distinguishing between the heterogeneous mechanisms through which different types of misinformation affect markets and business organisations. Third, previous studies do not systematically include null cases - situations in which verified misinformation has no effect on prices - as a tool for internal validation of the methodology. Fourth, the relationship between fake news, organisational vulnerability, and the rationality of economic decisions remains insufficiently explored empirically.
This paper addresses these gaps by constructing a dataset comprising 30 confirmed fake news events targeting U.S.-listed companies between 2020 and 2025. The events are classified into five categories based on mechanism and target: company-specific direct impact (Category A, n = 14), contagion and propagation effects (Category B, n = 3), market-wide systemic shocks (Category C, n = 3), null/control cases (Category D, n = 4), and SEC-documented "pumpand-dump" schemes (Category E, n = 6). Each event is validated through regulatory actions, peer-reviewed publications, or established fact-checking organisations.
The empirical analysis uses the standard event study methodology (MacKinlay, 1997), applying a unifactorial market model estimated over 252-day windows. Seven hypotheses are tested, addressing the existence, direction, and persistence of effects, heterogeneity across categories, contagion mechanisms, cross-sectional determinants, and validation via null cases. From a broader perspective, the results show that misinformation disrupts evaluation and decision-making processes in the economic environment, affecting not only market efficiency but also the ability of organisations to protect their credibility and reputational capital in an increasingly volatile information environment.
By introducing a multi-category classification framework, the paper demonstrates that the effects of fake news are not homogeneous but depend on the propagation mechanism and market context, thus offering a relevant contribution to both the academic literature and practitioners and policymakers.
1. Review of scientific literature
1.1. Efficient market hypothesis and information processing
The theoretical foundation of this study is based on the Efficient Market Hypothesis (EMH), formulated by Fama (1970), according to which asset prices fully reflect available information. In its semi-strong form, prices should adjust quickly and accurately to public information, including news regarding corporate fundamentals. However, this hypothesis assumes that investors can distinguish true information from false information, a premise that is increasingly difficult to uphold given the speed and scale of information dissemination on social media (Obadă and Dabija, 2022). In this regard, Vosoughi et al. (2018), analysing 126,000 rumour chains on Twitter, show that false information spreads faster and more widely than true information, undermining the assumption of rational information processing. Behavioural finance provides the explanatory mechanisms for these deviations. Kahneman and Tversky (1979) highlight loss aversion, Shiller (2000) describes her behaviour, and De Bondt and Thaler (1985) demonstrate overreaction to dramatic news. Together, these mechanisms suggest that false information, particularly negative information, can generate immediate and amplified price reactions, followed by partial corrections as the information is clarified.
The literature often uses terms with distinct meanings interchangeably. Wardle and Derakhshan (2017) distinguish between misinformation (false information without manipulative intent), disinformation (false information deliberately disseminated), and malinformation (true information used harmfully). In the financial context, fake news falls predominantly under disinformation (Allcott and Gentzkow, 2017). Market manipulation involves the intentional distortion of prices (Clarke et al., 2021; Kogan et al., 2023), reporting error is an unintentional inaccuracy with reversible effects (Palmrose et al., 2004), and a rumour is characterised by a lack of confirmation from authoritative sources (Vosoughi et al., 2018). The sample of this study deliberately covers this spectrum, justifying the need for the proposed multi-categorical classification framework.
1.2. Fake news and financial markets
Against this theoretical background, the empirical literature on the effects of fake news on financial markets remains relatively limited. Arcuri et al. (2023) represent the main methodological benchmark, demonstrating through an event study applied to 19 cases (U.S. and EU, 2007-2019) the existence of significant negative abnormal returns, which are more pronounced for small firms and the financial sector. Other recent research highlights the role of social media in amplifying investor reactions and the dynamics of price adjustments following misinformation (Hirshleifer et al., 2023; Zhong et al., 2024). However, their analysis does not cover the recent period and treats the phenomenon as homogeneous.
Clarke et al. (2021) examine SEC-documented pump-and-dump schemes on the Seeking Alpha platform, highlighting positive abnormal returns during the promotional phase, followed by corrections. Although relevant, the study focuses on a single manipulation mechanism. Louchez (2025) makes an important recent contribution by analysing the effects of the fake Eli Lilly tweet regarding insulin and demonstrating the existence of contagion within the pharmaceutical oligopoly. The present study extends these results by integrating the case into a multi-category framework, which allows for comparisons between different types of misinformation, including events with no effect and alternative mechanisms.
1.3. Social media, information asymmetry and market manipulation
The spread of fake news is closely linked to the role of social media in price determination. Jiao et al. (2020) show that sentiment on social media can predict short-term returns, and Kogan et al. (2023) demonstrate that fraudulent information directly influences trading activity and prices, while exposure to fraud reduces trust in the entire information flow. Allcott and Gentzkow (2017) highlight the scale of the fake news phenomenon in the digital ecosystem. These effects can be explained by the theory of information asymmetry (Kyle, 1985). Misinformation creates temporary asymmetries between informed and uninformed investors, and the speed at which these are corrected determines the persistence of abnormal returns.
Beyond the impact on prices, these mechanisms directly affect business organisations. The rapid spread of false information implies additional costs for monitoring, communication, and reputation management, turning fake news into an issue of information governance and organisational sustainability (Sariarei et al., 2024).
1.4. Contagion and spillover effects
A key mechanism through which misinformation affects markets is informational contagion, whereby false news targeting one firm also influences the prices of related firms. King and Wadhwani (1990) provide the theoretical framework for cross-market contagion, while Forbes and Rigobon (2002) refine the distinction between contagion and interdependence. In the context of fake news, Louchez (2025) provides empirical evidence of contagion in an oligopolistic market, demonstrating that competing firms are affected even in the absence of direct exposure. Hong et al. (2023) extends the analysis to the COVID-19 context, highlighting systemic risks generated by misinformation.
Within this framework, our analysis contributes by testing contagion across multiple sectors and comparing it to direct effects and null cases.
2. Research methodology
2.1. Research design and data
This study (Figure 1) uses the event study methodology developed by MacKinlay (1997) to measure the market impact of 30 confirmed fake news events on U.S.-listed companies between January 2020 and December 2025. To investigate these effects, the literature predominantly employs the event study methodology, which has been the standard in financial economics since Fama et al. (1969), who established the framework for market models and the testing of abnormal returns. Brown and Warner (1985) analyse the statistical properties of these tests, including under conditions of non-normality and cross-sectional dependence. Boehmer et al. (1991) and Patell (1976) develop the statistical tests used in the present analysis. The present study utilises these established methods, adapting them to the specific context of confirmed disinformation events.
The dataset includes adjusted daily closing prices for 25 unique tickers and the SandP 500 ETF (SPY), used as a market benchmark, resulting in 43,748 firm-day observations for the period January 2019-March 2026. The data comes from Yahoo Finance for all securities except Twitter (TWTR), which was delisted following its acquisition in October 2022; for this security, historical data is sourced from Investing.com.
For each event, the estimation window covers 252 trading days [-257, -6] prior to the event, and the event window covers 11 days [-5, +5], resulting in a total analysis window of 263 days per event. Daily logarithmic returns are calculated as rt = ln(Pt/Pt-1 ). Events are classified into five categories based on mechanism and target, as shown in Table no. 1.
The inclusion of each event meets four criteria: (i) the information has been confirmed as false by authoritative sources (SEC filings, peer-reviewed publications, or established factchecking organisations such as Reuters, AP, Snopes, or PolitiFact); (ii) the security in question is listed on a U.S. stock exchange, with data available; (iii) the date of the event is precisely identifiable; (iv) the event generated or had the documented potential to generate temporary information asymmetry in the market, regardless of the issuer's intent-a criterion that justifies the inclusion of both disinformation and misinformation cases, as well as false disclosures, under the common analytical umbrella of fake news, understood broadly as informational disorder (Wardle and Derakhshan, 2017). The type of disinformation follows this taxonomy: cases #9, #13, and #23 represent misinformation (unintentional error without manipulative intent); cases #10 and #14 represent false disclosure (intentionally misleading disclosure in official reports). All other events represent disinformation (deliberately distributed false information). These five cases are deliberately included to test the robustness of the methodology by contrasting it with disinformation proper and to reflect the actual spectrum of information disorder in financial markets. The source column provides an abbreviated verification reference.

The primary event window is [-5, +5] (11 trading days). Alternative windows of [0, 0], [0, +1], [-1, +1], [-2, +2], and [-3, +3] are analysed for robustness.
2.2. Statistical tests
The significance of individual events is assessed using Patell's t-statistic (1976): t = ARi0/σi^, where σi^ is the residual standard error from the OLS regression of the estimation window. Aggregate significance across events is assessed using four complementary tests: (i) the standardised cross-sectional BMP test (Boehmer et al. 1991); (ii) the binomial sign test for directional dominance; (iii) the signed Wilcoxon rank test; and (iv) cross-sectional t-tests on category means. The cross-sectional regression of CAR [-5, +5] on firm and event characteristics (log volume in dollars, category dummy variables, stock exchange) uses HC3 robust standard errors (White, 1980).
Based on the literature reviewed above, we formulate the following hypotheses.
* H1: Fake news events generate statistically significant abnormal returns on the day of the event.
* H2: The effects of fake news persist beyond Day 0, producing significant cumulative abnormal returns over the [-5, +5] window.
* H3: Company-specific fake news (Category A) produces higher absolute CARs than market-level shocks (Category C).
* H4: Fake news generates significant contagion abnormal returns in competing firms that were not directly targeted.
* H5: SEC-documented pump-and-dump schemes (Category E) generate significant abnormal returns consistent with the direction of the manipulation.
* H6: Firm-level and event-level characteristics moderate the market impact of fake news.
* H7: Null-event cases (Category D) do not produce significant abnormal returns, serving as a placebo control.
3. Results and discussion
This section presents the empirical results organised by hypothesis. For events in Category C, the DIA is used as the test title. In relation to the broader theme of the paper, the results should be interpreted not only as market reactions to misinformation, but also as indicators of business organisations' vulnerability to informational shocks, with implications for corporate credibility, the rationality of investor decisions, and the stability of competitive ecosystems. Before testing the hypotheses, two characteristics of the dataset are worth highlighting.
3.1. Individual event results (H1)
Table no. 2 reports the Day-0 abnormal returns and the cumulative abnormal returns over the [-5, +5] window for all 30 events.
The results indicate substantial heterogeneity. Twelve events (40%) show statistically significant ARs on day 0 at the 5% level, and 16 (53%) at the 10% level. Under the null hypothesis, approximately 1.5 events would have been expected to be significant at the 5% level by chance alone. Therefore, the observed rate of 40% is eight times higher than expected, suggesting that fake news events generate abnormal returns as a class.
The sign test also confirms a negative directional bias: 20 out of 30 events (66.7%) produce negative ARs on day 0 (p = 0.049). Excluding SCWorx, the proportion rises to 69.0% (p = 0.031). In contrast, the standardised cross-sectional BMP test for Day 0 is not significant (t = 0.16, p = 0.875), a result explained by the deliberate inclusion of heterogeneous types of events. Categories A and B tend to generate negative standardised ARs, while Category E frequently produces positive standardised ARs. MacKinlay (1997) shows that aggregate tests lose power when event-induced effects differ in sign. Following the same logic, a comparison with Arcuri et al. (2023), who report significant aggregate effects in a more homogeneous sample of negative events, suggests that the sample structure decisively influences the outcome of the aggregate test.
Consequently, H1 is partially confirmed. The sign test (p = 0.049) and the high proportion of individually significant events (40%, compared to the expected 5%) provide robust evidence that fake news generates abnormal market reactions. The predominantly negative direction is consistent with loss aversion, and the fact that the BMP test is insignificant reflects intercategory heterogeneity, not the absence of effects.
3.2. Category-level patterns and persistence (H2, H3)
Table 3 summarises the statistics on abnormal returns by event category and serves as the primary evidence supporting the central argument of this paper: different types of fake news produce systematically different market effects.
The strongest result is found in Category B (contagion). The Day-0 AR mean of -4.48% is significant at the 1% level (t = -10.10, p = 0.010), and all events in this category have a negative sign. The standardised BMP test independently confirms this result (t = -7.23, p = 0.019), making Category B the only category that is significant when aggregated using both parametric approaches.
Category A exhibits the highest intra-category variance (SD = 34.99%), reflecting the heterogeneity of direct misinformation mechanisms. After excluding the SCWorx outlier, the CAR mean shifts to -4.89%, and 69.2% of events remain negative, although the aggregated statistics do not reach the significance threshold. Category C records low magnitudes (mean CAR = -1.05%), with no statistical significance. Category E exhibits the highest dispersion (SD = 68.37%), suggesting the coexistence of opposing pump-and-dump dynamics.
Regarding H2, seven events (23%) exhibit CARs significant at the 5% level. The analysis of alternative windows, presented below in Table 4, indicates a clear pattern of attenuation: the [-1, +1] window produces 15 significant events (50%), a number that drops to 7 for the [-5, +5] window. This result is consistent with the existence of information shocks concentrated around day 0, followed by partial corrections. The pattern of gradual attenuation is consistent with Brown and Warner (1985), who demonstrate that informational effects are concentrated around the event date and dissipate over broader time windows. The high intra-category variance in Category A is consistent with Arcuri et al. (2023), who report similar heterogeneity based on firm size and industry.
Regarding H3, the absolute CAR average for Category A, after excluding SCWorx, is 15.5%, compared to 1.1% for Category C. The ratio of approximately 14:1 suggests that firm-specific information shocks produce much stronger effects than systemic market-level shocks. This finding is consistent with Kogan et al. (2023), who show that targeted fraudulent information produces stronger and more persistent effects than diffuse informational shocks.
3.3. Contagion effects (H4)
The fake Eli Lilly tweet about insulin, dated November 11, 2022, provides a natural experiment on information contagion. All three pharmaceutical companies show significant negative Day-0 ARs, with Eli Lilly (the direct target) at -5.29% (t = -3.32, p < 0.01), Novo Nordisk at -4.22% (t = -2.14, p < 0.05), and Sanofi at -3.87% (t = -2.54, p < 0.05) (Figure no.2).
The magnitude of contagion accounts for 73-80% of the target firm's AR, suggesting nearly complete pass-through within the insulin oligopoly. The result is consistent with Louchez (2025). The UnitedHealth Group event extends this logic to the health insurance sector: the Day-0 AR of -5.34% (t = -3.40, p < 0.01) is followed by a persistent CAR of -16.29% (p < 0.01). It is also relevant that AbbVie, although affected on the same day by a Twitter Blue impersonation but outside the insulin market, shows no significant effect (-0.17%, t = -0.13). This contrast suggests that mere temporal co-occurrence is not sufficient for contagion; proximity within the product market appears to be a necessary condition. The significance of the BMP test for Category B (t = -7.23, p = 0.019), in contrast to the non-significant result obtained on the full sample (t = 0.16, p = 0.875), directly supports the paper's central methodological argument: aggregating heterogeneous types of events can hide category-specific effects that are relevant both statistically and economically. Therefore, H4 is confirmed. All contagion events exhibit significant negative ARs, and transmission reaches 73-80% within the insulin oligopoly. The results indicate that product market proximity functions as a threshold condition for the occurrence of contagion.
3.4. Pump-and-Dump, Cross-Sectional Analysis, and Null Cases (H5-H7)
Two of the six events in Category E exhibit significant Day-0 effects: GameStop (+87.48%, t = 11.72, p < 0.01) and TWTR "deal on hold" (-12.81%, t = -4.65, p < 0.01). The opposite directions reflect distinct mechanisms: classic pump schemes generate positive ARs, while Musk's tweet worked as a sell signal, producing a negative AR. Consequently, H5 is only partially confirmed: there are significant individual effects, but the category-level means remain insignificant (p = 0.362) due to sign heterogeneity. The pump-and-dump dynamics identified for GameStop are consistent with Clarke et al. (2021), who document positive abnormal returns during the promotional phase followed by corrections, and with Desiderio et al. (2025), who confirm the causality between Reddit posts and price movements. The negative effect of the tweet reflects a distinct manipulation mechanism that warrants separate investigation in future research.
Regarding H6, the cross-sectional regression of CAR[-5, +5] on log-volume in dollars, category, and exchange dummy variables does not identify significant predictors (all p > 0.30; R2 = 0.106; Adj. R2 = -0.127). Given the small sample size (N = 30) and the presence of outliers ranging from -136% to +108%, statistical power is insufficient to detect moderating effects. Therefore, H6 is not confirmed.
Category D, used as the null set, clusters around zero, as predicted: the mean Day-0 AR is -0.74% (t = -0.51, p = 0.645), and the mean CAR is +1.10% (p = 0.725). Three of the four events produce individually insignificant Day-0 ARs and less than 2% in absolute value. The exception, Berkshire Hathaway (-4.57%, t = -4.91), coincides with the market crash on April 4, 2025 (SPY -6.03%), and the insignificant CAR of -0.26% indicates a complete reversal.
By showing that events for which no effects are expected do not produce systematic effects, the analysis provides important internal validation of the methodology, which is largely absent from previous literature on fake news. Consequently, H7 is confirmed. The absence of effects in null cases is consistent with Jiao et al. (2020), who show that market reactions to social media content are determined by the perceived relevance and credibility of the source.
3.5. Robustness checks
Table no. 4 presents the aggregated significance tests for all specifications and summarises the main robustness checks.
First, the standardised BMP test applied at the category level yields a different picture from the non-significant result obtained on the full sample. Category B reaches significance on day 0 (t = -7.23, p = 0.019), while no other category does, which directly supports the proposed multi-category framework. Second, the decreasing number of significant events as the windows widen-from 15 in [-1, +1] to 7 in [-5, +5]-confirms that the effects are concentrated around day 0 and subsequently attenuate, although the rate of this attenuation differs across events. Third, excluding the SCWorx observation strengthens the sign test, from p = 0.049 to p = 0.031, and shifts the BMP on the CAR toward marginal significance (t = -1.42, p = 0.165). Fourth, substituting DIA for Category C events avoids regressing SPY on itself, while maintaining a high correlation with the benchmark (ρ ≈ 0.97). Fifth, the BRK- B event, disrupted by the tariff crash on April 4, 2025, is properly identified and documented: the significance of Day-0 AR disappears over wider windows, suggesting market noise rather than effects attributable to fake news.
Conclusions
This study provides a multi-category event study analysis of confirmed fake news events in U.S. financial markets, covering the period 2020-2025 with a sample of 30 verified misinformation events. Beyond its contribution to the empirical finance literature, the paper highlights that fake news poses a real risk to business organisations, as it simultaneously affects market value, stakeholder confidence, and the quality of decision-making processes in an economic environment increasingly dependent on the speed of information flow. First, fake news generates economically and statistically significant abnormal returns at the individual event level. Twelve out of 30 events (40%) produce Day-0 abnormal returns that are significant at the 5% level, eight times the expected rate under the null hypothesis. The sign test confirms a significant negative directional trend (66.7% negative, p = 0.049), consistent with the loss aversion and overreaction mechanisms predicted by behavioural finance theory. This result suggests that misinformation rapidly erodes confidence in the targeted companies and amplifies market participants' irrational reactions. Second, the nonsignificant aggregate cross-sectional tests, combined with the significance of the tests at the category level, directly support the multi-category framework proposed in this study. Different types of fake news produce systematically different market effects that cancel each other out in aggregate analyses. This finding has methodological implications for future research, as well as practical implications for business organisations, as it shows that the risk of misinformation cannot be managed uniformly; it must be understood in terms of mechanism, sectoral proximity, and market structure. Third, the inclusion of null cases (Category D) provides internal methodological validation absent from most previous research. Confirming that events where no effect is expected produce no measurable effect strengthens the causal interpretation of significant findings in the other categories and demonstrates that the methodology does not generate systematic false positives.
The study expands the existing literature in several dimensions. Compared to Arcuri et al. (2023), it covers a more recent period, a larger sample, and introduces the multi-category framework and validation through null cases. Compared to Louchez (2025), it integrates the insulin contagion case into a broader cross-sectional analysis that allows for comparison across misinformation mechanisms. Compared to Clarke et al. (2021), it includes SEC- documented pump-and-dump schemes as one of five categories, not as the sole focus.
Several limitations should be acknowledged. Small sample sizes at the category level limit statistical power for cross-category comparisons and cross-sectional regression. As confirmed fake news events continue to accumulate, future studies with larger samples per category may detect cross-sectional determinants that are undetectable in the current setting. Furthermore, the single-factor market model, while standard, may underestimate extreme market movements in contexts of information shock.
For practitioners and regulators, the findings highlight that the risk of misinformation is not uniform. Contagion effects in oligopolistic markets pose the most systematic threat, while large-cap firms with high institutional ownership demonstrate relative resilience. The documented contagion transmission rate of 73-80% within the insulin oligopoly suggests that misinformation can rapidly spread beyond the target company and affect entire sectors, with implications for competition, reputation, and stability. From a broader perspective, the results show that fake news affects the efficient functioning of markets by distorting the informational signals on which investors and other stakeholders base their decisions. In this sense, combating disinformation is not only about protecting investors, but also about strengthening organisational sustainability, communicational transparency, and an economic environment based on trust and rational decision-making.

Cognitive load and individual differences as drivers of health-related misinformation: A signal detection approach

Author: Puebla, Guillermo    ; Ferrer-Urbina, Rodrigo    ; Pérez-Zapata, Daniel    ; Alarcón-Castillo, Karina; Sepúlveda-Páez, Geraldy; Elgueta, Herman    

Publication info: Puebla, Guillermo; Ferrer-Urbina, Rodrigo; Pérez-Zapata, Daniel; Alarcón-Castillo, Karina; Sepúlveda-Páez, Geraldy; et al. 

https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/cognitive-load-individual-differences-as-drivers/docview/3379928721/se-2?accountid=14696

Abstract: The global spread of health-related misinformation during the COVID-19 pandemic has highlighted the need to understand the psychological mechanisms that make individuals susceptible to health-related misinformation. This study examined the impact of cognitive load and individual differences on susceptibility to COVID-19 misinformation using a Signal Detection Theory framework. A sample of 634 university students evaluated true and false COVID-19 headlines under working memory load and no-load conditions, while also completing standardized assessments of cognitive reflection, epistemically unwarranted beliefs, naïve skepticism, and bullshit receptivity. Results showed that, although the working memory load manipulation successfully impaired recall and increased response time, it did not affect participants’ tendency to accept false information as true. In contrast, individual-difference variables robustly predicted misinformation susceptibility. Specifically, beliefs in pseudoscience, epistemically unwarranted beliefs, naïve skepticism, and bullshit receptivity showed moderate positive associations with false-alarm rates and negative associations with discrimination sensitivity. Cognitive reflection was negatively associated with false-alarm rates and positively with discrimination sensitivity. Only small associations were found between individual-difference dimensions and response bias. These findings suggest that stable cognitive and epistemic dispositions play a significant role in shaping people’s ability to distinguish between accurate and false health information.
